# EPIGRAM
### AGAINST
## ZOILUS.
<note>Zoilus was a 4th-century BCE Greek grammarian known as the "scourge of Homer" for his hypercritical attacks. In the Renaissance and Early Modern periods, his name became a standard label for any envious or unfairly harsh critic.</note>

*O envious one, who has always sought to dishonor virtue,*
*Always having the skin of another between your teeth.*
<note>original: *dentibus esse cute*. This is a vivid Latin metaphor for backbiting or "slandering the skin" of another person.</note>
*These works are not adjusted to every man's scale,*
*These have been found blameless by the Sages of old.*
<note>original: *Sophis*. A reference to the "Sages" or ancient alchemical philosophers whose wisdom the author claims to follow.</note>
*They are not to be rashly attacked by any unpermitted whip;*
<note>original: *mastige*. From the Greek word for "whip" or "scourge."</note>
*Therefore, do no harm here, or else teach us better.*
<note>This is a play on a common scholarly challenge: "Either provide a better explanation or stop criticizing mine."</note>
*Guelders is my fatherland, but Venlo is my home soil;*
<note>The author identifies their origin in the Dutch province of Gelderland and the city of Venlo.</note>
*Know that I speak for myself, only by the law given to me.*
*Do not, however, turn your gaze away from the Pitch-black Wand,*
<note>original: *Piceo Bacillo*. This likely refers to the author's pen or perhaps an alchemical symbol for the "blacker than black" (*nigredo*) stage of the process.</note>
*But read on; perhaps there is something inside to stir your interest.*
*Nor pass judgment upon it with a grim scowl,*
*Until the final page has been read by you.*

<summary>A defiant prefatory poem where the author defends his alchemical work against potential critics, identifying himself as a native of Venlo and urging readers to finish the book before judging it.</summary>

# A Word to the Fit Reader

->*A Brief Discourse.*<-

1. My discerning brother, because today there is an infinite lust for speaking ill, and I have more than once been severely flogged in this regard—namely, because I had occasionally produced some nightly labors <note>original: "vigiliarum"; refers to the products of late-night study</note> for the public good, and perhaps there were some things therein used <term>metaleptically</term> <note>a figure of speech where one thing is referred to by something remotely associated with it</note> or <term>tropologically</term> <note>a method of interpretation that looks for a moral or figurative meaning</note> that were not immediately obvious to everyone’s understanding, and because I had not yet added an index of the more obscure words and phrases—therefore, having become more cautious through my own misfortune, I have now proposed to provide <term>glosses</term> <note>original: "gloſſemata"; explanatory notes for difficult words</note> and paragraph notes for the more abstruse vocabulary and sharper sentences.

2. For there are some who are such mere smatterers <note>original: "ſcioli"; those with superficial knowledge</note> and so stubborn that they easily condemn, nitpick, and despise everything they do not know or do not perceive; they approve of nothing except that which they have personally discovered and proven. Soon, when a sentence structure or a word occurs that they perhaps do not grasp at first glance, they say: "This is a fabrication; it is not accepted Latin, because I have never read or heard it before." By this, they wish to indicate clearly that such language is not to be tolerated at all. Truly, what a clever saying, worthy of a Platonic or Socratic mouth! As if indeed these little seekers of glory and gluttonous readers—or "know-it-alls" with big noses <note>original: "magnis naſis panſophi"; a classical metaphor for people who are overly critical or mockingly superior</note>—should have already read or heard everything hidden in the wide-wandering field of <term>Latinity</term> <note>the body of Latin literature and language</note>, which one may rightly call a most deep ocean, scarcely explorable by the measuring line of our few years.

3. Nevertheless, the malignant urge <note>original: "cacoëthes"; a Greek-derived term for a bad habit or incurable itch</note> for slandering and the poison of envy spreads and festers to such an extent that, in the face of this present, ulcerated age, nothing seems more common for one who brings his works into the light than to prepare a sort of table for detractors and the malevolent. They tear apart and gnaw at everything served to them—I do not say only with sour and stinging tongues and bites, but with violent outbursts and <term>Theonine teeth</term> <note>original: "Theoninis dentibus"; a reference to the Roman poet Theon, symbolizing vicious and slanderous criticism</note>—destroying not only what displeases them...

<summary>The author defends their use of complex and figurative Latin against "smatterer" critics, announcing their intention to include explanatory glosses to prevent further misunderstanding. This reflects the tension in Renaissance and Baroque scholarship between innovative language and traditionalist criticism.</summary>
<keywords>literary criticism, Latinity, tropes, philology, academic defense, Theonine teeth, metaleptic, tropological</keywords>

# A Word to the Fit Reader

...not only [those things they do not understand], but even those things which often please them greatly; they are not unlike cats, which are accustomed to growl all the more fiercely at someone the richer the morsel of food offered to them. For such is the current disposition of men that, by Hercules, no thing, no business, and no little work is undertaken for reasons so just that there are not those present to mark it with an obelisk <note>original: "obelent"; refers to the practice of ancient critics marking passages as suspicious or incorrect with a symbol called an obelus</note> or prick it with their thorns.

->By Pollux, no one will go more safely than Antimachus, nor Homer,<-
->And envious Fate even pinches the great Gods.<-

4. It happened not so long ago, about a year ago, that a certain treatise on <term>universal medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina universalis"; a theoretical "all-cure" or elixir sought by alchemists</note>, which is appended here at the end of the book, and which was translated by me in London <note>original: "Londini"</note>, England, from German into Latin, was shown to several men highly skilled in the matters of nature and art to be examined. They were to give their judgment and vote on whether or not it was worthy of being printed; among them, the majority were Doctors, and some were even of high rank, distinguished no less by their lineage than by their wisdom.

5. Among these men, there was one who was very sickly and is now entirely deceased (but who was otherwise a great <term>Lover of Learning</term> <note>original: "Philomagus"; from the Greek "philos" (lover) and "mathos" (learning)</note>, a patron <note>original: "Maecenas"; a reference to the famous Roman patron of the arts</note> of the muses, and almost an equal to <term>Hermes</term> <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and hermetic philosophy</note>). I had decided in my mind to dedicate the aforementioned treatise to him, because he knew me to some extent, and I knew him. To this end, I had composed another more secret little note <note>original: "pictatium"; a small scrap of paper or ticket</note> in which, in plain and brief words (for a special reason known only to God and myself), I had communicated to him my own thoughts regarding the <term>Philosophers' Discovery</term> <note>original: "Philosophorum Inventum"; likely referring to the secret of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Thus, I imagined in my heart that the matter would turn out entirely according to my wishes.

6. But alas, how often the firm hopes of mortals turn out quite the opposite! For three or four days later, when I asked the printer <note>original: "typographus"</note> whether he had any resolution regarding that work, he replied that a "black bean" <note>original: "faba nigra"; a classical metaphor for a vote of rejection or a "no" vote</note> had intervened. It had been judged and proclaimed that the Latin translation was not good, but rather swarming with <term>barbarisms</term> <note>original: "barbarismis"; words or expressions that violate the rules of classical Latin</note> and lacking in flavor. And yet, in that translation (although the whole thing was completed in more or less [a short time]), except for the title and a very few...

<summary>The author describes how his Latin translation of a German medical treatise, intended for a now-deceased patron, was rejected by a committee of scholars in London who deemed his style "barbaric."</summary>
<keywords>criticism, universal medicine, London, Philomagus, Maecenas, Hermes, Philosopher's Discovery, printer, barbarisms</keywords>

# A Fitting Word to the Reader

<warning>Significant ink bleed-through from the reverse side of the page creates mirrored text overlays in some areas.</warning>

<margin>1.</margin> My judicious brother, because today there is an infinite lust for slander, and I have been severely lashed more than once on this account—namely, that I had occasionally produced some "night-studies" <note>original: "vigiliarum"; referring to works written late at night, implying scholarly dedication</note> for the public good—and because there were perhaps several things present that were used <term>metaleptically</term> <note>original: "metalepticè"; a rhetorical figure involving a double substitution or a complex chain of metaphors</note> or <term>tropologically</term> <note>original: "tropologicè"; a method of interpretation that looks for figurative or moral meanings</note> which were not immediately obvious to everyone’s grasp, and yet I had not added an index of the more hidden words and phrases; therefore, having been made more cautious by my own loss, I have now proposed to set down glosses and explanatory paragraphs for the more abstruse vocabulary and sharper sentences.

<margin>2.</margin> For there are some who are such "smatterers" <term>scioli</term> <note>original: "scioli"; individuals who possess only a superficial or "smattering" of knowledge but act as experts</note> and so stubborn that they easily condemn, peck at, and spit upon everything which they themselves do not know or do not perceive. They approve of and commit to nothing except only that which has been known and discovered by themselves. Soon, when a construction or a word occurs which they perhaps do not grasp at first glance, they say: "This is a fabrication; it is not accepted Latin, because I have never read nor heard this before." By this, they wish to indicate—not obscurely—that it is therefore not to be tolerated at all. Truly, a wise saying, worthy of a Platonic or Socratic mouth! As if indeed these seekers of petty glory, these "greedy readers," or these <term>pansophs</term> <note>original: "pansophis"; literally "all-wise ones," here used sarcastically for those who believe they have universal knowledge</note> with their great noses, ought to have read or heard everything that lies hidden in the wide-ranging field of Latinity—which one may rightly call a most deep ocean, scarcely fully explorable by the measuring-line of our years.

<margin>3.</margin> Nevertheless, the "bad habit" <term>cacoëthes</term> <note>original: "cacoëthes"; a Greek-derived medical term for a malignant habit or uncontrollable urge, often used for the "itch" to write or criticize</note> of calumny and the virus of envy grows and becomes cancerous to such an extent that, in the present face of this ulcerated age, anyone who drags his works into the light seems to do nothing more than prepare a sort of table for detractors and the malevolent. These people tear apart and gnaw at everything that is served—I do not say only with sour and stinging tongues and bites, but with violent snapping and with <term>Theonine teeth</term> <note>original: "Theoninis dentibus"; a reference to the Roman poet Theon, famous for his biting and slanderous wit</note>—not only those things which displease them...

# A Fitting Word to the Reader

...only, but even those things that greatly please them from time to time; they are not unlike cats, who are usually inclined to growl more sharply at someone the more they feel a choice morsel <note>original: "ofellam"</note> is being offered to them. For such is the disposition of people today that, by Hercules, no matter, no business, or even the smallest work is undertaken for ever so just reasons, without there being those who will mark it with a <term>dagger</term> <note>original: "obelent"; referring to the 'obelus,' a mark used by ancient critics to denote suspicious or fake passages in a manuscript</note> or prick it with their stings.

->Truly, no one will go more safely than Antimachus, nor even Homer,<-
->And envious Fate even snaps at the great Gods.<-
<note>Antimachus was a Greek poet often compared to Homer; the verse suggests that even the greatest writers cannot escape criticism.</note>

<margin>4.</margin> It happened not long ago, about a year ago, that that treatise on <term>universal medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina universali"; in the hermetic tradition, this refers to a "panacea" or "elixir" capable of curing all diseases and perfecting nature</note>—which is appended here at the end of the book, and which was translated by me in London, England, from German into Latin—was shown to some men most highly skilled in the matters of both nature and art, to be examined. This was done so they might give their judgment and <term>vote</term> <note>original: "calculum"; literally a "pebble" used in ancient voting</note> on whether it was worthy to be printed or not. Among them, the majority were Doctors, and some were even noble, no less distinguished in their lineage than in their wisdom.

<margin>5.</margin> To one of these men—who was very sickly and is now entirely dead, but was otherwise a great <term>Philomagus</term> <note>original: "Philomago"; a "lover of magic" or "lover of learning"</note>, a patron of the muses, and almost an equal to <term>Hermes</term> <note>original: "Hermeti"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>—I had intended to dedicate the aforementioned treatise, because he knew me to some extent, and I him. For this purpose, I had composed a certain other more secret <term>leaflet</term> <note>original: "pictatium"; a small note or label</note> in which, in plain and brief words (for a special reason known only to God and myself), I had shared with him my own true thoughts concerning the <term>Philosophers' Invention</term> <note>original: "Philosophorum Invento"; a reference to the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Hence, I imagined quite deeply that the matter would turn out entirely according to my wish.

<margin>6.</margin> But alas, how often the firm hopes of mortals tend toward the opposite! For three or four days later, when I asked the printer whether he had any decision regarding that work, he replied that a <term>black bean</term> <note>original: "fabam nigram"; an ancient idiom for a vote of rejection or a "no" vote</note> had fallen between them; the matter was judged and "concluded" <note>original: "conclamatum"; a term used for a funeral cry, signifying that a matter is dead or hopeless</note>. They claimed the Latin of that translation was not good, but was full of <term>barbarisms</term> <note>original: "barbarismis"; errors in grammar or non-classical vocabulary</note> and lacked flavor—even though the whole task (except for the title and a very few [catchword: words]) had been completed in more or less the time it takes for a leaf to fall.

<meta>This page continues the author’s preface, where he recounts his struggle to get his Latin translation of a German chemical text approved by local scholars. It picks up from the previous page's discussion regarding the specialized terminology used in the work.</meta>

# A Fitting Word to the Reader

...words, perhaps not so common, yet most appropriate to the subject, not even a letter of which has been changed. I, however, dropping my ears <note>a Latin idiom for acting submissively or being dejected</note> and at the same time greatly astonished by such an unfavorable consensus, immediately approached these Athenian judges <note>original: "Atticos arbitros"; a reference to the refined but often severe critics of ancient Athens</note>, today this one, tomorrow another. I asked each one very humbly that he would not, I pray, stand in my light <note>an allusion to the philosopher Diogenes' famous request to Alexander the Great to move out of his sunlight</note>, but favor me a little and deign to offer his fair judgment; for three or four men, likewise not unlearned, had judged the matter quite favorably.

7. It was like telling stories to the deaf <note>original: "Surdis fabulas"; an idiom meaning speaking to those who refuse to listen</note>; nothing was achieved. Everyone seemed to be, as it were, in a ferment. Many, even while listening to me superciliously and hastily, finally did not blush to say openly to my face—for what will these "high-and-mighties" <note>original: "culmites"; literally "stalks" or "tops," used here derisively for people who think they are superior</note> not say?—namely, that that translator, whoever he may have been, did not understand the <term>chemical art</term> <note>original: "Chymicam artem"; referring to alchemy or early chemistry</note> at all. They claimed I was not of such authority that I could use archaic words <note>original: "archaïzare"</note> or display my own genius, and that the translation from German into Latin <note>original: "è germanismo in latinismum"</note> was done childishly. Oh, blind ones! Have you ever seen colors? And along with these words, they politely showed me their backs several times.

8. Furthermore, while I was once more, as if already at the door, entreating a certain one of them for the last time to weigh the matter fraternally and with judgment, he added, still slackly and lightly at the very moment of departure, that when the printer returned, he would see what he had to say. Above all these things, some had lectured me much about my "shoulders" <note>meaning his capacity or strength to handle a difficult task</note>, and if it had occurred to them, they would have recited that line of Horace:

> ->*Take up a subject, you who write, that is equal to your*<-
>
> ->*powers, and weigh long what your shoulders refuse to bear.*<-
<note>original: "Sumite materiam vestris, qui scribitis, æquam Viribus, & pensate diu, quid ferre recusent." Quoted from Horace’s Ars Poetica (The Art of Poetry).</note>

There is no doubt that they would have sung that out; for they seemed to want to indicate by this that I would be far unequal to completing such a great work—namely, the translation of something from one language to another, especially the Roman tongue <note>Latin</note>.

9. And although I freely [admit] my own power here is worth no more than a nutshell <note>original: "nauci"; a Latin idiom for something worthless</note>, and is nothing...

# A Fitting Word

9. I would acknowledge this, and I would not wish to compare myself to anyone, even the least, much less gloriously prefer myself; nevertheless, if humility were not such a beauty before God and such a utility among men, I would have almost dared to affirm that most of them—however much they may be of a **sharp nose** <note>original: "emunctæ naris"; a Latin idiom for being intellectually refined or, more often, fastidious and arrogant</note> and a **well-oiled hearth** <note>original: "obuncti Laris"; referring to a wealthy or prosperous household</note>—with all their wisdom and skill, would scarcely have succeeded even once in this way.

10. And this further still, you will say with me again, fair reader, if only you weigh the matter a little more strictly in the balance; for then you will find a most brilliant reason, not for accusing, but rather for greatly admiring: namely, how I—in so brief a space of time, with equal daring and fear—undertook this work, such as it is. I did so while **displaced and a stranger** <note>original: "exconditionatus, & peregrinus"; suggesting he was living outside his normal social standing or as a refugee</note>, without means or money on my journey; without fire in the deepest winter; and having no book, nor even a hearth of my own. I kept watch over such a "filing" <note>original: "limam"; a metaphor for the painstaking process of polishing and refining a literary text</note> as you see, even in the worst of days, which the burdens of extreme necessity and the most diverse cares of seeking food and clothing completely extort from me.

->*But my muse is unrefined; we sing what songs we can,*<-
->*The bird that is not learned often chirps what it has mended.*<-

11. I then, sometimes at noon, sometimes toward evening, having feasted in this way among those most skillful and wise **Aristarchuses** <note>original: "Aristarchos"; a reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, the famously severe critic of Homer, used here to describe harsh, pedantic reviewers</note>, returned home perpetually as empty in my belly as I was broken in my mind. Yet, as I went home religiously, I tossed and turned many kinds of thoughts along the way, drawing them through my mind. For sometimes, **tilting my neck** <note>original: "acquiniscens"; a gesture of dejection or deep thought</note>, I would cry out in a rough manner: "Oh, what a parasite, what a **world of false judges** <note>original: "pseudocrites mundus"; from the Greek for "hypocrite" or "false critic"</note> this is! Puppies are judged by moles. What an unregulated school! Ants are instructed by magpies. What a turbulent sea! Small fish are devoured by the large. How poorly ordered the stable is! Sheep are oppressed by oxen. The poor and men of good mind, oppressed in various ways, are rejected and neglected; others flourish, happy as much in their vices as in their riches. He does not obtain his right, but loses his case, who nevertheless defends a most just cause. Alas, for the [folly] of mortals..."

# A Fitting Word to the Reader
<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

...irritability, but oh, the wicked and deadly demons of the sons of Adam! The poor man speaks with pleas, and the rich man speaks harshly; for whatever the rich say, whatever they do, is praised and accepted by everyone, whether it be good or bad.

->*No evil man is happy, yet what rich man does not act fittingly?*<-

This one thing brings both tears and the most sorrowful thoughts to mind.

> *Ah, shameful poverty! You have nothing harder in you*
> *Than that you make men ridiculous and braying like beasts!* <note>The author is quoting the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire 3), who famously argued that the most painful part of being poor is the loss of dignity and the mockery of others.</note>

12. Sometimes I even said to myself, surely fortune favors the fools; in this modern day, it still happens in the world just as in the age of Solomon: animals are more highly valued than the learned and the literate.

->*Entire towns worship dogs, but no one worships Diana.*<- <note>original: "Dianas"; likely a poetic way of saying that people value hunting dogs or common pets more than the goddess of wisdom, nature, and the hunt.</note>

The "little lords" <note>original: "Dominelli"; a diminutive, perhaps mocking, term for the petty wealthy.</note> please the world, while the poor wretches are cast down; the learned and the wise are as good as buried. Great merchants of sulfur-matches <note>original: "sulphuratorum"; likely referring to street hawkers or traders in cheap commodities.</note> are held in higher value than Plato himself.

> *A man well-dressed is believed by a thousand to be skilled*
> *Because of his clothes, even though he may be an idiot.*
> *If you lack a garment, and are not dressed respectably;*
> *If your hat is worn out, if your cloak is foul and torn,*
> *If your gown is a little dirty, and your other shoe*
> *Gaping with broken leather, or if—the wound having been sewn up—*
> *More than one scar shows the thick and fresh thread,*
> *You are worthy of no praise, even though you grasp everything you hear.*

13. Meanwhile, however, while I am so wittily arguing with myself, there would occur to me again and again passages from that truly golden little book—which, in my own judgment, easily carries off the prize from all the volumes in the world touching upon similar subject matter, both due to its powerful essence of things and weight of its sentences, as well as the hidden pull of the Holy Spirit. Since the moment I saw and read it, it has always tasted unique to my heart...

### An Interjection

These words, from *The Imitation of Christ* <note>original: "de imitatione Christi"; the 15th-century devotional classic by Thomas à Kempis, which was a staple of spiritual life in the author's era</note>, are the constant companion of my life and my path:

14. *It is good for us that we sometimes experience some burdens and adversities, because they often call a person back to their heart, so that they may recognize they are in exile, and not place their hope in any worldly thing. It is good for us that we sometimes endure those who speak against us, and that we are thought of poorly and imperfectly—even if we act and intend well. These things often help us toward humility and defend us from vanity; for then we better seek God as our inner witness when we are despised by men on the outside and not well-trusted.*

15. Therefore, since I am so unrefined, dull, and ignorant, and the world judges so foolishly, and my efforts <term>specimina: refers to his writing samples or intellectual demonstrations</term> seem so worthless to men, I offer up this unformed firstborn of my spirit and meager talent <note>original: "genii & ingenioli mei informem Primogenitum"</note> for Your approval, O unchanging Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), often used by scholars to denote the unspeakable holiness of the Divine</term>! You, to whom the smallness of my person is not unknown, who never waver in Your judgment, and with whom the simple and uncultured often carry more weight than the prudent and the learned; before You, I say, I most heartily and emphatically acknowledge my infancy, childhood, and ignorance in the following two documents <term>syngraphis: originally meaning written contracts or signed bonds, here referring to the written sections of his work</term>.

# SOLILOQUY
## The Paraphrast's Morning Prayer,

->*By which he is accustomed to sacrifice to the Ruler of Nature <term>Physiarcham: a Greek-derived title for God as the "ruler" or "governor" of the natural world</term> as a daily offering, and to dedicate his vow to Him.*<-

<margin>1.</margin><image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>Awaken and spring forth from the melancholy of the mind, O my soul! Why are you torn apart by empty sorrow? Why are you exhausted by superfluous cares? Listen to what the Lord God wishes to distill into you. Blessed is the soul made poor and a pilgrim for the sake of Jesus. Blessed is the soul that reads Christ the Lord speaking within itself, and feeds on the honeycomb of consolation from His mouth. Blessed are the ears that obey the lips of the breathing God <note>original: "labellis inhalantis Dei"; an evocative image of God whispering or breathing life into the believer</note>, and fall asleep to the idle tales of this world. Blessed are the eyes that are closed to carnal things, but open to spiritual things. Blessed is the mouth that sucks milk from the veins of the divine breast <note>This maternal imagery for the divine was common in medieval and baroque mysticism, symbolizing the soul being nurtured directly by God's grace</note>, and becomes numb to the nursing-scenes of this life. Blessed indeed is the heart that awakens at once to the knock of the heavenly bridegroom, and notices nothing of the slipperiness of this world. Blessed, I say, are they who devote themselves to God and shake themselves free from every worldly dream.

2. Take heed of these things, my soul; rather, turn yourself more quickly with all your heart toward God. Lock the doors of your senses, breathe your soliloquies, and aspire to dwell alone with yourself. Seek the company of no one, but rather pour out a prayer devoted to God with a deep groan, so that you may be able to perceive what the Lord God whispers within you. Thus you may maintain a contrite <term>compunctam: a heart pricked by "compunction" or deep sorrow for sin</term> mind and a pure conscience. Regard the whole amphitheater of the world as nothing; place God's serious matters before all exterior things. For you cannot be free for Him and take delight in temporal things at the same time. If God is to approach you with the holy Angels, you must distance yourself from acquaintances, from dear ones, and from friends, and keep your mind secluded from all human consolation.

<meta>catchword: 3. This (original: Hæc)</meta>

<summary>In this opening to his morning devotions, the author exhorts his soul to reject worldly anxieties and sensory distractions in favor of an internal, mystical communion with God. He employs traditional ascetic language to describe the "blessedness" of a soul that finds nourishment in divine silence rather than human society.</summary>
<keywords>soliloquy, morning prayer, internal dialogue, asceticism, divine consolation, mysticism, solitude, Ruler of Nature</keywords>

### MORNING SOLILOQUY.
<sig>B 3</sig>

<margin>3.</margin> These things your most beloved says: I am your lot, I am your salvation, and your peace; keep yourself with me, and you shall find peace. Cut away the Siren-like <note>original: "sirenicam"; a reference to the Sirens of Greek mythology whose songs lured sailors to their doom, symbolizing worldly temptation</note> desire, abandon this bitter, this gall-filled, this wretched world, and you will find rest. Let go of things that perish, seek things that endure; for what are all transitory things, if not seductive? Follow me, because I am the way, the truth, and the life; without the way one does not travel, without the truth one does not know, without the life one does not pass through. I am the way you ought to follow, the truth you ought to trust, the life you ought to desire; I am the saving way, the all-encompassing <note>original: "sphæralis"; literally 'spherical,' suggesting the perfection and completeness of a globe</note> truth, the timeless life. I am the straightest way, the supreme truth, the true life, the blessed life, the uncreated life. If you sigh to inherit this, disdain the present life; if you wish to dwell in heaven, live as a pilgrim on earth; if you desire to triumph with me, bear the cross with me: for only the bearers of the cross find the way of blessedness and of true light.

<margin>4.</margin> O sweetest, O most honey-sweet first-martyr <note>original: "protomartyr"; while usually referring to St. Stephen, the author here applies the title to Jesus as the first to sacrifice His life</note> Jesus! Since Your way is so narrow and likewise despised by the world, grant me, I beseech You, to strive to follow You despite all the world's reproach. For the servant is not greater than his Lord, nor the disciple above the master. Let Your servant be continually exercised in Your life, because there is my salvation and my holiness; for You, Lord my God, have written me in Your hands. You are my only good, You stand in my heart, You are my desire, and therefore it is necessary to run after You, to weep, and to pray. But who am I, that I should dare to speak so confidently to You? I am a most poor, most lost, and most ignominious little man of Yours, a most dejected wanderer, and the most worthless filth—doubtless much more wicked and more contemptible than I know or would dare to say.

<margin>5.</margin> I am, O highest and most awesome Father, that shapeless, faithless, and spendthrift prodigal, who—swept away by the raging North Wind <note>original: "Aquilone"; the north wind was often associated with harshness or spiritual coldness in biblical allegory</note> of youth, and impatient with any yoke for the love of freedom—behaved insolently toward You. Following the violent impulse of my passions, and deserting Your house, I withdrew into distant and foreign regions, in which, by living softly and acting dissolutely, I squandered and mired all my faculties and substance.

### SOLILOQUY.
<sig>B 4</sig>

<margin>6.</margin> Teach me, however, today to conduct myself worthily and humbly in your presence, for you are my wisdom. You are the one who knows me in truth, and you knew me before the foundations were laid, and before I was born into the world. You also take a greater care for me, your humble little servant <note>original: "clientulo tuo"; a diminutive form of 'client,' implying a protective relationship like that of a patron and a dependent</note>, than a mother’s heart takes for her own precious child <note>original: "prolecula"; a diminutive of 'offspring,' used here to show deep affection</note>, or than I have or can even manage for myself.

<margin>7.</margin> See, therefore: my purpose hangs upon your judgment and stands at your good pleasure. I trust in your grace rather than in my own wisdom; for man proposes indeed, but you always dispose <note>original: "homo proponit quidem, sed tu disponis semper"; a variation of the famous Latin proverb 'Man proposes, God disposes'</note>, nor is a person’s way within his own power. The more humble someone is within himself and the more subject to God, and the more a person is at one with himself and inwardly simplified, the wiser and more peaceful he will be in all things. Such a person understands more things and higher things without labor, because he drinks the light of understanding from above. God walks with the humble, joins himself to the modest, and draws near to the little ones.

<margin>8.</margin> There is a wide enough difference between the wisdom of an illuminated and devoted man, and the knowledge of a literate and well-versed scholar <term>scholasticus: a student or teacher in the medieval university system, often associated with rigorous logic and intellectualism</term>. That doctrine which flows from above by divine influence <note>original: "influentia"; literally an 'in-flowing' of grace or light</note> is always much nobler than that which is laboriously acquired by our own cleverness. It is better to be wise in a small way with humility and little understanding, than to possess entire wagon-loads of the sciences <note>original: "plaustra"; literally 'wagons' or 'carts,' used here to describe a heavy, burdensome amount of intellectual data</note> with vain self-satisfaction. He will remain small for a long time and lie low beneath others, who considers anything to be great except the one immense eternal Good; for whatever is not God is truly nothing, and ought rightly to be counted as nothing.

<margin>9.</margin> Thus, he is truly great who is small in his own eyes and holds every peak of honor as nothing. He is truly prudent who considers all earthly things as filth so that he may gain Christ. And he is truly well-taught who carries out the will of God and ignores his own mind. He who seeks anything other than God alone or the salvation of his soul will reap nothing but some degree of nausea, anxieties, and bitterness; nor can he stand peaceful for long who does not aspire to be the least and subject to all.

<margin>10.</margin> Who <meta>catchword: 10. Qui</meta>

->### MORNING PRAYER.<-
<meta>catchword: 13. Blessed-</meta>

10. One who relies more on their own cleverness or their own reasoning than on the humble discipline of Jesus Christ will only rarely and slowly become an enlightened person. This is because God wants us to be entirely subject to Him, and to rise above all human reason through a heart set on fire with love. To always act rightly, and yet to hold a low opinion of oneself, is the sign of a humble soul <note>original: "parvuli animi"; literally "a very small soul," used here in the positive sense of being "little" or child-like before God</note>. Those who are humble in heart and simple in spirit dwell in a great abundance of peace, while those who are proud and puffed up are never satisfied. True peace of mind is not found by following one’s passions or chasing after one’s desires, but by resisting them. **Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart** <note>A quotation from Psalm 37:4</note>. If there is any joy to be found in this world, the person with a heart emptied of worldly things and made small in humility surely tastes it; and if, on the other hand, there is tribulation or distress anywhere, a heart burdened by conscience knows it best.

11. My son, because you know these things and have read them all, you will be blessed if you put them into practice <note>original: "piaveris"; literally to "atone" or "purify," but here meaning to perform or observe these teachings with devotion</note>. He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me; and I will love him and will reveal myself to him, and I will make him sit with me upon the **high throne** <note>original: "altithronio"; a poetic compound word for a throne in the highest heavens</note> of my Father. O generous and honey-sweet Lord Jesus, radiance of eternal glory, comfort to my soul wandering on its pilgrimage! Provided that my desire is right and not infected by my own self-interest—as you have said and promised—so let it be, and let it be my lot to be found worthy. My mouth is now silent before you, and my sighing speaks to you: how long will my most longed-for Messiah delay his coming? May he come to me, a lonely orphan, and make me glad; may he reach out his hand and rescue this poor wretch <note>original: "misellum"; a diminutive of "miser," used to evoke a sense of being small and pitiable</note> from every distress. Oh, how long and bitter is this delay away from the nest of my eternal home!

12. Away with everything else, but come to me! For without you no day or hour will be happy, because you are my joy, and without you my table is tasteless. Oh, my **Emmanuel**, "honey and milk are under your tongue" <note>A reference to the Song of Solomon 4:11, used here to describe the sweetness of Christ's words</note>! My Lord, most dear as my own eyes <note>original: "oculissime Domine"; a term of endearment suggesting someone is as precious as one's own sight</note>, your hungry little worm <note>original: "vermiculus"; a common medieval expression of extreme humility, referencing Psalm 22</note> licks up the droplets; for you sprinkle the honeycombs of eternal life. Unfolding me in the love of your most healing and perfect desire, **pierce** <note>original: "confaucia"; likely a variant of "confodere," meaning to strike through or wound with a weapon</note> my heart with your arrow, so that I may learn to taste with the inner mouth of the heart how sweet it is to love, and to melt and swim in your love. If anyone here loves, they surely know what this voice is crying out.

->### MORNING SOLILOQUY.<-

13. Blessed indeed is the one who understands what it means to love Jesus and to look down upon themselves for the sake of Jesus. For the love of Jesus makes a person trample upon their own ego <note>original: "seipsum calcare"; literally "to tread upon oneself," a common metaphor for overcoming self-interest or pride</note>. A soul that loves God finds everything beneath God to be distasteful; it is necessary to exchange one beloved for the Beloved <note>original: "dilectum pro dilecto"; the author suggests replacing earthly attachments with the one divine Love</note>, because Jesus wishes to be loved alone above all things. Do you see these vows, my little soul, and how your lover is so powerfully jealous <note>original: "masculè zelotypet"; suggesting a strong or vigorous protective love</note> for you? 14. O most tender suitor, O most wounded little lover <note>original: "amasiuncule sauciatissime"; a diminutive and intimate term referring to the "wounded" or "lovesick" heart of Christ</note>, tell me, I pray, where you tend your flock, O beautiful spouse who are born among the lilies. Where do you rise in the morning? Where do you rest at noon? Where are you, most sweet Jesus, who so pursues my soul? Let me kiss you just once with the kiss of my mouth, so that you might turn the diamond-bright and magnetic rays of your eyes toward me—rays that make my spirit take flight—so that I may find you always alone from now on. Let me reveal my whole heart to you alone and lose myself in love for you, just as my soul hungers for you. Let no one look down on me now, nor any creature distract or notice me; instead, let you alone speak to me and I to you, just as a beloved is known to speak to his beloved, or a friend to feast with a companion. Truly, you are my beloved, chosen from among all others, in whom my soul is well-pleased to have stored up its comfort for all the remaining days of its life. Amen.

# HOMILY
## His Evening [Soliloquy] with the Messiah,
->BY WHICH<-
### *He was accustomed daily to run toward that jealous little Monarch of his heart, and to cast himself at his feet.*

1. <image-desc>Ornamental initial L featuring floral or vine-like patterns within a rectangular frame.</image-desc> Grant to me, O most loving and most indulgent Jesus, your Spirit, that it may be with me, and work with me, and persevere with me even unto my final state <note>original: "habitum"; referring to the soul's enduring condition or final breath</note>. Grant that I may constantly desire and will that which is more acceptable to you and pleases you more; let your will be mine, and let mine always follow yours and be in perfect harmony with it. Let there be for me one "will" and "will not" with you, nor let me be able to want or not want anything except what you want or do not want.

2. Let me not care for the shadow of a great name, nor for the familiarity of many, nor for the private affection of men; let me always refuse to be uniquely loved or praised: these things nourish pride, generate distractions, and create the greatest darkness <note>original: "caligines"; mists or spiritual gloom</note> in the heart. You help the humble, and you humble the one who presumes of himself; you defend and free the humble, you love and console the humble; you incline yourself to the humble person, you bestow great grace upon the humble, and after their suppression <note>original: "suppressionem"; here meaning the humbling or casting down of one's worldly status</note> you raise them up to glory; to the humble you reveal your secrets, and you sweetly draw and invite them to yourself.

3. It is good for me, therefore, Lord, that you have humbled me and made me poor so that I may learn your justifications <note>original: "justificationes"; divine statutes or the ways in which God makes one righteous</note> and cast away the vain elations and presumptions of the heart. It is useful to me that shame has occasionally covered my face, so that I might seek you for consolation rather than men. O, how gladly and frequently would you speak your loving words to me and reveal hidden things, if only I would observe your coming more diligently, and to you knocking at the door of my heart as soon as—

# HOMILY

...at last I opened <note>The Latin suffix "-mùm" likely completes "postremùm" (at last) or "primum" (first) from the previous page.</note> [my eyes], oh, how great was my thoughtlessness and my neglect!

4. Truly, O loving Shepherd, I am that lost little sheep, whom you have hunted down after my winding wanderings, and have taken up as a brother upon your shoulders, readopting me into the lush pastures of your vineyard. Hosanna, therefore! Grace and thanks to you, my **Purple-clad Light-bringer** <note>original: "Purpurate Lucifator"; "Purple-clad" refers to Christ's royal and sacrificial dignity, while "Lucifator" is a rare term for a bringer of light.</note>, who quite some time ago—surely in the presence of the prayers and sighs of my mother **Monica** <note>Saint Monica (c. 332–387), whose persistent prayers led to the conversion of her son, Saint Augustine. The speaker here adopts Augustine's persona.</note>—humbly bound me to yourself. I beseech you, by that friendship which exists between you and me, do not deny my intellect this light: namely, that from now on I may give myself entirely over to your fatherly disposal and offer myself to your will. May I be just as willing to be poor, lonely, despised, and rejected for a lifetime as I would be to be wealthy, honored, favored, or famous in the mouths of men.

5. Ah, sweet Jesus, **Word-begotten** <term>Verbigena: a theological term for Christ as the Son born from the Eternal Word</term> beyond all reward, from this point forward turn all carnal consolation into bitterness for me, for such comforts draw me away from the love of eternal things and wickedly lure me toward themselves with the spark of some present, pleasant good. I pray that in exchange for transitory earthly knowledge and all the fading magnificence of this false world, you might grant me a crumb of **ambrosia** <note>In mythology, the food of the gods; here used to mean pure, divine sustenance.</note> and of your pure, heavenly wisdom, which rejects all these lowly things and burns with zeal for you alone. Your tablets and your letters are the most delightful wisdom—a wisdom so deep it surpasses all the teachings of the philosophers and the wise men of this world.

6. Let me always conduct myself as a stranger, as a hermit and an exile upon the earth, to whom nothing concerning the patterns of the flesh belongs. For whoever desires to reach the interior things and your spiritual delights must turn aside with you far from the crowd; it is certainly better to remain hidden and to set everything else aside, to take care of one's own soul and keep oneself alone before one's eyes, rather than to neglect oneself, chase after phantoms, and **plow another man’s field** <note>original: "alienum arare fundum"; a classical idiom meaning to meddle in affairs that do not concern one's own spiritual progress.</note> while one's own plot lies fallow.

7. Let me also not be ashamed or weary of always listening gladly to others for the sake of your love, and let me be seen as poor and without honor in this life, becoming a **fool for your sake**. Oh, that I might be a lover of myself in nothing, but instead be able to resign myself entirely to you—to fully abandon, annihilate, and cast myself away for your sake!

## Authority and Majesty <note>original: "Authoritas & Majeftas"</note>

<margin>1.</margin> *The great wonders of the whole world, the trophies on its stage,*

# TRIUMPHALIA OF THE GOLD-BEARING ART TO THE STUDENTS OF THE ART.

<meta>catchword: In- (likely for the word "Insuper" or "Indeed")</meta>

Wherever the earth lies open, let it crackle,
Wherever the whole world extends, let it roar.
Come now! By trying, by faltering, by blowing the bellows,
Feeding the Bosch <note>original: "Boscham"; likely referring to the city of 's-Hertogenbosch or a specific alchemical vessel/process named after it</note> with perpetual tears <note>in alchemy, "tears" often represent the distilled liquids or "mercury" of the philosophers</note>,
Cooking the Phoenix <note>the Phoenix represents the final stage of the Great Work, the Philosopher's Stone, which is reborn from fire</note> in much darkness,
You who, wavering too much among the shadows,
Live as exiles far from the path of truth,
And you who, while Jupiter <note>referring to the god of the sky, often representing the "spirit" or "air" in alchemy</note> remains silent,
Hold the Art in suspense and regard it with suspicion,
In whose mind, I say, the Labyrinth <note>a common metaphor for the confusion of alchemical texts</note> remains stuck:
Be steadfast, watch on, and be of good cheer.

<margin>3.</margin> Behold, the **SICAMBRIAN** <note>original: "Sicamber"; a reference to the Germanic peoples of the Rhine, often used as a pseudonym for alchemists from that region</note> was the first to attempt
The slippery battles of powerful Mars <term>Mars: the alchemical symbol for iron</term>
To stir up the wars of this sea:
The man from **VENLO** <note>a city in the Netherlands</note> first dared to enter
This winding path of the Daedalean house <note>the Labyrinth built by Daedalus to house the Minotaur; here used for the complexity of the chemical process</note>
With pitch-black wreaths and hollow wings;
Abounding in the home of a very powerful court,
Weighted with the omen of Phrygian zeal,
And strong in his natural genius, he strove and burned
To carry the torch with a favorable fate.

<margin>4.</margin> Just as he immediately blessed himself
By the obtaining of this gift,
So may we be blessed by the use of it!
Let **GUELDERS** <note>original: "Gelria"; a province in the Netherlands</note> applaud, and twenty times live
The **VANNISTS** <note>original: "Vannistae"; likely referring to a specific group of practitioners or a play on the word "vannus," a winnowing fan used to separate grain from chaff</note> in their charming flight.

*The Interpreter’s Exhortation*

->TO<-

# The lover of golden truth,

->CONCERNING<-

### *His Sibylline lots.* <note>original: "Sibyllinis ſortibus"; referring to the Sibyls, ancient prophetesses whose oracles were famously difficult to interpret. "Lots" refers to the oracular decrees or fates.</note>

Ignore for my sake, you who write, the trifles of the commentators <note>original: "Paraphraſte"; those who rewrite or interpret other texts, often making them more confusing</note>,
Who teach things more slippery than our famous arts.
And with me as your discourager, spare the Chemists <term>Chymiſtis: early modern term for alchemists or chemists</term>
Who deal in symbols and types; they sing only of naked names.
Flee, I say, the double-tongued and philosophical little books,
Which sound like riddles from the mouth of the Sphinx <note>the Sphinx represents the "philosopher’s stone" riddles that are impossible to solve</note>, hardly known even to the gods.
For as many as have written such things, they have almost always
Died through the shadows of trying to grasp things too difficult.
Always speaking in an ambiguous or figurative manner,
Quick with the empty brightness of a flowering fig tree <note>an allusion to something that appears fruitful but is hollow or deceptive</note>.
Using now these, now those, and various evasions,
Like will-o'-the-wisps <note>original: "fatuos ignes"; phosphorescent lights seen over marshes that lead travelers astray</note> which are seen to go off the path.
Do you think anyone can understand all the spirals
Which the first masters of magic established for their followers?
Who are you to me, the least of the crowd of Sages <term>Sophorum: the "Wise Men" or Sages of alchemy</term>
To be the one who will rightly perceive the book by the fates?
Tell me, how many could have held the secrets of the Stone of Geber <note>original: "Gebêri"; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century father of chemistry whose works were notoriously difficult</note>,
Or known the dogmas of the "Perfect Work" of Rhazes <note>original: "Rhaſis"; a prominent 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note>?
To whom, once read, could a true mind return after Plato <note>alchemical texts were often attributed to the philosopher Plato in the Middle Ages</note>,
Or for whom did the jeweled bird <note>original: "gemmina avis"; likely a reference to the "Bird of Hermes" or the Emerald Tablet, symbols of the alchemical process</note> create the matter?
Whose ears does Raymond Lull <note>original: "Raymundus Lullius"; a 13th-century polymath to whom many alchemical works were falsely attributed</note> feed with follies,
He for whom so many deceptive "waters" <term>waters: alchemical solvents or spirits</term> are listed?
Does Arnold of Villanova <note>original: "Arnoldúſne novâ de villâ"; a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> feed your eyes?
Far be it! What he reported is either sluggish, or it was all for himself.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;They have entangled everything more tightly in their folds.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But it is joined to a corrupt guide.

That spirit is from the pole <note>the heavens</note>, but not from those divine seats;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;More truly, that inspiration arises from deceit.
It is a wonder that the divine Art is held buried in perpetual darkness,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And that the glowing treasure lies hidden in the muddy soil!
the Golden Muse was given, not to suppress secrets,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But for the use of things was the Golden Muse given.
That species of bird, flying through a thousand rocky crags,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Will by no means make its nest in our field.
To hand down the secrets of the ancient Sages on pages—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ingenuously, nakedly, without envious speech,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rejoice, people of **GUELDERS**, live and thrive, **VENLO**. <note>The author identifies his home province as Gelderland (Guelders) and his city as Venlo in the Netherlands.</note>

Since among these massive waves of Tethys <note>original: "Tethyos"; the Greek goddess of the sea, used here to represent the "ocean" of difficult alchemical theory.</note>,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before Lead <note>original: "plumbum"; associated with Saturn.</note> ceases to smoke upon the pyre:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before the living Nymph of golden Jove <note>A poetic reference to the alchemical "Secret" or the "Philosophical Gold."</note> shall fall.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which is often a joke in place of an excellent name?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And so that you may be wise, take your place under this stern-ornament <note>original: "aplustre"; the decorative high stern of an ancient ship.</note>.
For through a short space, with light wings, instead of the Phoenix’s private wings,

### Forestalling rash criticisms.

1. I have thought it best, O seeker of golden truth, to place the summary of this **entire little work** before your eyes here in a visual image, as if in a "three-word motto" <note>original: "triverbio"; a concise or proverbial expression.</note>. I have done this to reveal the destined spirit and the value of the present work, so that being ignorant of our unusual method of proceeding and our intention, you do not judge the matter prematurely as irrelevant, or pass an immature judgment upon it. 3. *The Sibylline Oracles of the Magical Nights* <note>A section of the book likely containing cryptic, prophetic-style alchemical verses.</note> sets forth the cause and circumstances of this undertaking: namely why and how it was begun. 4. Therefore, he who does not wish nor desire to read anything here except what strictly pertains to the Art should skip over the prose-and-verse <note>original: "prosimetricum"; a literary style mixing prose and poetry.</note> Prelude along with *The Sibylline Oracles of the Magical Nights*, and only examine *The Grain Unearthed from the Chemical Winnowing Fan*. He will not need many hours for this; for once one ignores all the symbolic and "glyphic" apparatus of parables, circumlocutions, and metaphors with which it is overshadowed, the *Art* itself is extremely brief, easy, linear, and simple.

5. Now, however, a question may arise against me: to what purpose does it serve to introduce such a great structure of repeated things? I say I did it because it is not the custom, nor is it possible, for a book or booklet to be composed of a single page; and so that you may believe that the truth is true. You may hold the Nymph <note>A poetic personification of the alchemical secret or the "Matter."</note> in higher regard because she is more beautiful when adorned with gems and jewelry. For truly grave reasons, the Church employs ceremonies in its sacred rites and sacraments; for a thing proposed crudely and nakedly, however mystical or sacred it may be, quickly becomes a joke and falls into contempt.

6. *If a King were to walk through the streets in unknown dress, alone without any pomp or royal retinue, who would believe him to be a King? Who would pay him royal honor?* In the same way, if the Royal Art <note>A traditional name for Alchemy.</note> of the world were naked and stripped of all its ceremonial trappings, who would regard it as such? How many would believe <term>Gea</term> <note>The personification of Earth in Greek mythology.</note> or <term>Rhea</term> <note>An ancient mother goddess associated with nature and the earth.</note> to be a Goddess? Who would bend a knee in reverence to her? It was necessary, therefore, to sew an honorable tunic for our Nymph, so that she might appear in public with dignity and be able to enter the courts of Great men.

# PRELUDE

*Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within:*

As if it were a decree delivered from heaven and born divinely in one's soul—being the beginning of all knowledge and wisdom and the gateway to God—this phrase should rightly be written in golden letters. For it is a golden tribute, worth its weight in gold, and would that it were never erased from the tablets of our hearts, but rather fixed there and held within a mindful breast. It is brief indeed, but it suffices without anything else, even if all other things apart from this exist and yet offer little benefit. Irradiated by this supreme torch, as it were, we are reminded to fix our sight and the edge of our mind upon ourselves. We should strive to reach a knowledge of no other thing more urgently than that by which each person may consult and recognize himself.

For much indeed he knows, who knows himself; he alone is wise, and all others are fools. We must therefore enter the inner chambers of nature’s reality and see deeply into what she requires, for otherwise we cannot know ourselves. Because this precept was too great to seem uttered by a man, it was attributed to the God <note>The author refers to Apollo, the god of the sun and prophecy, to whom the maxim "Know Thyself" was attributed at the Temple of Delphi.</note> who wishes us to know ourselves. And since this knowledge is the most necessary of all, the Delphic oracle <note>original: "Delphica cortina," referring to the tripod or cauldron where the priestess sat to deliver prophecies.</note> is said to have delivered this fate to King Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia who sought the oracle's advice on how to be happy.</note> when he once asked by what means he might be happy: *if you know yourself.* This response is truly worthy of the memory of all ages and nations, for to be able to know oneself is the very pinnacle of the sciences. It encompasses a summary of the whole Christian life in its ancient praise, just as that **walking tree, man**, <note>original: "ambulatilis illa arbos homo." This is a common philosophical metaphor suggesting that man is an "inverted tree" with roots in the heavens (the mind) rather than the earth.</note> presents the proof of all created things. Evangelus <note>Likely referring to a specific Christian author or the "Messenger of the Gospel" (Evagrius or a similar figure); the text cites him as an authority on spiritual light.</note> has elegantly and exquisitely agreed with me on this point: that this is the first benefit granted by God to a sinner—to cast a ray of light into his heart so that he may know himself more intimately. The first gift, undoubtedly, he says, which is given to man in respect to the Light, is the knowledge of self;

->To know oneself, and what one's heavenly origin might be,<-
->This is the path that leads to the homes above.<-

These are noble verses, and truly worthy of not being sung from the earth; for I certainly do not see what could be more religious, what more holy

# PROSE AND VERSE
E 2

...nothing wiser could be expressed in poetry; for to know this one thing is to be ignorant of nothing, while to be ignorant of this is to know nothing at all. Even the ancient nations, though they wandered in the dark, murky mists of heathendom <note>original: "coeno Gentilitatis," literally the "filth of Gentilism," referring to the pre-Christian era.</note>, found this lack of self-knowledge profoundly distasteful.

As the first witness to this truth, let that oracle of philosophers and one of the Seven Sages of Greece, Solon <note>Solon (c. 630 – c. 560 BCE) was an Athenian statesman and poet, celebrated for his wisdom.</note>, step onto the stage. To humble the pride of the Alexandrians, to restrain the insolent, and to recall the arrogant and stubborn back to the rule of reason, he employed a single remedy: he inscribed that famous verse upon the doors and both walls of the Delphic shrine:

->*Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within,*<-

Walk, I say, with yourself; dwell with yourself, consult yourself, and know yourself. Know, specifically, who you are and where you came from; for "nothingness" itself is your father, mud and filth are your nobility, and worms are your true heraldry <note>original: "insignia," referring to the coats of arms or symbols of status used by the nobility.</note>.

Dressed in a gown of no lesser status, let Thales of Miletus <note>Thales (c. 624 – c. 548 BCE) is often called the first philosopher in the Western tradition.</note> follow him as the near-leader of this same procession. According to the historian Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, a 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note>, when someone asked Thales what was the most difficult thing in the world, he replied: "To have known oneself." Oh, these records of the ancient Theater! O men entirely admirable in their learning! For what does it help to embrace the heavens and the earth with one’s intellect if one does not grasp one’s own smallness and worthlessness? What profit is there in skillfully searching for the spots on the Sun <note>original: "rugas Solis," literally "wrinkles of the sun."</note> while never meditating on one's own stains? Of what use is it to observe the eclipses of the Moon and yet fail to see one's own defects? If you gain knowledge of all secrets and arts, what is this worth and what does it profit you, if you are ignorant of your very self? You wander abroad constantly, thinking you are well-advised and that you know much, when in fact you know nothing of who and what you are. If you know the height of the heavens and the depth of the sea, and possess all sciences at once, but do not know yourself, you are like one who builds without a foundation:

->*For indeed, when the foundation collapses, everything falls to ruin.*<-

Yet how very few follow and attain this! Which...

<meta>This page continues the "Prelude" (Præludium) from page 35. The previous page introduced the Greek sages, specifically Solon and Thales, as proponents of the maxim "Know Thyself." <header>PRELUDE</header>

Similarly, in the times of the prince and father of philosophers, Plato, it was noted—he says—that in the public square one can scarcely find one man in ten who knows himself. The poet Persius, however, finds not even a single one; censuring the habits of the age with his biting satire, he argues:

> ->No one attempts to descend into himself, no one;<-
> ->instead, the pack on the other man’s back is always watched.<-
> <note>original: "In sese nemo tentat descendere... Semper at alterius spectatur mantica tergo." This refers to Aesop's fable where humans carry their own faults in a bag behind them, out of sight, while carrying the faults of others in front where they are easily seen.</note>

Thus, wisely, Plato—though a pagan philosopher—crowned the aforementioned motto when he said that the knowledge and memory of oneself is an absolute and solid science. From this perfected verse:

> ->Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within.<-

From this, all the wisdom and justice of life sprouts forth without dispute. Hence that torch and flower of Roman eloquence, Cicero <note>original: "Tullius," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the famous Roman statesman and orator.</note>, says: "And so it happens that wisdom is the mother of all good arts." It is from the love of this wisdom that the name *philosophy* <term>Philosophy: from the Greek *philo* (loving) and *sophia* (wisdom).</term> found its name. No gift more fruitful, more flourishing, or more excellent than this has been granted to human life by the immortal gods. For this alone has taught us, among all other things, that which is most difficult: to know ourselves.

The power and meaning of this precept are so great that it was attributed not to any man, but to the Delphic God <note>The god Apollo, at whose temple in Delphi the phrase "Know Thyself" was famously inscribed.</note>. For whoever knows himself will first feel that he possesses something divine, and he will regard his own intellect as if it were a kind of dedicated sacred image. He will always act and feel in a way worthy of so great a gift from the gods. When he has looked into himself and tested his whole being, he will understand how he came into the light equipped by nature, and what great tools he possesses for obtaining and attaining wisdom. For in the beginning of all things, he conceives in his soul and mind certain "sketched-out" understandings; enlightened by these, and with wisdom as his guide, he perceives that he will be a good man and, for that reason, a happy one.

But while this supporting evidence has been drawn from elsewhere, let us also shoot an arrow from our own quiver <note>The author signals a transition from citing classical "pagan" philosophers to citing Christian or theological authorities.</note>: rightly, it seems to me—

# PROSIMETRIC WORK

...I believe I can [conclude] that the height of the knowledge of Christ consists in the consultation, habitation, cognition, and memory of oneself. Compared to this sublime wisdom, all other things are truly ignorance. It is a distinguished and sharp weapon that suddenly transforms even the most dull-witted men into wise priests! O, therefore, golden *three-word maxim* <note>original: "triverbium," referring to the three-part command: Consult, Know, Walk.</note>, oh majestic song, which must surely be hammered deep into the triangle of the human heart! <note>In Baroque spirituality, the heart was often symbolized as a triangle to represent the Trinity or the way the human soul (the triangle) cannot be filled by the circular world, only by God.</note> For in this magnificence of things, and in this sight and knowledge of that unspeakable Word—immortal gods!—how one will consult oneself and distinguish oneself, just as the Pythian Apollo <note>Referring to the god Apollo at Delphi, where the famous command "Know Thyself" was inscribed on the temple.</note> commanded! How he will despise, how he will look down upon, and how he will count as nothing those things which are commonly called "the greatest" by the crowd!

But with still other colors and with a new "charcoal," so to speak, I shall paint this same thing for you on a white canvas. That Antaeus, son of the Earth, born from the race of Giants—as long as he was thrown down to the ground while wrestling with Hercules and kissed that most indulgent mother [the Earth], his strength and power were perpetually restored. But soon, when he raised his head high into the air, his arms were weakened again, and he was laid low by Hercules <note>original: "Alcide," a common epithet for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alcaeus.</note>. But leaving behind the husk of the fable, let us extract the kernel of truth that lies hidden within it. We must say, therefore, that the very same thing happens to us when we carry giant-like spirits and presume a certain singular privilege for ourselves as "Earth-born" <note>original: "Terrigenis," those born of the earth; here used to mean mortals who become arrogant.</note> and forget ourselves. For as long as we hold to the earth and fix our eyes upon our own being, and at the same time often revolve that saying in our minds:

->Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within.<-

And as we weigh what we are, where we have come from, and into what we are to be reduced, no enemy can be found—nothing so difficult, nothing so "Herculean"—that it might conquer or prostrate us. Nothing is so secret, so suppressed, that it might lie hidden from us or pass us by. Indeed, if we allow ourselves to be carried away into pride and loftiness by some empty and vain wind of presumption and [false] wisdom, and if we chase after clouds and empty things, and exhaust ourselves trying to raise ourselves upward; if, finally, we are ignorant of what our origin is and from where we came, and if we do not keep always fixed...

This was indeed excellently devised, because to do what has already been done, to risk only easy things, to drift down a fertile river, to labor at trivialities—what glory could lie beneath such things? Or what kind of feat is it to undertake a task that can be handled with no effort?

# PROSE AND VERSE

Since, therefore, the nature of these mysteries is by no means of secondary importance, but clearly primary, then by necessity and the very character of the law, shapeless and enormous "trunks" <note>Metaphor for lazy, unformed individuals.</note> must never be admitted to the **Philosophical Rose Garden**; nor should those who linger and stretch lazily, allowing their lives to grow wild with sloth, ever be permitted entry. For what, by the Gods, could be more desirable than she? What more excellent? What better for man? # PRELUDE

Wisdom is most precious, according to the oracle of the Easterners, among whom was that wealthiest and most powerful prophet Job <note>The biblical Job was traditionally associated with the "East" (the land of Uz) and was renowned for his discourse on the elusive nature of wisdom in Job 28.</note> (whom some indeed believe to have been a King). He found nothing to be its equal, saying: *Pure gold shall not be exchanged for it* <note>original: "Non commutabitur aurum obryzum pro eâ." A reference to Job 28:17.</note>. For this reason, the "Omega" of Orators <note>The "Omega" or the ultimate/greatest of speakers.</note>, the Prince of Philosophers, and the Torch of Theologians—that sun of doctors, Thomas Aquinas—count wisdom among the greatest goods of man. She is called the *Torch of an honorable mind*, in whose glory and splendor even the most upright men are captivated.

For so great is the innate love of knowledge and science in all people that no one can doubt that human nature is drawn toward these things, even when invited by no reward. We see how children, even by the threat of lashes, are not deterred from contemplating and investigating things; how, though driven away, they return to their inquiries and rejoice that they know something; how they yearn to tell others; and how they are held fast by pageantry, games, and spectacles of that kind, even enduring hunger and thirst for that sake. Indeed, what of those who delight in noble studies and arts? Do we not see them take no account of their health or their family estate? Do we not see them endure everything, captivated by cognition and science itself, balancing the great cares and labors they spend against the pleasure they draw from learning?

To me, indeed, Homer seems to have seen something of this kind in those things he fabled about the songs of the Sirens <note>In the *Odyssey*, the Sirens were sea-nymphs who lured sailors to their deaths with song.</note>. For it does not seem to have been the sweetness of their voices or some itch for novelty and variety in singing that used to call back those who sailed past; rather, it was because they professed to know many things, so that men would cling to their rocks out of a desire for learning. For thus they invited Ulysses <note>The Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus.</note>:

What that Orator [Cicero] declared regarding the beauty of virtue may be even more rightly said of wisdom. It must be said, therefore, that wisdom contains so much beauty and so much grace that no one has ever looked upon her closely without admiring her and being spurred by her form toward virtue and a more watchful, fruitful way of life. "Sight," says Plato, "is our keenest sense, yet through it we do not see wisdom; how burning the loves she would stir for herself if she were visible!" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus* 250d, regarding the invisibility of true wisdom.</note>

As Antisthenes finally threatened him with a staff to drive him away, Diogenes said: *Strike if you wish, but you will find no staff so savage or so hard that you might drive me away from you, as long as you teach me something.* Oh, what zeal and fervor for wisdom, which every person should uniquely strive to emulate!

# P R E L U D E

...arrangements. The first was of those whom nature had enriched with a generous hand and with the beauty and dexterity of emerging gifts. Truly, the second was of those who stood in the middle, being neither beautiful nor deformed. The third, however, was of those rejected and abandoned, as if by nature, provided for so sparingly that they could be called deformed and unlovely without causing offense. Therefore, the young men coming forward, eager to have a bride, first desired the daughters of the first rank and beauty to be taken. This was permitted, however, under such a condition: that whoever received them was forced to provide a huge sum of money for a dowry, and that money was not bestowed upon those [beautiful] girls, but was kept for the marriage of the unlovely ones so they would not be left to complain; for whoever took the latter gained the money. Now, those "middle" ones, who were neither beautiful nor clever <note>original: "vafrosæ" — can mean crafty, subtle, or sharp-witted.</note>, were obtained without any gain or payment. Therefore, in their judgment, bodily beauty and riches could not be possessed at once; it was considered such a great thing to take a beautiful woman that not only was she to be obtained without a dowry, but a price actually had to be paid so that they might have her. By Hercules, a deed and custom to be proclaimed and truly praiseworthy! 

But come now, you suitors of the **Only-Begotten Daughter of the Philosophers** <note>referring to Wisdom (Sapientia)</note>, answer me: was there ever any girl so

->Beautiful, smooth-browed, snowy-white, tender, polished girl,<-

As wisdom? What little maiden, I ask, was ever as rare, dear, and distinguished as wisdom? What **Cynthia** <note>A poetic name for the moon goddess Diana, used here as a standard of feminine beauty.</note>, I ask, was ever nearly equal to the value or beauty of wisdom? She is the *brightness of eternal light and a mirror without blemish* <note>original: "candor lucis æternæ, & speculum sine maculâ". A direct quote from the biblical Book of Wisdom 7:26.</note>. When we wish to greatly praise someone for the gifts and goods of beauty, we are accustomed to compare them to the **Sun**, which restores and gladdens all things with the purple color of its clarity and the golden-haired beams of its splendors; but pay attention: wisdom is far more beautiful than the Sun. For she is more lovely than the sun, and proven to be prior to all the starry arrangement of the heavens.

Clinging to this one point, *Herillus* <note>A Stoic philosopher who argued that knowledge was the "Supreme Good."</note> maintained that wisdom is the highest good, and that no other thing is to be sought for its own sake, judging it fitting and appropriate that it should be loved for itself alone:

->Wisdom herself is indeed her own most beautiful reward;<-

groups; The first was of those women whom nature, with a generous hand, had enriched with the charm and grace of inherited gifts. Truly, the second group consisted of those who existed in the middle, being neither beautiful nor ugly.
