<meta>This page continues the argument regarding true nobility, following the anecdote of King Alfonso V of Aragon. The king's sentiment—that a monarch without learning is but a "crowned ass"—is expanded here into a philosophical meditation on the soul versus external status. The catchword from the previous page "No-" likely anticipated a word like "Nobilitas" (Nobility), though the text begins with a reflection on the vanity of false merit.</meta>

# PRELUDE
<note>Latin: *Præludium*. A preliminary section or introduction to the main argument.</note>

It is indeed ridiculous for someone to claim credit for something for which they were not the cause, or which they have not earned. Therefore, when you wish to see a true estimation of a man and know what he is really like, look at him "naked." Let him set aside his inheritance, set aside his status, set aside his honors and the other lies of fortune. Let him strip off the body itself and look into his soul: of what kind is it, how great is it, and of what value is it? Is it great by someone else’s merit, or its own? For he who praises his own lineage praises the merits of others. Setting boastfulness aside, tell me: what are all men, if not men? Once possessions, the splendor of clothes, gold, gems, and the rest are removed, men are only men; they do not change, except in their outward trappings:

> Why do they boast of ancestors? If they but look at their origins
> and God the Creator, then no one is base-born;
> The entire mortal race rises from a shared birth.
> <note>original: "Quid Proavos jactent..." These lines are from Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy* (Book III, Meter 6), a standard medieval and Renaissance text on the vanity of worldly status.</note>

True and recognized nobility consists in being distinguished by learning. This is consistent with Socrates, who, upon seeing a very wealthy and arrogant man who possessed no education, said: *“This is a horse covered in silver.”* For horses are often decorated all over with blankets, trappings, and silver studs, yet inside they remain nothing other than horses. Thus, reason and clarity itself declare that only the wise man is noble. For what use to a man is a famous lineage if his morals defile him? Or how does a lowly birth harm a man whom his morals adorn and ennoble?

> I would rather have Thersites <note>A figure from the *Iliad* known for being ugly, low-born, and foul-mouthed.</note> as a father, provided I am
> like the son of Aeacus <note>Achilles, the greatest Greek hero of the Trojan War.</note> and can wield the arms of Vulcan,
> than have Achilles beget me as a man like Thersites.
> <note>original: "Malo pater mihi ſit Therſites..." Quoted from the Roman satirist Juvenal (*Satires* VIII), emphasizing that personal virtue outweighs inherited status.</note>

Accordingly, whoever is inclined toward the good by their own nature is noble, even if born of an Ethiopian mother <note>In the classical world, "Ethiopian" was often used as a literary shorthand for someone from the furthest reaches of the known world, implying that virtue transcends geography and ethnicity.</note>. Most deservedly, therefore, I shall sing:

> A man's nobility is his mind and the image of the Deity,
> A man's nobility is the bright progeny of his virtues,
> A man's nobility is to lift up the wretched who lie prostrate,
> A man's nobility is to restrain the raging mind.

# PROSIMETRIC
<note>original: *Prosimetricum*. A literary work composed in a mixture of poetry and prose.</note>

Human nobility is to uphold the laws of nature,
Human nobility is to fear nothing except shameful deeds;
Human nobility is to despise earthly paths,
Human nobility is to seek the celestial springs;
True nobility is not provided by gems or gold,
Nobility demands that one possess something greater,
For the objects of wisdom are considered the only ornaments,
Which Fortune both gives and snatches away with her hands:
These things, therefore, cannot make anyone truly noble,
For learning preserves the ancestors of nobility within itself.

->§. 3.<-

Indeed, these rhythms are quite charming, and the little verses are worthy of Apollo’s tripod <note>original: *Phœbi tripode*. A reference to the three-legged stool of the Pythia at Delphi, symbolizing prophetic truth and divine wisdom.</note>; we who are bond-servants to <term>Christian Philosophy</term><note>A term often used by Renaissance and early modern scholars to describe the integration of classical ethics with Christian theology.</note> are all moved by them. We must always hold a greater regard for eternal things than for earthly ones. The things of the earth and of time are to be regarded as the least significant. If this is so, we must certainly strive—with all the mental effort we can muster and all the diligence we can achieve—not to be separated from those whose proper lot it is to enjoy a blessed and everlasting life. Anyone who wishes to accomplish this (and all who love themselves and wish to live in harmony with nature must wish it) will never allow themselves to pursue the very things they believe to be ruinous to others.

->For it would truly be a most mournful thing,<-

That any philosopher should reach such a point of recklessness and madness that, for the sake of a moment of shadowy and imaginary <term>little joy</term><note>The author uses a series of Latin diminutives (*gaudiolum, voluptatula, delectatiuncula*) to emphasize how small and pathetic worldly sins are compared to the vastness of eternity.</note>, he does not fear to subject himself, knowingly and willingly, to the most bitter tortures. He does not dread exchanging lasting goods for a fleeting little pleasure, nor does he fear being cast headlong into the abyss of all miseries for a passing delight that is barely even tasted. For the sake of a single disordered <term>little thought</term>, he does not shudder at being tortured forever in timeless fire. *Who would not weep for such a fate?* To be excluded from eternal joys for the sake of a momentary little delight—*Who, in telling such things, could refrain from* <note>The text ends mid-sentence. The catchword "lacry-" (from the Latin *lacrymis*) indicates the full quote is from Virgil's *Aeneid*: "Who, in telling such things, could refrain from tears?"</note>

...destined for the uses and delights [of others]; but as soon as the age has crashed into them, and they are thrown into the fire and reduced to ashes, who, I ask, can distinguish the bramble from the cedar, the broom-bush from the myrtle, or the sacred laurels from the wild heath? Who now of such slack and base judgment would deny that this world—this abyss of tumults and assaults—can be called a forest in the same way, and men indeed can be called plants? According to the old saying of our Divine Magician <note>original: *Theomagus*. This likely refers to a Hermetic or Neoplatonic philosopher who views the world through a spiritual-magical lens.</note>: *Man is an inverted tree*;

->And man is indeed called a turned-about little plant,<-

Since just as a tree has its roots in the ground, so man has his roots on high—that is, his hair, which veils the citadel of the whole body, namely the head <note>The "Inverted Tree" (*arbor inversa*) is a classic philosophical metaphor. It suggests that while plants draw nutrients from the earth, humans draw their life and reason from the heavens (the "roots" in the brain/head).</note>. And indeed, as long as this grove flourishes, it is marked by varied colors; for these can be discerned from the "leaves" of their words. Some men are indeed slow and dull; others are eloquent and articulate; some are even Philosophers, craftsmen, or makers of rarities. These can be known by their "flowers," for some are beautiful and others deformed, and the manner of growth is not the same for all. Finally, others can be distinguished by their "fruits"—that is, by their heroic works or deeds. Some we see are spirited and noble; others wealthy; others still fearful and timid, daring to attempt nothing because of their poverty. But as soon as that grim and violent Fury, Death <note>original: *Magæra mors*. Megaera was one of the Furies of Greek myth, usually representing jealousy or rage; here she personifies the violent "cutting down" of life.</note>, begins to make her incision and hurls the darts of her wrath at them, reducing them all to dust and rot, no further distinction is observed. All undergo an equal lot, and no mention is then made of any difference:

->But all are hewn alike by the same measuring-line.<-

Choose then, if you can, the heads which you once saw crowned with golden diadems; pick out then, if you are able, the corpses of bodies once covered in purple and scarlet. Pick out, I say, the tongues of such excellent philosophers, of such eloquent Orators of old. Point out then the faces <note>original: *tronias*. Likely referring to the features, masks, or countenances of the individuals.</note> of the lovely Nymphs, the "Dianas" and "Helens" <note>References to the goddess Diana and Helen of Troy, used here as archetypes of supreme female beauty.</note>, for whose adornment the gems of the East and all the groves of Arabia...

> Shaking the shacks of the poor and royal halls with an equal roar, 
> Leveling the crown and the diadem alike;

For Death is great, powerful, and terrible; she is no respecter of persons and accepts no bribes. She holds the poor and the rich in the same regard. Just as a cloth merchant measures out both fine silk and coarse linen with the same yardstick <note>original: *ulna*. An "ell" or yard-length used for measuring fabric.</note>, so too does she drag the master and the servant to the very same mill <note>original: *pistrinum*. Death by no means tolerates modest manners; she shows herself no kinder to Barons, Counts, Princes, Dukes, Kings, or Emperors than to the lowest of peasants or beggars. Indeed, she strikes with the same foot the peoples hardened by Arctic cold and those scorched by the sun in closer proximity—

> Those whom the rising sun sees, and those whom Phoebus <note>The sun personified as a god.</note> sees hidden in the sea,
> Those over whom the glowing axis wanders with a short or long beam.
> This is the law; here comes the King, and here the flock: here is the first and the last rank.
> This way is evil, but this mournful path must be trodden by all;

> Codrus <note>A traditional name in Latin poetry for a typical poor man.</note> enters the underworld alongside the wealthy Crassus <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus, a Roman general and politician famous for his immense wealth.</note>.

Just as, therefore, in a dense-leaved and diverse grove—as long as it flourishes—we behold very different kinds of trees: acorn-bearing oaks, shade-giving beeches, knotty junipers, prickly hollies, sublimely swaying Poplars, and the ever-blooming, bristling pines, and other trees, infinite in both size and number, and manifold in color and vigor. Some are prized for their flowers, some for their leaves, and others for their fruits; among which some are common and lowly, while others are indeed unique and noble—

<header>PRELUDE</header>

...were not sufficient; then cast away those cheeks, which once consumed so much antimony <note>original: *stibii*. A black mineral used as eyeliner since antiquity.</note>, myrrh oil <note>original: *stactes*</note>, mercury sublimate <note>original: *sublimati*. A toxic mercury compound used to whiten the skin.</note>, and purple rouge <note>original: *purpurissæ*</note>: then identify, just once, that beautiful Juno <note>A reference to a woman as beautiful as the queen of the Roman gods.</note>, whose elegance drew everyone into admiration and envy, for whom so many suitors perished, and who was always weighted with gems, stiff with gold, and covered in fine linen.

On this occasion, it pleased the Cynic philosopher <note>Diogenes of Sinope, known for his eccentric behavior and rejection of social status.</note>, having once become playful, to mock the pride of Alexander the Great: for as the latter walked past a certain temple, Diogenes was rummaging through a graveyard in the ossuaries of the dead among the skulls; and he was contemplating now one, now another; now having seized one he threw it away, now he seized another. Alexander, observing him, asked what he, a living man, was doing there among the dead? The satirical philosopher replied that he was searching for the skull of Philip of Macedon, Alexander's father, but so far had been unable to find it, because there was no distinction among them.

For just as various kinds of herbs and flowers live and flourish in sunny places during the fine springtime—how great is the diversity of colors, brilliance, and scents? How great the variety in width and length? How great the inequality in strength and greenness? But as soon as the reaper has cast in his scythe, and the flowers and herbs are cut down to the earth, no further distinction is recognized; rather, all have undergone the same fate together, the great and the small, the beautiful no differently than the lowly. Is not this world, under the monarchy of death, now like some meadow or garden? In which men perform the role of flowers and herbs; yet all these differ and stand apart from one another in size, and are unequal in honors and fortunes: indeed, as soon as the Gorgon-like Libitina <note>original: *Gorgonia Libitina*. Libitina was the Roman goddess of funerals; "Gorgon-like" emphasizes her terrifying, unavoidable nature.</note> has cast in her sickle, all very quickly become equal and the same:

->For death levels all things with a swift, merciless scythe,<-
->It is fated to die; death spares no honor,<-
->The weak and the strong come under the arrows of death,<-
->The great and the small, the rich, the young, and the old,<-
->Trembling death captures, savage death snatches away.<-

# PRELUDE

> No one arrives at it too late, for fate comes in its own time;
> once a person turns toward it, they can never depart.
> What use is it to forestall a harsh and miserable fate?
> All this world’s wandering crowd shall depart
> for the Spirits of the Dead <note>original: *Manes*, the souls of deceased loved ones or ancestral spirits in Roman belief.</note>, and set the sails of silent Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>.
> Everything that the Evening and the Sunrise look upon grows for you;
> spare those yet to come—we are being prepared for you, Libitina <note>The Roman goddess of funerals and burials.</note>.
> Even if you are slow, we ourselves break the threads <note>A reference to the three Fates of mythology, who spin, measure, and cut the thread of human life.</note>;
> the final hour, which gave us life, has taken it away.

Since, therefore, there is said to be such a great necessity for this "end" in natural matters that physicists do not hesitate to establish it as the primary thing in every situation—for although the end is the last thing in the execution of a task, it is the first in intention and in the mind—it is necessary that death, being the limit and final line of all things, should be first in all our actions and hold the chief place in all our works. Just as a sailor, while steering a ship through the dangers of the waves, sits in the stern <note>The rear part of the ship; the author is arguing that one must look to the "end" (the back) to steer the "front."</note> which is the furthest part of the vessel, so it is for the <term>Philomagus</term> <note>A "lover of magic" or "seeker of hidden wisdom," modeled on the word "philosopher."</note> who sails the ocean of this world's most hidden difficulties. To direct the ship of his life and his station rightly and dutifully, he must not put his trust in the prow <note>The front of the ship.</note> or the status of his office—admiring his own privileges because he was chosen for secret knowledge before others. For can the clay boast about itself, or say "Aha!" to the other vessels because it was spun on the potter's wheel into a cup of a more beautiful shape? Nor should he trust in the rigging <note>original: *anquina*, a technical term for the rope that fastens a yardarm to a mast.</note>, flattering himself in the middle of his "summer," counting his honors, dignities, and the abundance of his riches; rather, he should sit in the stern, recalling to mind the night of death and the final things.

This, this is what the prince of intellect and learning, Plato—whom I am commanded to call divine, most wise, most holy, and the Homer of the seekers of wisdom—used to say: namely, that the prudent and wise establish for themselves a school in which nothing else is taught but the brevity of life and the swiftness of death.

[continued from previous page] ...is concerned with it, and that the meditation upon death is a certain type of true and upright philosophy. But the dull and the foolish establish an "Academy of Oblivion" <note>A metaphorical school where people learn to forget their mortality.</note> because they never remember Libitina <note>The Roman goddess of funerals and burials.</note> or the final things, and they ponder extending their years at all times. 

For it is well known that the wise, the simple, and those who strive for virtue and wisdom die gradually while living; whereas the wicked, the haughty, and the nefarious live by dying, and by always promising themselves more life, they trample death underfoot. Clearly, therefore, it now becomes known that he who forms and devotes his mind to the studies of this gymnasium <note>original: *palæstra*; a place of training or competition, here referring to the school of life or the study of death.</note> ought to be greedy for nothing other than holy wisdom alone.

> Though you may be powerful in houses and vast lands,
> your empty shadow will carry nothing to its Spirits <note>original: *Manibus* (Manes), the spirits of the dead or ancestral souls.</note>.

All things will remain here, for all your heirs; and whatever you, as a private citizen, could desire in this life, you will enter a vile and narrow tomb.

> Carrying no riches to the waves of Acheron <note>A river in the underworld in Greek mythology.</note>,
> you will stand naked on the tragic shore of Cocytus <note>The "river of wailing" in the underworld.</note>.

Kings, the powerful, Princes, and the wealthy are gods only while on the earth. Hence the true lover of wisdom—even if they have only tasted wisdom with "the fibers of their lips" <note>original: *fibris labris*; a Latin idiom meaning to have only a superficial or slight taste of something.</note>, as they say—never goes after gold or the vain breeze of honor. Instead, they cling to the "Philosophers' Calm" <note>original: *Galena*; a term for a calm sea, used here metaphorically for the peace found in philosophical study.</note> which, according to the sound of Holy Scripture, is nature’s treasury. Indeed, having attained the value not just of one empire, but of all things and the whole world, the wise man can carry it in his own small pockets, and as if he were the Master of the entire machinery of the world, he possesses everything, and can rightly say: *I carry all my things with me* <note>original: *mecum omnia porto mea*; a famous Stoic saying attributed to Bias of Priene, meaning that true wealth is internal.</note>.

> Our riches shall fear no thief;
> let others mock, let the fool mix his jests.

For what use is it, according to the Writer of Proverbs <note>original: *Paræmiographo*; referring to the author of the biblical Book of Proverbs (Solomon).</note>, for a fool to have riches when he cannot buy wisdom?

### §. 4.

...isdom. Toward **wisdom** herself, therefore, I have committed myself to you in the theater of this prelude—provided that my Evangelus <note>Likely referring to a patron or a "bringer of good news," personified here as a divine guide.</note> does not disdain to direct my small boat through this stormy sea with his most august breath of help—to apply the spur and to point out the rare and clear path toward the highest honors and works. Behold, indeed, **Socrates**, the god and glory of philosophers, shines a torch for you from the open valley; having obtained human and divine <term>Adorea</term> <note>original: *Adoream*; an ancient Roman term for glory or a reward for valor, originally a gift of grain.</note>, and known by fame even above the heavens, he exhorts us to follow him in this way:

For once, when he had encountered the young **Xenophon** in the street on a certain day—as is noted in the *Apophthegms* <note>A collection of concise sayings or anecdotes.</note>—Socrates gazed upon him. Noticing from his <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The historical practice of judging a person's character or intellectual capacity from their facial features.</note> that his nature was steady and inclined toward the acquisition of wisdom, Socrates extended the staff he carried on his shoulders and immediately detained him. He uttered such words as: "Hey there, young man, where do you come from? Where is bread sold? Where are fish sold?" and other things of that sort. When the physiognomist <note>Socrates is being characterized here by his ability to read Xenophon's character.</note> perceived that the youth had responded to the questions in an orderly fashion, he immediately added: "In what place, then, do the wise live?" The youth gave his answer: he did not know. Then Socrates said: "Follow me, and I will instruct you; for it is shameful for you to be ignorant of that which is most worthy of being known, after you already know other things that are less necessary." Truly, a lesson worthy of a Socratic mouth! But adapting that story to my own purpose, I say:

That merchant of wisdom, my Mercury, constantly runs through the streets with his <term>caduceus</term> <note>The traditional staff carried by the messenger god Mercury, featuring two snakes winding around a winged staff.</note>. If he were to meet you and ask about nuts and similar trifles <note>original: *affaniis*; refers to nonsense, petty things, or children's games.</note> and less necessary things, you would undoubtedly know how to respond immediately and with the greatest expertise. However, if he began to inquire of any one of you about things most vital to know—namely, where in the world a simple and upright philosophy might be found, or where the records containing it might lie hidden:

> Surely the water would fail you <note>original: *aqua hæreret vobis*; a Latin idiom meaning to be "stuck" or at a total loss for words.</note>, and your tongue would stick to your palate;
> You would stand mute with a dull and strained brain,

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>original: *Prosimetricum*; a literary work that alternates between prose and verse.</note>

And indeed, under my leadership—so that I might not be stubborn in this regard (since so many diverse and fraudulent little refuges have been sent out and filled everywhere, to our grief)—you and the entire court might cry out as you pass by, *“O, what a lamentable art! And oh, our most desperate affairs!”* But look, rejoice! Be of good courage still! To me has been entrusted the task of **investigating nature in the Socratic manner** for you, *you gilded offspring of wisdom—not money-coiners, nor sophists suffering from a hunger for gold. Follow me;*

->*I will lead you into a broad Land, and one greatly approved,*<-

I shall be your future forerunner, leader, and teacher. You who strive with me to enter the *Apolline* <note>Referring to Apollo, the god of light, healing, and prophecy.</note> sanctuaries, to ascend like a lofty eagle to the highest **Cedar of Lebanon**, and to climb the **Golden-born Atlas of Alchemy** <term>Chrysogonum Alchymiæ Athlanta</term> <note>Atlas was the Titan who held up the heavens; here, he represents a monumental figure or pillar of alchemical knowledge.</note>; hasten to this sanctuary and oaken citadel, more impregnable than the **Roman Capitol**. Do so as if intoxicated by the harmonious tone of the *harp-players* <note>original: *Spaltriarum*; likely a misspelling of *psaltriarum*, referring to female lute or harp players.</note> in this music hall, or by a broth from the cup of *Lethe* <note>The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology; here used metaphorically for a transformative state of mind.</note>. I cherish with the greatest desire—indeed, I embrace with both arms—these **magical seeds** <note>original: *Magicos coccos*; 'coccos' refers to grains or berries used for dye, here symbolizing the 'seeds' of wisdom.</note> unearthed from the chaff, these vintages of my harvest scraped away from the scraps and weeds; these small "Night-fruits," I say, or the **Phrygian** <note>original: *Phrygios*; the Phrygian style was often associated with complexity, religious ecstasy, or intricate embroidery.</note> offspring of my spirit and intellect, approved by the solemn and **Ambrosial** <note>Divine or heavenly.</note> choir.

For we are not those to whom nothing seems to be true, but rather those who say that certain falsehoods are joined to all truths with such similarity and such entanglement that there is no certain mark for judging or assenting to them. For the inquiries of the Philosophers, because they are entirely thorny and hieroglyphic, and obscured by the dark complexities of riddles and opinions, cannot be understood through themselves except by a divinely illuminated man, or an **Adept philosopher** <term>Adepto philosopho</term> <note>A term in alchemy for one who has successfully achieved the 'Great Work' or transformation of base matter into gold/spirit.</note>.

> *If only it will please you to listen to me a little while,*
> *From the very cradle of budding Magic* <term>Magiæ</term> <note>In this context, 'Magic' refers to 'Natural Magic' or the deep study of the hidden laws of nature.</note>
> *(If one may use small examples in great matters)*
> *I will trace the matter deeper for you, and provide a model:*
> *I shall sing of facts, yet there will be those who say I have made them up,*

# PRELUDE

### §. 4.

Therefore, for that very reason, I have taken it upon myself in the theater of this prelude to spur you on—provided that my Evangelist <note>original: *Evangelus*; likely referring to a guiding spirit, a personification of "good news," or divine inspiration</note> does not disdain to direct my small boat through this stormy sea with the most august breath of his help—and to point out the rare and clear path to the highest honors and riches. Behold, Socrates, the God and ornament of philosophers, shines a torch for you from the open valley; having attained both human and divine Glory <note>original: *Adorea*; a Roman term for military reward or renown</note>, and known by fame even above the heavens, he exhorts us to follow him thus:

For on a certain day, having once met the youth *Xenophon* in the street, as is noted in the *Apophthegms* <note>A collection of concise sayings or anecdotes, often those of ancient philosophers.</note>, Socrates gazed upon him. Observing his **physiognomy** <term>physiognomia</term> <note>The historical practice of assessing a person's character or mental qualities from their outward appearance, especially the face.</note>, he realized that the young man's nature was perfectly suited and inclined toward acquiring wisdom. Extending the staff he carried on his shoulder, he immediately stopped him, speaking these words: "Hey there, young man, where do you come from? Where is bread sold? Where are fish sold?" and other things of that kind. When the "face-reader" <note>Referring to Socrates</note> saw that the boy had answered his questions in an orderly fashion, he immediately added: "And in what places do the wise dwell?" The youth replied that he did not know. Then Socrates said: "Follow me, and I will instruct you, for it is shameful for you to be ignorant of that which is most worthy of being known, after you have learned other less necessary things." Truly, a teaching worthy of the Socratic mouth! But adapting that to my own purpose, I say:

That merchant of wisdom, my Mercury, runs constantly through the streets with his **caduceus** <note>The winged staff entwined with two snakes, carried by the god Mercury as a symbol of commerce and secret knowledge.</note>. If he were to ask you who cross his path even once about trivialities <note>original: *nucibus*; literally "nuts," a common Latin metaphor for children's games or unimportant trifles.</note> and such nonsense and less necessary things, you would undoubtedly know how to answer him most exquisitely at once. However, if he began to inquire of any one of you about the most vital knowledge—namely, where in the world simple and upright philosophy, or the records containing it, might be hidden or found:

Then truly **you would be at a total loss** <note>original: *aqua hæreret vobis*; literally "the water would stick to you," a Latin idiom for being stuck or paralyzed by a problem</note>, your tongue would stick to your palate, and you would stand mute, empty and paralyzed in your brain.

# PROSIMETRICUM 57

And indeed, under my guidance—lest I should be stubborn in this regard (since, alas, so many multiform and deceptive little retreats <note>original: *receptiunculis*; small hiding places or intellectual refuges</note> have been sent out and filled everywhere)—since you might cry out that you and the whole assembly could pass this by; Oh, then, what a deplorable art! And oh, how desperate are our affairs! But look, hurrah! Still honored, for my sake and yours, *golden offspring of wisdom*, you who are not money-grubbers nor sophists suffering from a hunger for gold. It has been entrusted to me to philosophize in the **Socratic manner** <term>Socraticè physiculare</term> <note>To study natural philosophy or the "physics" of the world using the questioning, moral method of Socrates.</note>; follow me:

->I will lead you into a broad land, and one greatly approved,<-

I shall be your herald, leader, and teacher—you who strive with me to enter the shrines of **Apollo** <note>The Greek god of light, prophecy, and the arts, often associated with the "light" of alchemical revelation.</note>, to ascend like a sublime eagle to the highest Cedar of Lebanon, and to climb the Golden-born Atlas of **Alchemy** <term>Alchymia</term>. Hurry to this sanctuary and this oaken citadel—more impregnable than the Roman Capitol—as if intoxicated by the harmonic tone of the harpists <note>original: *Spaltriarum*, likely a misspelling of *Psaltriarum*; female musicians playing stringed instruments.</note> of this Music Hall, as though by a broth from the cup of **Lethe** <note>The mythological river of forgetfulness; here suggesting a cleansing of prior false knowledge.</note>. I contemplate with some desire—nay, I embrace with both arms—these Magic kernels <note>original: *coccos*; berries or grains of truth.</note> unearthed from the chaff, these vintages of my harvest carved out from the scraps and weeds; these "little fruits of the night," I say, or these Phrygian offspring <note>original: *Phrygios fœtusculos*; "Phrygian" refers to an ancient style of music or mystery rites, often considered ecstatic or profound.</note> of my genius and talent, approved by the solemn and heavenly choir.

For we are not like those "smokes" <note>insubstantial or deceptive people</note> to whom nothing seems true, but rather like those who say that certain falsehoods are joined to all truths, with such similarity and such rivalry that there is no certain mark within them for judging or giving assent. For the inquiries of the Philosophers, because they are deeply rugged and hieroglyphic, and obscured by the dark perplexities of riddles and opinions, cannot be understood through themselves except by a divinely illuminated man, or an **Adept philosopher** <term>Adeptus philosophus</term>.

# PRELUDE

I am gathering ancient tokens <note>original: *symbolas*; can mean contributions to a shared feast or symbolic emblems</note> and the "song of the cuckoo" <note>An idiom possibly referring to repetitive or well-known alchemical truths</note> into these new centuries <note>Books or collections organized into sets of one hundred.</note>.

Form a round circle from the man and the woman, and from that extract a square, and from the square a triangle, and from the triangle likewise make a cyclic circle, and you will have completed the **Great Work** <term>magisterium</term> <note>The "Mastery" or completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. For this artifice is a thing whose head is of **Carbuncle** <note>A deep red gemstone, likely signifying the "Red Stage" or Rubedo.</note>, eyes of **Jet** <note>Black stone, signifying the "Black Stage" or Nigredo.</note>, and feet of **Diamond** <note>Signifying the fixed, indestructible nature of the final Stone.</note>; and a thousand other things of that kind occur everywhere. Of these, this present work is not the last, but rather a supplement to the others (if we may walk in the **shoes of the Stoics** <note>original: *Stoicorum soccis*; an idiom for using the rigorous, concise logic associated with Stoic philosophers</note>, who are accustomed to tighten their arguments to the very summit).

Purple-haired **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, representing the Sun or Alchemical Gold.</note> begat a little son in the lower world, whom he gave to the **Son of Maya** <note>Mercury, the messenger god.</note> and to **Mulciber** <note>Vulcan, the god of fire/blacksmithing.</note> to be nursed, and to the **Son of Philyra** <note>Chiron the Centaur, tutor to heroes, representing the guidance of nature.</note> to be instructed. First, we command all posterity to take this up with the blood of the **Eastern Lion** <note>A symbol for the "Fixed" sulfur or a specific mineral acid.</note> (which was conceived upon the continent from celestial dew and earthly warmth, and brought forth in the streams of the Mediterranean Sea by **Lucina** <note>Goddess of childbirth.</note>, with **Aeolus** <note>God of the winds.</note> and the **Earth-shaker** <note>original: *Ennosigæóque*; a title for Neptune/Poseidon.</note> acting as midwives). For this exhibits the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <term>Mercurium Philosophorum</term>, that secret spirit of the world, and the **Syrian dew** <note>A metaphor for the "universal solvent" or the pure moisture of the prima materia.</note>, because its spirit has surrounded the face of the earth, and from its inner parts the twisted serpent shall be led forth.

Afterwards, separate it from the useless rot of **Amphitrite’s** <note>A sea goddess, here representing the "salty" impurities or the bitter sea-water of the initial matter.</note> saltiness, and purge it with lye—not indeed made from beech or oak ashes and their salt, but from a metallic salt, which is more durable than the rest. Nor should you use common water, but rather that which is sought from the spring of **Parnassus** (which exists at the peak of the mountain, separate from the nature of other springs, born from the **hoof of the Medusan steed** <note>Pegasus, whose hoof-strike created the Hippocrene spring, a source of poetic and alchemical inspiration.</note>). This water, under the **Trojan youth** <note>original: *Iliade*; referring to Ganymede, the cupbearer of the gods, often associated with the zodiac sign Aquarius and the process of distillation.</note>, has turned into ice and crystal, inasmuch as it is made of subtler parts than stagnant or marshy waters. Because of this, it can penetrate more deeply into the innermost parts of the black and squalid "philosophical body" to wash it clean.

Finally, cherish the **Goddess who bears twins** <note>Latona/Leto, mother of the sun and moon.</note> while she is pregnant, with a gentle warmth and a benign fire for so long, until, through the wheels of the elementary orb, by a stratagem of art and nature, the **flower of the Sun** <note>original: *Cynthii flos*; Apollo's flower.</note> and the **dew of the Moon** <note>original: *Cynthiæ ros*; Diana's dew.</note> rise up together into a certain undivided little body in the form of a **hexagon** <note>The six-pointed star, representing the union of Fire and Water.</note>.

...acle, and a doubling of stupendous powers, they brought forth a male and female child. You must then immediately and separately nourish both of them decently, according to the specific nature of each, whitening them with the **soap of the wise** <note>original: *sapone sapientum*; a metaphorical term for an alchemical purifying agent</note>, and reviving them with **Virgin’s Milk** <note>original: *lactéque Virgineo*; likely referring to a white mercurial solvent or a specific stage of distillation</note> until they reach a solid age. Then, betroth them to their brother **Paean** <note>An epithet for Apollo, representing the Sun or Alchemical Gold</note>, in a robe of **Cinnabar** <note>A bright red mineral (mercury sulfide), signifying the "Red Stage" or Rubedo</note> and with a rough **Coralline** retinue; join them by the wedding torch. This Phoenix is able not only to perpetuate life for itself, but also to prolong human health and truly recall the **Golden Age**.

By Hercules, what a deep sea, so tangled and unswimmable even for the most learned! What whirlpools and abysses are here! Oh, what depth!

->Here is the Charybdis of Zancle, Scylla, and the rocks of Caphareus,<-
->Here are the Cyclopean crags with a thousand winding paths;<-

And I know not what is more inextricable than this labyrinth itself. How can the understanding of beginners cross over such rising waves of entanglement, where even the mind of an **Oedipus** <note>The mythological hero famous for solving the riddle of the Sphinx</note> is almost suspended and halted? How, I ask, shall the sails of mortal intelligence be spread, where even immortal things are weakened and shrunken? Ah, the labor of all labors, the highest and last of **Hercules’** <note>original: *Alcidæorum*; referring to Alcides, another name for Hercules</note> trials! Oh, the steep cliffs! Oh, the shipwrecking bends! Oh, the labyrinthine windings of imperceptible circumlocution! Everything in this great monument is subject to crosses, snares, and misfortunes; nothing here is intelligible, but in every direction we see the inhospitable peaks of **Dindymus** <note>A mountain range in Phrygia associated with the goddess Cybele</note>. Oh, how many altars of **hyperbaton** <note>A rhetorical device where words are placed out of their natural order to create confusion or emphasis</note>, how many images and echoes! Alas, how many halls are built in this courtyard, how many emblems marked here and there with painted and fictitious letters! *Who will read these things?* Oh, what a knot! Truly more indissoluble than the **Gordian knot** itself; by Pollux, it is difficult and entirely like the **Herculean knot**, in which neither beginning nor end appeared—just as the Gordian knot is said to have been, which, when **Alexander** could not untie it, he cut with his sword. Experience...

# PRELUDE

...highly intricate, or by Argus of the hundred eyes, and even by the Delphic sword <note>original: *rhomphæâ Delphicâ*; an ancient term for a multipurpose tool or a divine weapon, suggesting a "silver bullet" solution</note>, to dissolve these bonds of Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcania hæc vincula*; an allusion to the unbreakable net Vulcan used to trap Mars and Venus; here meaning the "knots" of alchemical secrets</note> and these riddles. So much are the mysteries of secrets wrapped in fabulous and winding sentences and words by those authors; the books of the philosophers are full, and nearly all their pages are stuffed with allegories and stretched with parables, with such a great abundance of metaphors that nothing could be more overloaded.

I, therefore, lest anyone brand me with a similar mark of envy <note>The "envy of the philosophers" (*invidia philosophorum*) was a common trope where authors claimed others hid the truth out of spite or greed</note>, will not entangle the Decrees of the Past Magicians of Philosophy with such repetitions of circumlocutions and involvements. Instead, having broken the Pythagorean silence <note>The five-year vow of silence required of students in the school of Pythagoras</note>, I will declare the whole matter to honest and chosen disciples in a few plain words.

We shall therefore fulfill this neglected task with the support of no one, but, as they say, by our own Mars <note>original: *Marte proprio*; an idiom meaning by one's own strength or individual effort</note>; for nothing concerning this specific part has been strictly published that met my approval among those things that have come into my hands. Since, therefore, some appearance of utility has newly presented itself, I felt it necessary to be moved; nor indeed have we undertaken the defense of things entirely abandoned; for arts do not perish with the death of men, but only desire the light of an Author. 

You shall therefore receive this <term>little Work of True Magic</term> <note>original: *Orthomagiopusculum*; a Greek-Latin hybrid meaning a small work on "straight" or "true" magic</note> worked upon during these now-shorter nights, since that larger duty of longer vigils shall be forged later under our auspices; and you will rejoice in this opened treasury <note>original: *cimeliarchio*; a repository for valuables or a museum cabinet</note> of my verses, which I have composed as fate allowed. Since those things which are treated scatteredly by others—rare and excellent as they may be—I shall transfer all alike to this, my metrical and concise style of writing. 

Indeed, it will seem incredible how many great things I intend to sing here to you: to prophesy the chief point of human desires, and to offer the most hidden treasure of all the secrets of this world, not diffusely, but nakedly and concisely. This shall be, evidently, my rule or certain token, by which you may walk as if guided by a thread. Oh, I shall bring forth to you an elegant <term>love of learning</term> <note>original: *philomathiam*</note>, by which, as if with the jawbone of an ass <note>A biblical reference to Samson (Judges 15), who used this unlikely weapon to defeat his enemies</note>, you will be able to put the Philistines to flight and lift the gates of Gaza. I intend to provide, as I believe, a most brilliant guarantee of my promise; therefore, it is fitting that you grant me such faith in your attention as I here offer you a strong introduction to science.

# PROSE-POETRY <note>original: *Prosimetricum*; a work written in a combination of prose and verse</note>

Nevertheless, to enjoy these golden feasts, it is necessary above all else for those who, with the highest glory, intend to devote their efforts to this pleasant dust and to take an equal risk with fortune, to act as leaders <note>original: *Archimandritas*; literally "heads of the fold" or abbots, here used to mean those who take a leading, disciplined role</note>. They must not slacken their pace like Diogenes running in the stadium. It is told that even amidst the business of public disturbance, having cast aside his little cloak and girded himself, Diogenes began to roll his tub—his versatile roof—to and fro with great ardor. In this tub, like a snail <note>original: *domiporta*; literally "house-carrier," a poetic name for a snail</note>, he was perpetually enclosed, living a life of the mind rather than the body, much like a mind fixed to a wooden heaven. Here he sweated; here he was busily occupied in leisure; here, by acting much, he achieved nothing, yet all in such serious play that within the tub, as if within the Trojan horse, the safety of Greece seemed to be contained. Indeed, many citizens began to marvel and feel indignant at this, and when they finally asked him what he intended by it, he explained: "I am moving my tub so that, while everyone else is busy, you might see me being active as well; *for he who does nothing, seems to be nothing.*"

Truly a magnificent and divine saying of Diogenes! Through it, that clever philosopher seems to have wished to indicate clearly that even if nature did not produce "Anacharsides" <note>Followers of Anacharsis, a Scythian philosopher known for his plain-spoken wisdom and rigorous lifestyle</note> at home, many are still capable of becoming, through much art and exercise, even more Hermetic than the Egyptian Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> themselves, and more Platonic than the very Platos. Such men, broken by no labors and sparing no expense, felt no regret for any difficult deed, provided that their undertaking might succeed according to their heart's desire; such a great fire of this philosophy had risen within them.

Three animals are found (says Solomon, the wisest of the sons of Adam, since he had obtained wisdom from above) which are indeed the smallest living things on earth, yet are wiser than the wise: the ant, the rabbit, the locust, and the lizard <note>original: *stellio*; a spotted lizard or newt</note>. Concerning this last one, a small verse exists: *the lizard leans on its hands, and stays in palaces.*

However, the commentators on the Proverbs of Solomon hold from the Hebrew: *the spider leans on its hands*; and they form this sense: The spider, with the busy webs of its delicate little hands, prepares its own livelihood; nor, as the writer of the Proverbs says, should we overlook these four...

<header># PRELUDE</header>

...indeed, these animals can provoke even the most prudent men to a contest of skill, and judge the ignorance of even those who wish to both appear and be heard as the wisest; *and they themselves are wiser than the wise.*

In what does the wisdom and art of the spider—that cheap and slender little beast—reside? It lies in this: that although she dwells in the halls of Kings, she makes no use at all of the luxury around her to prolong her life for many years through the labor of her hands. Instead, she might seem to invite a judgment of imprudence; for if she lives in the houses of Kings, where there is such a copy of food and every abundance of provisions, she nevertheless always, with such care, such diligence, and such toil, weaves nets within the workshop of her own viscera <note>The author uses "viscera" to highlight that the spider produces the silk from her own body, just as the alchemist must find the "matter" within a single source.</note> to catch unwary flies, so that she may preserve her own life with their blood. If this is so, why did the wisest <term>Paræmiastes</term> <note>The "Paræmiastes" refers to Solomon, the traditional author of the biblical Book of Proverbs (see Proverbs 30:28).</note> attribute such a great title of wisdom to this little animal? This little creature most perfectly deserves the august praise of the prudent and the glorious epithet of "wise" because of her manner of acting, by which she fruitfully teaches and instructs the "Wise-Chemists" <note>original: *Sophochymicos*</note> in the ways of <term>Spagiria</term> <note>Spagiria (Spagyrics) is a term for alchemy, specifically the art of separating and recombining elements to reach a purified state.</note>.

> *For the spider leans upon her hands, and dwells in the houses of Kings:* <note>A translation of Proverbs 30:28.</note> as if to say: what does it matter if the palace abounds in delicacies, flows with delights, and has storerooms where one thing overflows into another, if I do not seek a living for myself with my own hands? I would promised myself nothing from that luxury of all the court's resources if I did not eviscerate myself <note>In this context, to "eviscerate oneself" means to pour out one's internal substance and energy into the work.</note>, and spend every night and day drawing threads, weaving nets, and hunting flies, seeking nourishment for myself through equal labors and cares.

This very thing, by a certain silent example of its own nature, calls out to and teaches the *industrious ones consecrated to Golden wisdom*. A Pygmy or a Satyr compared to a Giant; a man of Chios compared to one of Cos; Dares against Entellus <note>Dares and Entellus were two boxers in Virgil's *Aeneid*; the younger Dares was defeated by the aged but powerful Entellus.</note>: what indeed can a little lamb do among wolves, or a small boy hiding in the midst of great hounds, if a mother or nurse does not protect him? Therefore, I shall strive to touch only upon mechanical matters, and those whispered through <term>Hermogenes</term> <note>Hermogenes may refer to the Greek god of eloquence and secret knowledge (Hermes), or a specific rhetorical authority; here it implies a messenger of secret wisdom.</note>, by joining our smallness to the sublimity of the Great Giants who came before us. I would be never-ending if I wished to match every single thing that can be sketched in the vast estate of this subject matter with the clear truth of the thing and experience, according to the sense of Authors and their interpreters. It shall suffice that we pursue our purpose: to more fully untangle those fated and inner lines which the finger of God has inscribed upon the Earth.

For it is no concern of mine to know whether fish breathe under water or not, or whether the herring or the whale is King of the scaly flock. Or whether the sun is a fiery stone or instead a chariot of fire? And whether there is a true face in the lamp of the moon, and why? And six hundred other such things, from which there is no fruit but labor and affliction of the spirit <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:14, suggesting the vanity of trivial pursuits.</note>, and the mere waste of precious time. > The loss of things is nothing, but the loss of days is greater,
> Property can always come to the aid of property, but nothing can aid lost days.

<header>PRELUDE</header>

Thales of Miletus, a man unique and quite distinguished among the Seven Sages of Greece, was once absorbed in contemplation. Having seized with his eyes the pinnacle of the universe <note>original: *cosmocolophonem*; a rare term implying the summit or finishing touch of the world's order.</note>, the winding paths of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and that flashing army of the stars, he looked quite intently to foretell something of the future from them, provided the Gods might give a sign. While doing so, he fell into a muddy pit that lay before his feet—as he had moved them quite carelessly— and, having broken his shins, as the saying goes, he returned home as a laughingstock. For this reason, he was deservedly mocked by a certain sharp-tongued old woman standing by, who said he rightly deserved to suffer this: that while he was senseless to what lay right at his feet, he wished to explore the celestial realms. Is it pleasing to hear how the Swift Poetaster <note>likely referring to a minor poet or a specific satirical style</note> likewise sharply thins out that tale?

> Perhaps while Thales observes the fires of the high heavens,
> With a stumbling foot <note>original: *pede cæcultante*; literally "a blinding foot," implying one that cannot see where it goes.</note>, he slips into a muddy pit;
> When a certain lowly woman saw him fallen there,
> Who by chance had come to fetch water with her vessel,
> Thus insulting him from above, when she reached him,
> She addressed that head with a mocking, trembling voice:
> "Why, O fool, do you traverse the heavenly stars with your eyes,
> Do you not see enough earthly comforts for yourself?
> And while you strive to predict future fates for others,
> Are you unable to see the ditch that lies before your feet?"

In this way, many "keen-nosed" <note>intellectually arrogant or over-critical</note> men still contemplate the heavens and a thousand trifling subtleties; this one gapes at omens, while that one and another hunger for quarrels over names,

> Another often brawls about a lock of goat’s wool, <note>original: *lana caprina*; a Latin idiom for an argument over something utterly trivial or non-existent (as goats have hair, not wool).</note>
> Armed with trifles he fights, so that, forsooth,
> My word might not be believed first, and what truly pleases me,
> That I might not bark it out sharply, but let him be learned against all;

And meanwhile, they pay no heed to the ditch of errors in which they are continually blind, until at last they are driven to madness as their end; for here, while one more accurately searches out the labors of the stars and the rotations of the heavens,

I say: "Tell me, you who so curiously and scrupulously scrutinize the emptiness of the stars, the wandering paths of the heavens and the planets, and the constellations—how does a beautifully feathered bird come from an egg? And what of that bird for whom iron is a feast? <note>Referring to the ostrich, which in medieval and early modern lore was famously (and incorrectly) believed to eat and digest iron.</note> Why do the hands go numb as soon as the Torpedo fish <note>original: *Narcus* (likely for *narkē*). And why can that numbness be prevented by those carrying something in their hands? If you cannot grasp these and countless other things by chance or instinct, how will you comprehend things above? Can you—who claim for yourself an all-encompassing and 'circular' wisdom <note>original: *sapientiam encycliam*; the root of our word 'encyclopedia.'</note>—answer how the earth, which hangs downward with the swirling mass of its own weight, sustains itself with balanced weight in the midst of the waters? Or how bees weave their honey, spiders their webs, or silkworms their threads? If you do not grasp the works of tiny animals and worms, why do you grant yourself so much as to presume that the most admirable hand of the Divine can be known by you? Truly, such 'glorious' wisdom is of little value; indeed, it differs not much from madness."

# P R E L U D E #

->Led by the guiding star of this heavenly lamp and the ruler of this difficult path, let us hasten in a race toward the very temple of Minerva <note>original: *Tritonia*, a title for the goddess of wisdom, referring to her mythical birth near Lake Tritonis.</note>. Here I desire to follow the industry and experience of the ingenious honey-making bees, which pack their cells with thyme-scented honey gathered from the most excellent and fragrant juice of <term>bee-balm</term> <note>original: *apiastrum*, a plant traditionally favored by bees, often identified as lemon balm.</note> and flowers, collecting it bit by bit, separating the best honey-producing parts from the rancid ones, and handling only what is useful. And so it is for this reason that I have chosen to give a title to these <term>Little Works on True Magic</term> <note>original: *Orthomagiopuscula*.</note>, and decided to present them under the torch of the <term>Alchemical Winnowing Fan</term> <note>original: *ventilabri Chymici*. A winnowing fan is a tool used to separate grain from chaff; here, it symbolizes the process of refining knowledge.</note>.<-

For just as by this instrument worthless things—husks, clippings, scraps, rinds, and thick outer skins—are driven off and cast out, and whatever tastes of the <term>stale wine</term> <note>original: *vappa*, wine that has lost its flavor and become flat.</note> and <term>bitter dregs</term> <note>original: *amurca*, the watery, bitter residue left after pressing olives.</note> of vine-cuttings is thrust out and weeded away, leaving behind the pure, naked kernel and core. In no different way, from this center and heart of the <term>Body of the Adepts</term> <note>original: *Adepti Corporis*.</note>, I have sifted out and utterly eliminated the monstrous, confused, and discordant practices and fabrications—not to say delusions—of many petty masters and false craftsmen. I have retained only the sweet, whole, and essential core of knowledge, purified of all the skins of parables and the layers of metaphors, and brought it together into the storehouse of the triumphant harbor; *for we do not perform the threshing for the sake of the straw, but for the sake of the grain.*

Nevertheless, I do not wish to light this <term>fiery lamp</term> <note>original: *empyria lampas*.</note> in such a way as to suggest that there are no other great and extraordinary wonders than those found here. For I am not so sluggish, nor of such a base mind, dull or shameless, that I could or would want to deny that in all this vast hospitality, there is no study so filled with benefits—which so blesses us and makes us heirs to so many goods and gifts—as that single practice of the <term>Love of Magic</term> <note>original: *Philomagia*.</note>. It is a practice which, like a theater of mysteries and a mirror of secrets, preserves a man as heroic and whole, restores the weak to health, brings to light the hidden things of nature, calms the mind with solid knowledge, and honors and enriches the body with all the treasures of life, and finally to the [Creator...]

For the work which is touched upon here is of such virtue and energy, and is so powerful in its many wonders, that it is kept not in the power of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but in the will of a merciful God. ### PRELUDE

Grant, O God, that these coffers swell with joyful money;
This is the only cry, and this is the only love.
Accordingly, the wise **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BC), the famous Cynic philosopher who lived in a barrel and valued self-sufficiency over possessions.</note> was once asked why gold was so pale? He replied: "Because it has found so many plotters lying in wait for it."

> And the seeds of cares are born from your very skin.

> For all things obey wealth; he who has amassed it
> Shall be famous, brave, just, wise, and even a King.

If you please, step outside and look around the marketplace; whatever is convenient and suitable for human use is all for sale for copper. Enter the workshops, look upon the fairs; whatever is delightful to the eyes, whatever is acceptable to desire—it is all purchasable with money.

->The nostrils are touched by the scent of a greater little profit;<-

# MIXED PROSE AND VERSE
<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>PROSIMETRICUM <note>original: *Prosimetricum*. A literary work composed of a mixture of prose and verse.</note></header>

...destitute of all things, I was at times far more miserable than he <note>Referring to Diogenes the Cynic, mentioned on the previous page.</note>. For while he always had his revolving tub—which was turned about like the leaves of a sun-following plant to face the sun—I, alas, due to my frequent and excessive beggary, was supplied with scarcely a wicker coop <note>original: *porca viminea*. A small enclosure or basket.</note> under which a hen might huddle with her chicks. He had his tunic and a little cloak to wrap around himself, the meager tools of a beggar: a staff and a bread-bag. But I often had none of these. Not only did I not look like Diogenes, but I was poorer than any ragged beggar. After a little while, though "too late like the Phrygians" <note>original: *cum Phrygibus*. Refers to the proverb *Sero sapiunt Phryges* ("The Phrygians learn too late"), suggesting the author only realized his folly after disaster had struck.</note>, I began to groan deeply over my status and my misfortunes. I often struck my empty palms together and shook my feet with uncertain steps; I would scratch first one part of my head and then another, though they did not itch, and with a half-closed mouth, sobbing, I would stammer out I know not what complaints. Weary in the day of my distress, frequently moaning with a sad soul, I cried out to myself:

> Woe is me! Why did I ever learn, or open a book?
> Why did any letter ever linger before my eyes?

"I ask," he said, "for a talent of gold, and then I will satisfy your objection." When he had received the gold, he said: "Do not wonder, O King, because the Philosophers <term>Philosophi; those who love wisdom</term> teach that nothing can ever be lacking to the wise. They say this reasonably, for they are always able, without great difficulty, to find those who may come to the aid of their necessity."

But for one shouting these and similar things, his mouth is ready and remains for remonstrating; for first of all, such times do not appear now.

->The earth now brings forth evil and stingy men,<-
->More truly now all things are done in reverse order,<-
->As much money as each man keeps in his chest,<-
->So much faith he now holds, for he is stripped by the world,<-
->Much fraud now, no faith; the world is turned upside down,<-
->The lowest things are leveled with the highest in this ruined world,<-
->The series, status, and order of things are reversed,<-
->While sincere offspring are postponed for the sake of the wicked, and while<-
->Worthless people are carried through every honor,<-
->The world <term>Mundus</term> is mocked by its own struggle.<-

Today it seems to happen in the world just as in the age of Salmoneus <note>original: *Salmonico*. Salmoneus was a mythological king who tried to imitate the gods; the author uses this to suggest an age of hubris and falsity.</note>, that animals are indeed valued more than the learned and the literate.

->(Everywhere towns worship the dogs, no one the Dianas)<-
<note>Diana was the goddess of the hunt; the author suggests people now value the hunting dogs more than the goddess they serve.</note>

Cooks <term>Coctores</term> are valued more than Doctors <term>Doctores; meaning teachers or learned men</term>; simple Arcadians more than Aristotle; the fickle Glaucuses more than Socrates; buffoons and the bold more than the honest and the modest, because iniquity rules the world <term>Mundum</term>, and hypocrisy commands. The unworthy possess dignities, the ignorant dominate the learned, the wise indeed are ruled by fools, and horses are judged by donkeys. The wicked stand at the summit, vices flourish, virtue is a disgrace; the liars and those skilled in deceptive speech <term>logodædali; literally "word-crafters" or sophists</term> are praised, while truth and honesty <term>honestas</term> are exiled. The wise wait before the doors of the rich, rather than the rich at the door of the wise.

<note>The author uses the image of the greatest philosophers of antiquity acting as lowly servants to a wealthy man to illustrate the degradation of wisdom.</note>

In the house of the wealthy Feaster <term>Epulo; often used to refer to the rich man "Dives" from the biblical parable</term>, the dogs and other beasts were feasting sumptuously, while poor and ragged Lazarus, a most innocent man and God's particular delight, lay dying of hunger before his gate. Indeed, matters are conducted even worse in the house of the World today than they once were in the Feaster's palace; for the cruel, the wicked, and the ungodly—who live in the manner of dogs and beasts—abound in delicacies and delights; they gorge themselves and feast. But the merciful and the servants of God, the poor and the humble, almost perish from hunger and are crushed by extreme necessity. 

Alas, what disorder <term>ataxia; from the Greek for "lack of order"</term> and dysfunction <term>dyspraxia; ill-conduct or mismanagement</term> there is in the world! What abuse, what turmoil, what chaos! *Fortune favors fools* <note>original: *Fortuna favet fatuis*</note>: the unfit gain honors, the dull are elevated and appointed to high dignities, while the genuine and worthy live in infamy and reproach. The wise are rejected and driven from their duties, while the ignorant and unskilled are gifted with crowns of honor. Dullards and pimps are enriched, but those as skilled as Daedalus <term>Dædali; referring to the mythical Greek inventor, signifying master craftsmen or intellectuals</term> are treated as common servants, and the wise fall into extreme poverty. 

Horses <note>Likely referring to those of noble spirit or high birth</note> must beg for favors, while promises are made to asses. The worthy are neglected, and the unworthy are judged as capable. The inventions of the learned and the honest are laughed at as trifles or old wives' tales, while the advice of fools is embraced like oracles. Therefore, can the World not best be baptized as a "democracy" <note>The author uses "democracy" in a pejorative sense, common in his era, to mean a state of lawless equality where no one respects true authority or merit.</note>, in which everyone wants to be supreme and in charge? Is it not, I say, to put it bluntly, a brothel?

->In which everything is done for the sake of hellish coins,<-

Truly, who can know the human heart, so full of diversions and windings, so wicked and inscrutable? <note>original: "pravum & inscrutabile"; this alludes to Jeremiah 17:9, "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"</note> Who then can penetrate it with thought, or who can see through it? Now indeed, of all the heart’s inventions, the evil ones are the most difficult to recognize, for man always seeks to hide and cloak them as much as he can. If you once "fish out" a failing <note>original: "Expiscamini semel in deliquia"; a metaphor for catching someone in a mistake or sin.</note> and confront this or that person with their evil intent, soon a thousand shadows of reasons, causes, hiding places, arguments, and cloaks are ready at hand, with which the crooked intention and the fox-like soul <term>vulpinus animus; a mind characterized by the cunning or "craftiness" traditionally attributed to a fox</term> may be most honorably dressed. For no perversity, no cunning, lacks its reasons; hardly any vice lacks its little cloak <note>original: "palliolum"; a small cloak or cover-up.</note>, almost no wickedness or fallacy is without a beautiful pretext for excuse, and none is left without its hiding place. Everyone offers some argument for why they have gone astray—truly, for every little jar, its own lid is found. In the very middle of the day, when the light is clearest, the thickest darkness is drawn over us, and the day is often wrapped in such an artificial scheme of night that you would swear it was a most certain eclipse. We Alchemists <note>original: "Chymistæ"</note> experience, and it is most true, that there is a great conformity between gold and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>. Indeed, it is so great that when gold is outside the fire, no matter where the quicksilver may be, it seeks the gold out, so that it might unite and adhere to it. Yet, when we "quicken" <note>To "quicken" or "vivify" in alchemy often refers to the process of restoring life or motion to a substance through heat or chemical reaction.</note> and purify it in the furnace, the quicksilver turns into smoke and deserts the gold. It happens exactly this way in every friendship of this world; regardless of previous closeness, when you enter the fire of tribulation, adversity, or distress like gold, the false and deceitful friend—acting like Mercury, or like that other fugitive slave—abandons you and vanishes into smoke. Thus, you are left alone in the furnace of your sorrows.

# PREAMBLE

...to still pluck flowers from there; when that most profound sea of Spagiric <term>Spagiric: a term for alchemy, specifically the art of separating and recombining natural elements to produce medicines</term> philosophy, Theophrastus <note>original: "Theophrastus"; referring to the famous Swiss alchemist Paracelsus, whose full name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim</note>, once saw a noble pair of friends, of whom one was overflowing with wealth while the other was afflicted by a meager state of affairs, he jokingly said: *“If they are friends, why then is one so rich and the other so poor?”* He wished to show that where sincere friendship is sealed, adversities and prosperities ought to be shared in common, and that it is not right—indeed, it is against the laws of friendship—for the poor and needy friend to be abandoned by the wealthy one.

->*True love never abandons a friend in misery.*<-

Let us enter this rose garden more deeply and see what our Plato—a philosopher like a god—says regarding love; in his dialogue on love, he says: *“Love is the parent of excess and of will.”* Indeed, I do not quite grasp what he said here: if it is the parent of *excess*, why is it immediately also the parent *of will*? I, on the contrary, would rather say: *“Love is the parent of will and of excess.”* But far be it from me! The divine Plato spoke divinely here when he said, *“Love is the parent of excess and of will,”* which is as much as if he had declared that, in one who truly loves, after all has been poured out for the one he loves, after all has been spent and paid out for that person's honor and reputation, there remains only the desire to pour out, spend, and pay out even more. This desire is so great and so pure that it is as if he had poured out, spent, or paid out nothing at all: *“the parent of excess and of will.”* This, this is the touchstone <term>original: "lapis Lydius"; a Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold and silver</term> of true and authentic love.

But I shall pick only one more flower as a conclusion and, as it were, a final gift <term>original: "corollarium"; literally a small garland, used to mean a finishing touch or an added deduction</term> before leaving this Rose Garden. Regarding the Heliotrope <note>The sunflower or "sun-turner"</note>, to which the Ancients also gave various names because of its hidden, stupendous, and varied properties of nature, it is widely known that it is a *lover of the Sun*, such that it never ceases to watch the Sun with greedy eyes from dawn until dusk, and from the first rising until the setting, as if its whole life depended on the sight of the Sun. To the Heliotrope, to live is to see that most serene and illustrious planet. But perhaps [we should ask] whether it then only turns toward the sun...

By no means, says Pliny <note>original: "Plinius"; referring to Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note>, that curious and studious observer of nature's secrets; for how small would this benevolence be, if it only worshipped the shining Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbum"; a common name for the sun god Apollo</note> with a bowed head?

We have many times recalled the miracle of the heliotrope <term>Heliotrope: literally "sun-turner," a name used in the past for flowers like the sunflower or marigold that physically turn to follow the sun’s path</term> which turns itself with the sun, even on a cloudy day. Even if a cloud places itself in the way and hides the sight of that most grateful and bright star—as if out of the greatest envy—so that the flower, most eager to see it, cannot look directly upon it, it nevertheless does not cease to follow it. Even on a foggy day, when the wind stirs everything up, amidst these injuries, it turns toward its friendly planet. Why so? How is this? Pliny responds: *so great is the love for the star* <note>original: "tantus sideris amor est"</note>. From this it happens that it follows the sun no less in clouds than in clear weather. If this admirable plant followed the glowing planet only when it smiled brightly upon it, it would give no proof of its arising friendship. But because even on a cloudy day, it inclines toward it from every direction with its head lowered in reverence—even though the storm prevents sight by the intervention of clouds—that is the most brilliant sign of true and sincere love, because *so great is the love for the star*. Thus, by the silent warning of this flower,

Someone expressed this quite skillfully regarding such people: *They are in truth vultures waiting for a corpse; bees flying toward a feast. For in the manner of vultures and bees, they gape for prey and soft pickings* <note>original: "pappis"; refers to soft food or "pap," implying they seek easy benefits</note>. Ah! This is a matter worthy of a just rebuke, not to say a harsh, stepmotherly one! O pestilence and crime to be anathematized <term>Anathematized: formally cursed or denounced</term>! Like swallows, they build their nests among men for three or four months, even warbling in the homes of the poor; but when the chilly winter approaches, they desert people and, like flatterers, depart in the time of trial! And so, from the sole of the foot to the top of the head, you will find a thousand proofs of lies in a man.

> Whoever you are, then, do not trust in the World,

# MIXED PROSE AND VERSE

[The world] is most shameful in its pretense, tricks, hypocrisy, frauds, lies, and masks; everywhere is filled with crowds of masked hucksters <note>original: "mangonicis personatorum gregibus"; "mangonicus" refers to a deceptive dealer who fakes the appearance of goods</note>. Everywhere there is an abundance of words and ceremonies, but little charity and faith. The words are beautiful and the ceremonies are charming, but the heart swims with bitter gall. Therefore, not without reason, this workshop of hypocrisies—the world—is baptized in Holy Scripture as a dissembler, a liar, and an imposter. For on its exterior face, it shows everything as truly beautiful, charming, and sincere, yet it cheats the buyer while hiding foulness, loathing, deceit, and lies within. Oh, what a crafty world!

And certainly, has this not happened to me in reality quite often? Indeed, I have experienced it—especially when I arrived in Amsterdam in Holland in the year of our Lord 1657, and in London in England in 1662. My travel money, which had been meager, was nearly exhausted, nor did I know how I might earn enough for my expenses;

> For I was not often a "son of a white hen," <note>original: "gallinae filius albae"; a classical Latin idiom for a person favored by fortune or born into privilege</note>
> Like a swallow anticipating the spring time,
> To whom resources not won by labor were abundant enough,
> But I left them behind.

# PRELUDE

2. Therefore, following in the footsteps of my predecessors and our elders, I wished to make known by this simple observation that I intend to interpret the sayings of the ancient <term>Magi: Ancient wise men or priests, often associated in this period with the origins of alchemy and natural magic</term> for orthodox and select minds. I will focus on their mystical, yet most true, meaning, which they have gone about covering and veiling with eternal types, allegories, parables, and circumlocutions. This meaning concerns that tempered substance which the violence of fire cannot separate, nor the dregs of earth defile, nor the muddiness of water alter, nor the touch of air overshadow. By this substance, every hard body becomes soft, and the soft becomes hard; the fleeting is fixed, and the foul is illuminated with a marvelous brilliance. This was called by the father and prophet of philosophers the *strong strength of all strength* <note>original: "totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis"; a famous phrase from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, describing the "One Thing" or Philosopher's Stone</note>. It is likewise that truth hidden by the poets, specifically in the fables of the Gorgon, Jason, and Medea concerning the Golden Fleece. It is of the nature of the Sun—the heart, form, and flower of the Sun, and the Golden Tree, from which if the fruits are plucked, new ones grow back immediately. And this is that clay-like representation which always hardens in the fire, and this is that waxen image which melts in the same:

->*As the clay hardens, and the fragrant wax melts*<-
<note>original: "Ut lutum durescit, odoráque cera liquescit"; a reference to Virgil's Eclogues (8.80). In alchemical literature, this quote illustrates how a single "fire" or process can produce opposite effects—fixing the volatile and softening the hard—depending on the nature of the material.</note>

By one and the same fire, in short, this is that strong and strongest thing which conquers all and draws all to itself; and this is that thing separated from its own body, about which the philosophers, prophets, poets, and others have sung such wonders.

3. Come then, *sons of doctrine*, proceed! Now, now I say, the door stands ajar. Approach boldly to perceive the stupendous and abstruse things of nature. Therefore, just as it is accustomed to happen among the locals, or those who are well-known in the city—who rarely seek profit through writing or small pages, nor do they signal the state of their business through any <term>paper indicators: "philyraceis indiciis"; referring to "philyra," the inner bark of a linden tree once used for writing material</term>, partly because everyone knows their holiday schedules, and partly due to a certain reluctance or, more truly, a swelling of a modest mind, because what is laughed at by a guest or stranger always grates in one’s own fatherland—so, on the other hand, it is the custom of foreigners and newcomers that, as soon as they have licked the threshold and reached the hearth or the place toward which they were sailing, they signify the roles of their life by various consultations or undertakings close at hand.
