# MIXED VERSE AND PROSE #

I am now playing the part of <term>Diogenes: "Diogenizo"; meaning to act like the Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope, known for his rejection of social norms and material wealth</term> entirely, laughing at all things and holding them in total indifference, just like Diogenes. When he was once asked by Alexander whether he wanted anything from him, he said nothing else except, "only that you step a little out of my sun," for you cast an annoying shadow while I am basking. They say Alexander was so delighted by this response that, having returned to his companions, he said he would wish to be Diogenes if he were not Alexander. Thus, it has seemed a deep paradox, or even unintelligible, to many that I have replied nothing else to those offering the most lavish conditions than *that they should stay a little away from my light*. That is to say, it pleases me to live in my own way;

And this is especially because I knew that there is nothing—however useful, glorious, or pleasant it may be—in which the heart of man may find rest, except in God alone. From this, it seems to me that I can rightly take the opportunity to propose a most pious question here: namely, why did God, having established all other things, create man? He had created the heavens and filled them with angels; also the earth, into which He sent the animals; and the air, which He assigned to the birds. And when He had already established all things, only then at last did He create man. But why, I beseech you, Lord, do you now create a being so noble and of such great dignity, when no place remains among created things to assign to him, and in which he might dwell? Where, then, will you place man? What position will he occupy? What element will he enter? Will you insert him into heaven? But the angels will resist, crying out that heaven was destined for them. Will you transfer him into the air? But the birds will struggle against it. Will he dwell in the sea then? But the fish will not bear it. Will he inhabit the earth? But the animals will stand in the way. Tell me, then, disinherited man, what shall become of you? But let us not go too far; wait a moment, and you shall hear the reason.

Without a doubt, God, the Creator of all things, wished to create man at the very end—after all other things were established and their places assigned—to show that He alone is man’s inheritance and possession. He intended to show that He Himself is the only <term>center: "centrum"; the focal point or fixed point of rest</term> for man, in which man ought <term>to keep Sabbath: "feriari"; to rest or take a holiday, here referring to the spiritual rest of the soul</term>, if he wishes to find rest for his soul. # PRELUDE #

...this? What kind of philosophy is this? What does a thing possess in its own center? Three things answer from my ears: rest, preservation, and union. For all things indeed find rest, are kept safe, and are united in their center; hence, with a full throat, the delight of God and glory of the Doctors <note>A reference to St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the "Doctors of the Church."</note> cries out: *“You have made me for yourself, O Lord, and my heart is restless until it rests in you!”* <note>original Latin: "Fecisti me Domine ad te, & inquietum est cor meum, donec resideat in te!" This is one of the most famous lines from Augustine's *Confessions*.</note> Truly, these words are emphatic and swollen with a spiritual vein; while we examine the occasion of these words with a sagacious mind, we see that every thing takes its ease in its center alone, and nothing is content until it achieves its appointed end. For all the works of divine goodness are circular and perfect, rotated spherically toward Him from whom they came forth.

From the beginning, before the first dawn of His creation, God, placing nature before all things, made four simple bodies <note>The "four elements" of ancient and medieval physics: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, from which He later established all mixed bodies. Of the mixed bodies, He made some instinctive, some sensitive and vegetable <note>Refers to plants and animals that possess life and sensation but not human reason.</note>, and some intellectual only. But some He created solely from the <term>rarity: "raritas"; in medieval physics, this refers to the "thinness" or lack of density in substances like air or fire, which were believed to naturally rise.</term> of the elements, and therefore, by grace of this, our heart is restless until we come to Him; for the rarity of all the elements ascends to the fire which is above the stars. Therefore, we too, created from that same rarity, rightly strive upward toward God as toward our sole beginning. 

But all sensitive things, as well as vegetable things, made from the <term>density: "spissitudine"; the opposite of rarity, referring to the "thickness" or weight of substances like earth and water.</term> of the elements, are distinguished into different species. When they are dissolved by death, they are not without reason returned to the earth and water as if to their mother; for the density of the elements naturally and continually tends downward toward its center, namely the earth. This is just as our lower fire here always creeps upward until it reaches its elemental kin <note>Ancient physics held that fire sought to return to the "Sphere of Fire" above the atmosphere.</note>. So the philosopher applies himself entirely to studies until he obtains knowledge; the sun hastens diligently until it arrives from the East to the West. The winding rivers flow until they reach the Ocean to which they are tributaries. In short, every thing naturally inclines toward its goal, and once that is obtained, it rests in it. Therefore, since the center of our heart is that sole Creator of the entire universe, eter-

# PROSE AND VERSE #

->One world does not suffice for the youth of Pella.<-

# PROSIMETRIC WORK #

<note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM." This title indicates a work composed in a mix of prose and verse.</note>

For this whole life of ours is nothing but a lying dream, in which we do nothing but sleep; and while sleeping, we see nothing except empty and false images. Death itself, however, is the awakener; by opening our eyes, it discloses and reveals the truth of all things. That which we thought to be good, or pleasure, or honor, or joy and delight while we were sleeping, we shall recognize to be nothing but evil, pain, toil, hardship, infamy, and reproach once Death itself has awakened us. Therefore, when we lie down in a bed of delights and fall asleep upon the feathers of pleasures, our mind fashions wonderful phantasms for itself; we seem to ourselves rich, sublime, happy, and the most blessed of mortals. But once that ultimate **Morta** <note>The Roman goddess of death, one of the three Fates (Parcae).</note> has awakened us, [we shall recognize] the truth...

From this, we lovers of the world <term>cosmophili: from the Greek *kosmos* (world) and *philos* (lover)</term> and worshippers of this world seem to experience daily what happened to the Patriarch Jacob. <note>Referring to Genesis 29, where Laban deceives Jacob by substituting his elder daughter Leah for his younger daughter Rachel.</note>
It happens no differently to us, the lovers of this world, who—where after losing oil and effort <note>original: "post oleum & operam perditam." A Latin idiom meaning "to waste one's time and labor," derived from the oil burned in a lamp while working.</note>, after enduring immense labors, we hoped we would abundantly fulfill our desire for our goods, riches, and pleasures—are mockingly deluded, leaving behind, instead of a sweet fragrance, a stench,

->Carrying nothing but a great void.<-

# PRELUDE #

For our nest, which we call the world, is a certain deceptive merchant <note>original: "mango." In Roman times, a *mango* was a dealer who used tricks to make slaves or goods appear more valuable than they actually were.</note>, an angler, and a most clever forger; he incites every person to chase after the honors he disguises with paint, to seek the riches he covers in soot, and to pursue the delights and pleasures he offers. But he lies and mocks us, for whatever he polishes and alters is empty, useless, futile, and mutilated. Away with such intolerable stupidity and greatest folly—of those, clearly, who are blinded by the passions of the world and driven mad by their own foolishness.

->Because of so many anxious little works of this Stygian <note>Pertaining to the River Styx in the underworld; here meaning hellish or death-bound.</note> world,<-
->Which I know to be nothing, but purely empty,<-
->And phantasms more vain than a vain vapor.<-

For the world passes away, and its desires with it. Its pleasures indeed shine like a lit candle, whose flame is beautiful and lasts as long as the fuel remains; but once it is burned down to the bottom, everything vanishes into smoke and stench.

->Smoke is wealth, and stench is honor, while pleasure is a thorn-bush,<-
->And whatever we love has the appearance of smoke and thorns;<-
->And yet, what person is not baited by this smoke?<-
->What person does the bait of smoke and thorns not press down with a yoke of weeping!<-

Such is the end of all worldly things; for although the splendor of their vanity may gladden us now, in the end it will give birth to much nausea and remorse. All things are:

->Destined to turn into dust, and a breath, and ashes,<-
->And thin smoke.<-

Pluto and Juno <note>Pluto was the god of the underworld and mineral wealth; Juno was the queen of the gods, often associated with the atmosphere and material prosperity.</note> were therefore considered two deities of wealth, to whom altars were dedicated and gifts offered under that title. However, in the case of Juno, the air also

# PROSE AND VERSE #

...was being prefigured; and just as Jupiter represented fire, Neptune water, and Ceres earth, so Juno displayed the air in the "Comedy of the Gods." Consider now the twin Saturnian duties <note>Referring to Juno’s lineage as the daughter of Saturn, the god of time and cycles.</note>, in that she was both the Goddess of riches and she represented the air, presiding over that region in which we breathe. What, indeed, did learned antiquity intend when it fashioned this same Juno as the Goddess of both the air and of wealth? Without doubt (saving the mystical sense of the philosophers), it intended to signify that in this world, riches and air, majesty and summer, pleasure and wind are one and the same:

> ->The world indeed anoints the outer lips with honeyed things,<-
> ->And it is fashioned to move along on wheels more than enough charming,<-

But inside it pierces with a thousand thorns, and fills the vitals with destruction and bitterness, because,

> ->As Juvenal says, it overflows more with aloe than with honey:<-
> ->The joys which the world creates with a friendly appearance are deceptive,<-
> ->O boy, they lead toward your punishments by the art of Cypris <note>An epithet for Venus, the goddess of love; here used to imply that lust or worldly love leads to ruin.</note>.<-

That Almighty Creator of things constantly mingles delights with sorrows and prosperity with adversities: where there is abundance, there is a tumor; where there is a nut, there is a cross; where there is wealth, there is strife; where there is honey, there is gall <note>original: "ubi uber, ibi tuber; ubi nux, ibi crux, ubi Dis, ibi lis, ubi mel, ibi fel." Its conceptions breathe of pain, its births reek of restlessness, the womb is a mere workshop of frauds, and the private parts <note>original: "interfemineum," a late Latin term for the groin or thighs.</note> are nothing but a dunghill and a nursery of deceit. The cheeks and breasts of women are nothing but drops of funeral dirges; outwardly they appear beautiful and desirable, but once you turn the sack over, inside there is nothing but wickedness and falsehood.

> ->Go now, and catch the lethal arrows of the world,<-
> ->If such vain joys should swim in so much gall.<-

Rightly, therefore, all these sublunary <note>Literally "under the moon"; a traditional term for the earthly realm which is subject to change and decay, unlike the "eternal" heavens.</note> things and all the goods of the world are to be considered as nothing; and I leave this motto to be carved upon a tombstone as a perpetual monument for those born hereafter:

# PRELUDE #

> Let it remain stored deep in the mind of every person,
> That all earthly things are vapor, breath, smoke, and shadow,
> A mere theatrical appearance, or nothingness, to speak plainly.
> In the world there is no house of protection, no altar of safety,
> But all things are vanity and emptiness:
> He who created everything from nothing is the only All,
> For whatever God made from nothing, is in itself nothing <note>original: "Nam Deus ex nihilo quod fecit, id omne nihilum." This reflects a common Baroque philosophical theme: because God created the world out of nothing, the world has no inherent substance without Him.</note>.

To flee that most deceptive *nothingness*, it is told that the most serene maiden, Isabella, in a more secluded corner of the court, used to read these verses daily from the golden censer of her heart:

> Suppose I have strength and elegant wealth, what of it?
> Suppose I have an overflowing mass of silver and gold, what of it?
> If I have children from a royal lineage, what then?
> And a long chain of servants crowding around, what then?
> Let the wheel of fortune lift me to the stars, what of it?
> And if I should reign happily for a thousand years, what then?
> For all these things quickly vanish, so that nothing remains,
> Therefore, it is safer that I serve God, for that is enough:
> Because whoever has looked well upon all things from every side,
> And seen again the lightness <note>In this context, "lightness" refers to lack of substance or "frivolity."</note> in every part of the universe,
> Will say that in the entire world, there is nothing at all.

While I weigh these verses with a more attentive edge of the mind, I cannot help but agree with the aforementioned heroic woman; for solitary women are overwhelmed by as many and as great evils as exist in the entire universe, seeing as all evil took its origin from them <note>A reference to the biblical narrative of Eve as the source of original sin.</note>. Thus it is fair and just that it returns to the head from which it springs. And indeed, to weigh this matter a little more at length according to its own merits: tell me, I pray, what delight can there be for a wife joined to her husband—who possesses her as his own physical center—except to be honored with the title of mother, and to rejoice in the growth of children similar to herself? Furthermore, however, that moment and point of "little joy" <note>original: "gaudioli." # PROSIMETRICUM #

...in fact, it is entangled in a labyrinth: for the tender little sprouts <note>The author uses "germina tenellula" (tender sprouts) as a metaphor for young children.</note> have need of constant lifting up, refreshing, and watchful care; those reaching puberty require continuous guarding, and those who have reached adulthood are often nothing but a heartache <term>cordolia</term> <note>A Latin term for "sorrow of the heart" or "heart-ache."</note>.

What pleasure then, I ask, if we consider the matter from its foundation through the entire span of life, is there for the female sex? Once their seed is settled in the mother's womb and endowed with the gift of every perfection and of life, it suffers violence in that workhouse <term>ergasterio</term> <note>Originally a Roman term for a slave prison or workhouse; here used to describe the womb as a place of confinement and labor.</note>, drawing breath through slippery cords, floating in putrid and foul-smelling waters, and is enveloped in the dismal wallowing-place of the womb. Once these enclosures are burst and the bars of that dark prison are broken so that the child may enjoy the sun's beam and the glowing lamp of the world, for a space of at least two years it is bound round with ribbons and cradles—as if with shackles and handcuffs. Afterward, for the whole remaining time of life, a woman is always restrained by the strictest yoke, partly of her parents and partly of her husband, and is buckled in by the tight pressures of her garments. Their youth is spent not for their own sake, but to please men; and while they please them, they are meanwhile goaded by perennial torments. If there is perhaps any little delight for them while men neigh after them <note>original: "viri adhinniunt." A vivid, biblical metaphor (from Jeremiah 5:8) comparing male lust to the neighing of horses.</note> and they are a source of pleasure to those men, that joy is so vain and fleeting that in the course of only nine months, the lethal punishment for this little bit of pleasure daily approaches. They cannot perform this duty without a violent risk to their lives and the exquisite torture of all their limbs—as if that supreme Upright Judge <term>orthocrites</term> <note>A rare term derived from Greek meaning a "just" or "upright judge."</note> and seeker of criminal acts, the just God, seems even now to demand from them an account for the great offense by which they cast down all men and themselves <note>A reference to the Fall of Eve and the subsequent biblical "curse" of painful childbirth (Genesis 3:16).</note>.

Therefore, you might rightly call a woman a heap of calamity, the origin of lament, and the beginning of groaning. If, then, as is the truth, so many and such great evils surround and envelop that weak sex, then by Hercules! <note>A common Latin exclamation (mehercle) used to emphasize a point, similar to "By heavens!"</note> those untainted virgins are born under a fortunate star who, free and secluded in a blessed courtyard, dwell in their sacred cloisters before they can know the value of this world's amusements and the allurements of fleeting pleasure.

Ah, therefore! Not for nothing do I groan; rightly happy—three, four, and a thousand times blessed—are those virgins and inviolate maidens to be called, who, breathed upon by a kinder West Wind <note>The "Zephyr," a gentle and favorable breeze in classical literature.</note>, have entered the longed-for harbor in the land of the living. ...[with their] burdens, and joining themselves by a solemn wedding torch to Christ—who on earth is a beggar, naked and crucified—so that they may possess Him in the heavens: He who is the King of the heavens and the sun, the father of light and life, and the one who measures out death. They betroth themselves to Him for perpetual eternities, and by this spouse, they will be gifted with all those inconceivable rewards which the human mind cannot even grasp. That most faithful and most tender lover, God, will not merely give, but will pour out at their feet majesty, wealth, and whatever else seizes human souls. Instead of a hair-shirt <term>cilicii</term> <note>A garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a penance.</note>, they shall have a hem more excellent than the very celestial belt <note>Refers to the Zodiac or the starry firmament.</note> painted with glowing constellations. 

For indeed, what an incomparable reward! Oh, thrice-noble prize for these tender young maidens! It is that they may cling to Him alone and meditate upon His service, His praise, and His glory. To Him they will offer sacrifices with a pure and chaste melody and a wonder-sounding voice, while the lung <term>pneumone</term> <note>original: "pneumone"; here referring to the breath of the soul or the spirit inspired by God.</note> is inflated by the swelling breeze of divine love. Anointed by the secret nectar of this heat, they will be drenched to the very marrow with super-celestial delights—and indeed, by a far longer and brighter torch of honorable pleasure than can be enjoyed by those who are shut up in this earthly dwelling and foul prison of the World.

Indeed, if you were to weigh all those things—and whatever delectable things the world possesses—against the joys and delights that are in heaven, they would seem like filth and stench. For whatever is in this stinking pit of Venus or of [earthly] love ought to be called a seducer arising from the regions of the brothels.

Because this lower Globe of ours is like a false and deceptive workshop, all of its goods—I mean even the most noble and distinguished creatures—are nothing but signs, types, and certain marks of the riches and wares contained in that most ample storehouse of divine majesty. Who is there, then, provided they are wise, who would not most willingly toil and fight for that heavenly abundance <term>polyplusiâ</term> <note>From the Greek "polyplusia," meaning great wealth or opulence.</note> of Jerusalem? Consider how much is endured for tiny little cities—which cost so much effort, calamity, and blood—or how much is suffered for a small scrap of earth or a minute fortification! And yet, the entire World is but a tiny point <term>punctulum</term> compared to the measure of that heavenly City.

# PRELUDE

Therefore, if the earth—which seems so vast and wide to us—is so tiny compared to the axis around which the sun revolves, how small and insignificant must other lesser bodies be? This is especially true if they are compared not just to that prince of planets <note>The Sun.</note>, but to the even grander things held within the inner heavens. I say even more: if all of Greece stood in arms, if they wore themselves out in a ten-year war for Troy and burned the entire city, and if the blood and death of so many noble youths and heroes were spent for the sake of one Helen—alas, what a plague! I burn with a worthy indignation for this reason:

> A foul adultress is sought by such a great war! <note>original: "Expetitur tanto tam turpis adultera bello!" A common sentiment in moralizing literature, likely echoing Ovid or similar classical poets criticizing the vanity of the Trojan War.</note>

What, then, is right for us to do in order to contemplate that uncreated beauty of God, or that most transcendent form of eternal truth and divinity? For the *holy service* <term>hierodulia</term> <note>From the Greek "hieros" (holy) and "douleia" (service/servitude).</note> of Christians is incomparably more beautiful than the Helen of the Greeks; yet here, alas, an imaginary shadow <note>original: "umbella imaginaria"; literally an "imaginary parasol" or "veil," suggesting a superficial distraction that blocks the light of God.</note> often robs us of heaven, of God, and of all good things, and wraps us in eternal evils!

> Man, a creature of God, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Why, since you are soon to die,
> And to rise again in the flesh, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Do you have so little care,
> ->For eternal glory?<-
> If you knew how great it truly was, &nbsp; You would surely not waste away,
> Nor thus pursue worldly things, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Nor thus thirst for human affairs,
> ->Vain and transitory.<-

By Hercules, what a honey-sweet discourse flowing from a river of honey! For what is more glorious, or what is more victorious, than to have the whole world under one's feet while leaving the world behind? O incomparable light! O spark from an unquenchable firebrand! You, a heart brave and unconquerable—you can do what no one else can: to bring about, to entice. For who could tear an adulterer, trapped in the snare of his usual lust, away from the long-standing habit of foul slipperiness? In the skin of a mistress <term>pellicem</term>, for whom all the baths of the world are not enough for cleanliness...

<page-num>117</page-num>

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM," a term for a literary work that alternates between prose and verse.</note>

->(Baths do not clean the crow, nor the prostitute;<-
->For neither does the crow become snow-white,<-
->nor the prostitute pure, by water.) <note>original: "Balnea cornicem non purgant..." A Latin proverb suggesting that external washing cannot change a corrupt nature; only internal transformation—grace—can do so.</note><-

Can one be pulled from the deep filth of vice by prayer or by a price? Divine grace and love, reaching even to the very division of the soul, have pulled and torn such souls away. It has led away the Mary Magdalenes, the madams, the Pelagias, the Laides, and the Thaides <note>The author lists famous reformed sinners and courtesans from history and hagiography: Mary Magdalene, St. Pelagia the Penitent, and the famous Greek courtesans Lais and Thais who were often used in moralizing literature as examples of worldly vanity.</note>. Daily, it leads so many tender daughters, raised in Sybaritic <note>Luxurious or self-indulgent; named after Sybaris, an ancient Greek city famous for its hedonism.</note> luxury, away from their parents, their inheritances, their marriages, their riches, and their delights. It leads them, as if from the very breasts of the world, to the wounds of Christ. 

Therefore, if the "medicine of the philosophers" <note>A reference to worldly wisdom or secular philosophy as a cure for the soul's ills.</note> were offered to me in place of such a transformation, I would refuse it. To speak plainly, I would value it no more than the humble gift given by the poorest Hecale <note>In Greek mythology, Hecale was an impoverished old woman who offered simple, sincere hospitality to the hero Theseus.</note>. To put it briefly: I am now enriched solely by the knowledge of these spiritual things, resting peacefully in my own skin:

->Now I support and strengthen myself by my virtue alone,<-
->And I seek honest poverty without a rich dowry;<-
->This is the one remedy most suited to my pain.<-

I know that for many—and especially for me—it is not helpful for salvation to possess the freedom of wealth and honors alongside physical health. Is this not a well-worn truth, found not only in divine but also in human literature? Are not the holy writings <term>hagiographa</term> <note>From the Greek for "sacred writings," referring here to the scriptures or the lives of the saints.</note> and the sacred books full of this persuasion?

Does a man not feel his brain reel when he climbs too high, so that he cannot judge correctly the small things existing below him? Similarly, the owl—does it not see less the higher it flies during the day? It is no different for us. When we are placed in high positions of majesty, or in the bright "day" of worldly dignity and prosperity, we lose the vision of true wisdom. *When man was in honor, he did not understand* <note>original: "Cùm esset in honore homo, non intellexit"; a reference to Psalm 49:20, suggesting that prosperity often blinds people to their own mortality and spiritual needs.</note>. For it is most true—truer than truth itself—that pleasures, riches, and the flatteries of this world are the primary cause of the fall of so many wicked men and the horrible damnation of their souls.

### PRELUDE

> For did not swollen fortune deceive Croesus? <note>original: "Crœsum"; Croesus was the King of Lydia, legendary for his immense wealth. His story was a standard moral warning that riches do not guarantee lasting happiness.</note>

The foolish and insane World-lover <term>Cosmophilus</term><note>A constructed name from the Greek *kosmos* (world) and *philos* (lover), representing one who is obsessed with earthly life.</note>, for whom everything flows according to his wish, who enjoys the prosperous wind of fortune and delights in a charming calm in his affairs—he, I say, who is outside the storm and swims in rivers of delights and pleasures—cares nothing for God. He does not think of death, does not fear judgment, does not shudder at the underworld, and has no concern for his soul or his salvation. The Ancients indicated this very thing, and not ineptly, under the veils of mythological mysteries. **Apollo** was desperately in love with the beautiful **Daphne**; she, scorning her lover, rejected all his attentions as if she had been hardened into flint. She was so implacable, unbending, and pitiless that she would not allow herself to be swayed by prayers, nor would she listen to any words of persuasion; she was not led by any bribe, nor moved by threats—even the most terrifying ones—to grant any of his desires. Apollo, somewhat ashamed because he saw the power of his divinity frustrated, transformed the woman into a laurel tree—she whom he had been unable to fill with love for himself. Just as Cupid was already depicted with wings, so his mother [Venus] trod upon a tortoise according to the Ancients. But what was the reason that they painted wings on Cupid and a tortoise at the feet of Venus? The messenger of the Gods <note>Mercury, known as the messenger god.</note> addresses Venus in wonder:

> O Paphian! <note>An epithet for Venus, referring to her famous temple at Paphos in Cyprus.</note> What is this appearance? What does that

It is common knowledge that wings signify swiftness, while the tortoise is a sign of slowness; it is so well-known that no one is ignorant of it. For that reason, the tortoise is called:

> Slow-stepping, grass-stepping, house-carrier, and thick-blooded,
> Which Apelles of Cos <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece.</note> painted under the feet of Venus.

Since she has little blood, carries her home around forever, and is hindered by the grass as she walks only in the meadows, what wonder is it that she moves so sluggishly and slowly? Now the question returns: why, I ask, did learned antiquity add wings to the armpits of Cupid, and a tortoise to the feet of Venus? I will explain (interpreting this fable now in a moral sense; though in a natural-philosophical and most literal sense, the wings designate the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>A key substance in alchemy representing the volatile or spirituous principle.</note>, and the tortoise designates the <term>salt of the world</term> <note>The "sal mundi," representing the "fixed" or physical principle that resides beneath the spirit.</note>, or the central salt, which arises as something fixed within or under it). He did this so that by this emblem <note>A symbolic picture accompanied by a motto and explanation.</note> he might ingeniously sketch two effects of love. He intended to indicate that the one who loves has wings by which he can fly with the swiftest flight into the house of the one he loves; but to depart from there is done so painfully and slowly, as if he had the feet of a tortoise, heavily burdened or hindered.

Therefore, the softness of the flesh miserably blinds and enchants men, and keeps them from the pursuit of sublime things—especially those pertaining to the salvation of the soul—and most painfully of all...

Wherefore it is all too true, as I have said, that the vice of **lust** <note>original: "luxuriæ"; in this context, it refers to sexual excess or debauchery rather than material wealth.</note> is sometimes most difficult to unlearn and to keep hidden. What did Jupiter intend when he turned the girl into a cow? Was it not so that he might secretly carry out his thefts of passion with a transformed mistress, and thus the maiden for whom he was dying of love might lie hidden? Indeed, he certainly intended this, but take note of how his own cleverness mocked him, and the caution with which he busied himself to cover her up actually revealed the matter. In the same way that he had proceeded to hide her, he led others to the knowledge of his own lust and wickedness. For that same girl, transformed into a cow, wherever she pressed her tracks, silently and cleverly

> She revealed herself, and suppressed her name and her misfortunes;
> A letter instead of words, which her foot drew in the dust,
> Carried out the sad evidence of her changed body.
<note>These lines are from Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Book I, lines 647–649.</note>

For just as a cow has a round and split foot, so as often as she stepped on the sand or grit, she formed an **I** with the split and an **O** with the roundness. Therefore, with every step, and as often as she fixed her feet in the earth, she expressed and, as it were, wrote out her name **Io**. Thus, by the very same path through which Jupiter wished his dear little friend to remain unknown, she became known. She never placed her feet upon the ground without simultaneously crying out, as it were, "**Io! Io!**" <note>The author notes a pun: "Io" is both the girl's name and a common Latin exclamation of greeting or ritual shouting.</note> and saying with a clear voice: "I, I am that Io beloved of Jupiter; I am his darling; I am his delight; I am the rival of Juno," and so forth. The sacred pages likewise teach us that this same wanton spirit is stirred up in times of prosperity; for was not that portent of men, the wonder of the world, and victor of many battles:

> Samson, known above the heavens for his Herculean strength,

He was resting in the lap of **Delilah** when he was seized and bound by the Philistines, and was not this lack of vigilance the occasion of his ruin? So it is, in truth; and just as many of us who are still distinguished by works of virtue, because we are too careless and do not look out for ourselves, we are sometimes...

### ->PROSIMETRIC WORK<-
<note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM"; a literary style that mixes prose and verse.</note>

And while we lie in the lap of pleasure and of the flesh—which is that Philistine and treacherous **Delilah** <note>original: "Dalida"; the biblical figure who betrayed Samson by cutting his hair while he slept in her lap.</note>—we are often overwhelmed by enemies and fall into the deepest captivity, which finally becomes the occasion of our exit, our destruction, and our perdition. I shall place this matter skillfully before your eyes once more; hear these wonders.

One day, towards sunset, a wealthy man of great reputation retired with his entire family to a most pleasant villa for a **sumptuous banquet** <note>original: "polluctum"; refers to a lavish or even sacred feast.</note>, intending to indulge more freely in pleasure with his own people. Here the house was choice and abundant; the chambers, especially the Master's, were decorated with various tapestries; the beds were draped with canopies; nothing was missing that was excellently prepared for pleasure. However, among the servants there was a wicked man who, during such a cheerful drinking bout, mixed a **sleeping potion** <note>original: "lethargum"; a medicinal or poisonous draft inducing heavy sleep.</note> for the Master and his fellow servants. Thus, most were consigned to a deep stupor, as much by the wine as by the drug.

In the middle of the night, while they slept almost like the dead, that worthless traitor of his Master admitted into the house, through the unbarred doors, **thieves** <note>original: "laverniones"; a term for robbers derived from Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves.</note> and plunderers—the very scum and dregs of humanity. Once they had pillaged the residence, they turned all their violence upon the Master of the house. It was not enough for them to have inflicted such great loss unless they also added a horrible spectacle: therefore, they carried the Master out of his bedchamber and the house in his stupor, as if he were a corpse, and left him abandoned in an open field. Meanwhile, the sky began to churn with foul storms; lightning flashed, thunder roared, and rain clouds burst. Finally, the Master awoke from his stupor; he looked around, trembled, and thought himself transported to another world. He was horrified and stunned to find himself on the bare earth, outside his room and his house, without servants, without any help or comfort, amidst the rains, the swirling injuries of the air, and the tempests—stiff with cold, abandoned by an angry heaven, and utterly ruined in all things.

Do you now wish for me to name this man? Forgive me: each of us is that most lost man when we devote ourselves to pleasure, for whom that most wicked traitor servant—namely, the **luxury of the world**—pours out a **trance** <note>original: "catalepsin"; a medical term for a seizure or loss of consciousness, used here to describe spiritual blindness.</note>. Thus we, as good Masters, [are led] toward ruin—

->PRELUDE<-

It is characteristic of one who is drowsy not only to nod off, but to begin to suffer notably from **lethargy** <note>original: "lethargo"; a state of profound spiritual or physical apathy.</note>. We may be moved, plucked at, warned, or pushed, yet we are not roused from our stupor. The **eyes of the intellect** <note>original: "oculos intellectûs"; the capacity for spiritual or rational perception.</note> do not open for those whom cataleptic inclinations overcome; nor do we feel anything while we fall asleep, intoxicated, in the bed of the **delicacies of the flesh** <note>original: "cupediarum carnis"</note>. To be sure, a hawk sometimes flies high into the air, yet it continuously turns its eyes back toward the earth so that it may snatch the prey it desires from there. We imitate this nature and these habits of the **kite** <note>original: "milvi"; a bird of prey often used in moral emblems to represent greed or earthly focus.</note> when we imagine ourselves wise in our finery and luxuries. For we sometimes seek high things by thinking lofty thoughts and transcending the very clouds of heaven; yet, gasping with desire for human things, we perpetually gaze at the ground.

### §. 13.

Through the subtlety and breadth of his words, let that greatest **Teacher of the Church, Aurelius** <note>Refers to St. Augustine of Hippo (Aurelius Augustinus), the influential 4th-century theologian.</note>, provide this more delicate matter which my own lack of skill and insignificance cannot. *Here, the trifles of trifles and the vanities of vanities, pleasures, riches, and friendships hold us back and ensnare us, which tear the garments of our flesh. Riches divide us, and they grant us pride, arrogance, and vanity.* <note>original: "nugæ nugarum, & vanitates vanitatum... fa-ſtus, flatus"</note> I was once asked by a certain student of mine—one more modest and better than the rest—what I might perhaps become if I were to suddenly become rich. I immediately replied with a question of my own: "Tell me, my son, what would you be if you were secretly to become a **lion**?"

> You often ask, my son, what I might happen to be,
> When I become wealthy and suddenly powerful;
> Do you think I can predict my future character?
> Tell me, if you were to become a lion, what kind would you be?

I would have answered with just as much: a lion and a rich man are the same thing, and not without reason. For as long as we are powerful through the means of money—which is the **root of all evils**—and we overflow with a torrent of riches, we then grow proud in the manner of a lion and go beyond our proper bounds. Then the worm of pride in our wealth wounds our soul, intoxicates it, and removes the light of reason; then in...

> In favorable times, man is almost never without arrogance;
> For strong indeed are the feet that can bear the weight of banquets.

> The usual clothes or the old palace please no longer.

Guardians of **silkworms** <note>term: "bombycum" (silkworms). Frequently, they interrupt the work of spinning they have begun and die. We are exactly the same: accustomed to "greener" things—that is, feeding on pleasures—we remain so tender and soft that if we ever begin a good or pious work, we abandon what we started as soon as the first opportunity to sin is offered or the first thunder of temptation strikes. Thus, we mostly die while coddled in our own comforts. 

Therefore, that flower and torch of **Insubria** <note>Refers to the region of Milan. > Abundant things have tripped up and enticed many
> Whom cruel punishments could not break.

The flow of these lines may be slender, but the beauty of these divine meters lies in their virtue. Alas, then, for our madness! But oh, the immense ocean of divine mercy and the unrewardable goodness of God! # PRELUDE

...happens to us; for like a nurse, who, in order to wean an infant, smears her nipples with gall, mustard, or wormwood so that the child, sensing the bitterness, might turn away from sucking the milk; in the same way, God, our most kind nurturer, leads us away from the breasts of this world and the sweet milk of carnal pleasures. He constantly brings our own weakness to our memory, and leads us to a perpetual meditation on death—in which the entire happiness of our life consists—deliberately and with forethought anointing riches, pleasures, and honors with wormwood, aloes, and bitterness.

But to loosen this cord more widely in passing, and to extend it as if through a triad; the first of the three actors presents himself in this theater: the Spartan General **Pausanias** <note>A famous military commander during the Greco-Persian Wars.</note>, who was once puffed up by a certain empty whirlwind of pride in a great assembly of men. He had asked **Simonides the Magus** <note>Simonides of Ceos, a celebrated Greek lyric poet known for his wisdom.</note> to declare to him some noble dogma drawn from the chests of philosophy, or some memorable precept by which he might direct his life, his morals, and his entire way of acting. Simonides, according to the prudence with which he was endowed, and having perceived the King's insolence, wished to render him both holier and wiser. To make those insane swellings of pride subside lest he become too arrogant, he advised that he should keep death always in his mind, and always think that he lived as a mortal, and was therefore exposed to various miseries and soon to die. Indeed, what else did the Philosopher wish to say by this utterance than that no law is more approved, no precept more healthy; no medium or remedy can be more effective for blunting someone's arrogance and defiance than to place before his eyes the vileness of his origin and the nothingness of his condition, and to recall to his mind his end, **death** <term>Libitina</term> <note>original: "Libitinam"; the Roman goddess of funerals and burials, here used as a poetic name for death.</note>, and the funeral rites themselves? A truly distinguished eulogy and an excellent dogma! But rarer things follow. Queen **Semiramis** <note>The legendary and powerful Queen of Assyria.</note> once decreed in the tablets of her will that these characters should be inscribed upon the monument of her tomb: **T. Q. Q. F. R. N. I. A : D. L. S. Q. Q. O.** <note>These initials represent a cryptic Latin puzzle often associated with the vanity of earthly power, likely to be decoded on the following page.</note>

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>A literary term for a work composed in a mixture of prose and verse.</note>

> Whoever you may be of Kings, now in need of gold,
> By rolling back this stone, take as much as you need.
<note>original: "Tu QuisQuis Fueris Regum Nunc Indigus Auri, Devolvens Lapidem, Sumito QuotQuot Opus"</note>

However, when **Darius**, the King of the Persians <note>Darius I (the Great), who ruled the Persian Empire at its peak.</note>, had read these characters and perceived their interpretation, he was spurred on by a greed for gold. With the hope of finding an immense treasure, he proposed to open the tomb and ordered it to be unsealed; but he was deservedly mocked in his hope and fell short of his wish. For nothing was found there except bones, a foul stench, and a decaying corpse, along with these short verses:

> Unless you were wicked and possessed an insatiable hunger for gold,
> You would never have wished to pick the pockets of the dead.
> Such as I lie here rotting, so shall you be,
> You who tread upon my tomb on foot.
> Whether you be Caesar, or the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great.</note>, ruler of the whole world,
> Or Cato, or Cicero, in the end, you shall be just like this.
> Learn to die, traveler, whoever carries back these writings;
> Equal deaths await all men: learn to die.
> Learn to die, O wealthy man; let the King and his flock <note>The common people.</note> learn with the poor,
> The learned and the unlearned, the youth and the elder alike.

And although this was a mockery, and this Queen <note>Though not named here, historical tradition (Herodotus) identifies her as Nitocris of Babylon.</note> had ordered it to be done only for the sake of striking him with shame, we are nonetheless mystically taught here that no better treasure is held in the world, none more splendid, than to have occasionally stirred the bones of the dead. And truly, if anyone wishes to listen to the counsel of death, he would soon become the richest and wisest of men; for he would love all virtues, bid farewell to all vices, send them away, and disregard all the vanity of the world. However, so that the triad <note>The author's structure of three historical examples: Pausanias, Darius, and Zeno.</note> may be made complete, receive with impartial ears this appended saying. It is told of **Zeno** the philosopher <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> that when he once inquired of **Apollo’s** curtain <note>The prophetic tripod or sanctuary of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> by what means he might lead an honest life, direct his morals, avoid vices, pursue virtues, and in what way he might pass the span of his life with honor, he received this response from the inner sanctuary: *That he should consult with those released from their bodies.* <note>A famous philosophical riddle meaning he should read the books of the dead (the ancients).</note>

As I now more carefully weigh and examine this oracle of the **Delphic God** <note>The "Delphic God" refers to Apollo, whose temple at Delphi bore the famous inscription "Know Thyself" (Gnothi Seauton).</note>, it seems that truthful God wished to teach him, and after him all mortals without exception, that there is but one way to lead a holy and praiseworthy life and to close one's final day in the highest happiness: to keep that rapacious and scythe-bearing **Fate, Death** <note>The author refers to the "Parcae," the three Fates of mythology. Here, Death is personified as the one who cuts the thread of life with a scythe.</note>, continually before one's eyes, and to **know oneself**. To know, I say, the moment; to know that he is a man who, from the moment he is born, is already dying; **an example of weakness**, since nothing is weaker than man; **the robbery of time**, because in a single year, month, or day, time snatches him away and strips him now of beauty, now of sight, now of hair, teeth, and bodily strength:

-> Man is a fleeting mushroom, who collapses at the slightest breeze, <-
-> Who remains in no place, however firmly he tries to stand. <-
-> For now he is pressed by the cold, now dissolved by the heat, <-
-> And the burden he carries today, tomorrow will be a funeral. <-

**A game of Fortune**, because when the dice are cast, she makes the rich man poor, and conversely, the honored man contemptible, and vice-versa, according to the quality of the fall of the dice:

-> If Fortune wills, you shall become rich from being poor, <-
-> If this same lady wills, you shall become poor from being rich. <-
-> If Fortune wills, you shall become a leader from a soldier, <-
-> If this same lady wills, you shall become a soldier from a leader. <-

**The scales of calamity**, because man experiences misery and prosperity placed and weighed in an equal balance of the scale;

-> It is said that the Monarch of gods and men <note>A reference to God or Jupiter as the supreme ruler of the universe.</note> <-
-> Once fashioned life for mortals mixed with many griefs. <-

Therefore, as long as we enjoy this light, we seem indeed to live, but more truly we are constantly dying, or at least we retain "life" in name, but in reality we have lost it. Oh, how a certain man—not less in holiness than in **erudition** <note>The text cuts off here. The catchword "dition" completes the Latin word "eruditione."</note>—described this fleeting life of ours in such polished and elegant speech...

<header>A MIXTURE OF PROSE AND VERSE</header>

...most famous in his description, sketched it out when he said: *“Such is our life, brothers, we who lead a fleeting existence; it is like a game played upon the earth, so that while we are nothing, we are born; and once we are born, we are dissolved again. We are a dream that barely holds together, a ghost that cannot be grasped, the flight of a passing bird, the trackless path of a ship on the sea, dust, vapor, morning dew, a flower blooming in its time and in its time withering away.”* Therefore, our life is the mockery of the ages and of time. We draw our shameful origin from a most base matter, and we have scarcely emerged from that filth when we return to it as if with great momentum.

*“A dream is the smoke of a wretched man, whom his own imagination mocks by night, so that in his rest he sees himself as a sublime King on a magnificent throne; yet, when he wakes—having spent the night under the open sky and at a crossroads—he finds himself broken by the hard ground, stiff with cold, naked from poverty, and famished from long hunger.”* A sunshade <note>original: *umbella*</note> is but smoke; if you wish to grasp it in your hand, you cannot. Are not birds and ships also smoke? The birds plow the winds with the rowing of their feathers, and ships plow the sea with the wings of their sails; but they leave only certain traces behind in their passage—traces such that no radiant or sharp eye, however piercing, can follow or survey them.

A tiny grain of dust is smoke, which prepares for itself a fall all the more heavy the higher it allows itself to be carried by the breath of the winds. A little drop of dew is smoke, which scarcely catches sight of the sun before it either yields its place out of reverence, or is consumed and wasted away out of fear and wonder at such splendid majesty. A little flower is smoke, which the sun alone sees open, fragrant, and then dead. Since we and our lives are so many things, it must indeed be said that we are therefore nothing; and we must rightly cry out:

-> How mortal threads hang by such a fragile string, <-
-> As the burden of our wretched living rolls along! <-

For if we look at our body, it is a narrow house, a workshop of miseries; by anagram it is a **pig** <note>The author notes that in Latin, the letters of the word *corpus* (body) can be rearranged to spell *porcus* (pig), a common moralizing wordplay of the era.</note>, a dung-heap covered in snow, which a slight fever uncovers in a single day:

# A MIX OF PROSE AND VERSE
<note>original: *Prosimetricum*. This refers to a literary work that alternates between prose and poetic meter.</note>

It is said that he possessed such power of eloquence, and was able to speak so effectively about the evils of this life, that men were moved to hang themselves. <note>The author likely refers to Hegesias of Cyrene, a philosopher nicknamed "the Orator of Death" because his lectures on human suffering reportedly led his listeners to commit suicide.</note> I do not doubt that you already know that long ago two famous philosophers existed among the Ancients, very different in character and temperament, though little different in doctrine and dogma; one of whom

->Was always loosening his deceptive lips with perpetual laughter,<-

namely, Democritus of Abdera; <note>Democritus (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) was known as the "Laughing Philosopher" because he mocked the follies of mankind.</note> but the other

->Was constantly renewing his loud sighs with continual weeping,<-

whom they called Heraclitus. <note>Heraclitus (c. 535 – c. 475 BCE) was known as the "Weeping Philosopher" due to his melancholy view of the world's transience.</note>

->The former did nothing but laugh, and the latter nothing but weep;<-
->Should the former be laughed at more, or the latter be wept for?<-

The former hissed at the vanities and false follies of this age; the latter wept for human miseries. And rightly so, indeed, and with great reason; for I believe there is no one who does not feel certain depths of sighs and laments erupting in their heart if they walk in their mind through those most abject exclamations <note>original: *epiphonemata*. Rhetorical flourishes or striking summaries.</note> regarding our nature, by which the chief of poets deplore our lot: "A tiny bubble of a bubble, a little shadow of a shadow, a dream of all things," <note>original: *Bullulam bullæ, Umbellam umbræ, Somnium omnium*. If finally one silently ponders so many passages of Holy Scripture where our nature is so far brought down that it seems to be ranked even below worms; would that we sometimes weighed ourselves—the "innards of the earth"—on the fairer scale of reason, and frequently and ardently considered that because we are earth, rot, dust, ash, dung, and pure nothingness, I do not doubt that we would soon fold our wings <note>An idiom for humbling oneself or ceasing to be proud.</note>:

**Others** hold that the present life is more a death than a life; from this, the leader of the moral philosophers, **Seneca**, acutely brought forth the idea when he said, *We die daily*. To those looking more deeply at the truth, however, all life is a punishment: *For what is it to live a long time, except to be tortured for a long time?* <note>Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher whose writings often focused on the preparation for death and the endurance of suffering.</note>

> Is a long day anything to us, if not a long heap
> of sorrows, an age of enduring a long prison?

As the **Royal Songwriter** says: *In the morning it flourishes and passes away; in the evening it falls, grows hard, and withers.* <note>The "Royal Songwriter" or "Citharedo Regio" refers to King David; the quote is from Psalm 90.</note> Ah, a three-day life! A life more shadowy than a shadow, and truly like glass! Swifter than the wind, more unstable than smoke! A life, I say, exposed to ruin; a life for which death constantly spreads its snares! **Others** say that we are all driven to the very same end; that death respects neither the priest’s headbands, nor the bundles of office, nor scepters, nor the executioner's axes. Rather, as the saying goes, death shears us "with a white rule," <note>original: "albâ amuſſi." > Blind Death, alas, knocks with an equal club at the hovels
> of the wretched and royal palaces; it equates scepters with hoes.

It pays no heed to the helmets of Counts, nor the tiaras of Prelates, nor the miters of Popes, nor the crowns of Kings. # PROSIMETRIC PIECE

Finally, the reward of life and honor depends upon the moment of death. In short, all people seem to become philosophers when affliction has fixed its chair among them; by establishing its school, it has tempered its disciples. And thus, as distress—which is the mother of philosophy and wisdom—shapes them, they quickly emerge as wise men and continually seek God.

That huntress of flies, and ingenious weaver and spreader of the snares in which she entangles them, the spider, is said to be endowed with this marvelous property: when the sky is clear, she does not work; but when the air is cloudy and dark, she works very diligently and carefully, perhaps so that she might enjoy the serenity of the ether and the brightness of light later. Just so, a human being is best likened to her in this regard: in the serene and tranquil time of prosperity, living idly, he refuses to work; but on a dark day, covered with clouds, when anxiety presses him, he cries out to the Lord and invokes His name. Then he delights in vigorously sweating over labor and good works, allowing no time to be wrongly wasted. And thus, placed in the chair of affliction and of the cross, he courageously sustains the conclusions of his love toward God and excellently displays the demonstrations of the sciences. <note>The author uses academic language—"conclusions" and "demonstrations"—to suggest that suffering is a rigorous logical proof of one's faith.</note>

->And thus ingenuity comes to miserable affairs.<- <note>original: "Atque venit sic tunc miseris solertia rebus." This is a common Latin sentiment suggesting that necessity is the mother of invention.</note>

From this long series of examples it is now rendered manifest that the "university" <note>The author uses "universitas," meaning the totality or the whole collection of arts.</note> of all arts and sciences is penury and adversity; for it teaches all things so perfectly and exactly that nothing remains imperfect. Likewise, all arts are learned in the <term>phrontisterio</term> <note>From the Greek *phrontisterion*, meaning a "thinking-shop" or a place for deep study and reflection.</note> of poverty: for need has made the most distinguished and numerous philosophers, orators, and poets:

> Bold poverty, deprived of home and land, 
> Drove me to write verses, and to study night and day. <note>A quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 2.2.51–52), describing how he turned to poetry only after losing his inheritance.</note>

And indeed, it has been called by some, not ignorantly, the school of virtue; for it is an effective <term>gymnasium</term> <note>In the classical sense, a place of rigorous training and exercise, both physical and mental.</note> of virtue, forcing even the unwilling to learn. It was just so that it forced Zeno the Scythian <note>This likely refers to Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism. According to legend, he became a philosopher after losing everything in a shipwreck.</note>, whom I brought onto the stage a little earlier when I was reciting the "senate of philosophers"; for he, having been made a merchant from a philosopher, <note>The Latin text says "de philosopho mercator effectus" (made a merchant from a philosopher), though historical accounts usually say he was a merchant who became a philosopher through poverty. # MIXED PROSE AND VERSE

For the entire universe is a home to the poor man, since he has no place of his own. Oh, what excellence, what a prerogative of grace! Where the lowly Christ—Governor of the heavens, Monarch of the Angels, he who is beautiful in form among the sons of men, that sweet bridegroom of virgins—is found, there the poor man shall likewise be! ->We judge you to be wretched, who have never<-
->been wretched, being ignorant of adversity.<-

And thus the reason is now clear why the aforementioned Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BCE), an Athenian statesman who fled to Thebes after being deposed from power.</note>, having been expelled from his leadership in Athens and having traveled to Thebes, began to reason with the philosopher Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a famous Cynic philosopher known for giving away his wealth to live a life of virtue.</note>. > Cursed fate, which favored my sails with a happy wind,
> Yet deprived me until now of the company of so great a man! <note>original: "Sors maledicta... Quæ me huc ufque viri privâfti fœdere tanti." Demetrius ironically calls his former "good luck" cursed because it kept him from the wisdom found in poverty.</note>

Oh, blessed, holy, and thrice-blessed condition of poverty! 
Therefore, the poet wrote not far from reason:

> Indeed, renowned virtue flees riches as its companions.

Or should he not be called dull and insane who, being about to climb the highest mountain, would take up a heavy burden upon his shoulders? Would not everyone cry out that he is thinking of anything less than ascending the slope? A philosopher must be judged to do exactly the same; for if he, chosen for knowledge and sublime things, entangles himself in the anxieties of wealth, the waves of civil life, and the cares of the court, he clearly demonstrates that he labors not at all for God or wisdom, nor does he even dream of them. Therefore, I shall sing about riches with no unworthy voice:

> Flee riches, for they are a heavy weight to one who loves heaven,
> For they destroy the soul and do not allow one to wish for the good.

# PRELUDE

*Heaven, I say, is a heavy burden to a lover [of the world];* <note>original: "Cœlum inquam grave pondus amanti." A variation on a common poetic sentiment that worldly attachments weigh down the soul.</note> because of this couplet <term>distich; two lines of verse</term>, which was cited at the beginning of our Prelude on behalf of poverty, we can also adapt it to wealth in this way:

->*By my genius I was able to transcend the heavenly seats,*<-
->*Were I not turned back and cast to the ground by riches.*<- <note>original: "Ingenio poteram superas transcendere sedes, / Per nisi versus humum praecipitarer opes."</note>

Anaxagoras, that most famous philosopher of Clazomenae <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who famously abandoned his family's estates to live a life of poverty and contemplation.</note>, seems to have understood this very well. In order to better and more quietly devote himself to philosophy, he renounced his wealth and resources. For from this side, the World—like Briareus <note>A giant from Greek mythology with a hundred arms and fifty bellies, used here to represent the overwhelming demands and appetites of a worldly life.</note>—attacks the rich with a hundred arms and fifty bellies; from the other side Argus the sleepless <note>A many-eyed giant from myth who never closed all his eyes at once; here he represents the constant anxiety and vigilance required to manage wealth.</note>, the wakeful dragon, and the lion sleeping with open eyes, blind the wealthy by showing them "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" <note>A reference to the biblical temptation of Christ in the wilderness (Matthew 4:8).</note>. Indeed, the riches and desires of the world are a kind of sweet fodder <note>original: "sagina"; a term often used for the fattening of animals before slaughter.</note> under which the hook of deception and enticement is hidden. It is a fodder that always captures its prey; for wherever there is bait, and birdlime <note>A sticky substance spread on branches to catch small birds.</note> is placed on the branches, and nets are spread out, a catch is usually made. Those who wish to live luxuriously and become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil.

It happens to the wealthy just as I have often observed happens to flies: though they greatly desire honey, they do not know how to set a limit on their appetite for its sweetness. And so, if they find honey anywhere, they immerse and entangle themselves in it to such an extent that they can no longer rescue themselves from it with their feet or wings, as if from a net:

->*Thus those whose chest is heavy with refined gold,*<- <note>original: "Sic quorum gravida est obryzis arca metallis." The term "obryza" refers to gold that has been tested and purified by fire.</note>

Those who dream of nothing but riches night and day; once they have discovered its very pleasing sweetness, they fill, stuff, and gorge themselves so immoderately that they cannot later free themselves from it with heart or soul, as if from a snare. Instead, they perish in the traps of greed and do not achieve the end for which divine providence made them rich. Since, indeed, as if voluntarily, now twice, if I am not mistaken, concerning...

### PROSIMETRICUM <note>A work composed of a mixture of prose and verse.</note>

<center>S 3</center>

Since a discussion of providence has arisen, by Hercules, my memory is opportunely refreshed; for I have heard more than once certain fools ascribing wealth to themselves and their own wisdom because they are rich. Ah, what a bald and insane sketch of Adam’s descendants! <note>original: "Postpartorum Adæ hypotyposis." An <term>hypotyposis</term> is a vivid description or sketch; here, the author uses it to describe the flawed nature of humanity after the Fall.</note> O you who waver in faith, giving more credit to the eye than to the oracle! You certainly rave more enormously than cows, whoever is led and misled by this opinion; let him hear that greatest of friends, Job, speaking and teaching:

> Nothing happens on earth without a cause,
> But all things exist created by number, measure, and weight; <note>This verse alludes to Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>
> As many mortals as we are, we all hang upon the One,
> And the orbit of heaven holds its prescribed laws;

The bad and good things of life, death, poverty, and honor are from God.

> Therefore, it is not to be thought that the rich
> Are found in the world by chance; whatever the Powers Above willed has been done;
> Just as the worrying prudence of men does not bring wealth,

But rather divine providence; *The rich and the poor have met one another, but the Lord is the maker of them both:* <note>A translation of Proverbs 22:2.</note>

> God made both, neither without the will of the Divine. <note>original: "Fecit utrumque Deus, neuter sine numine Divûm."</note>

Yet I wish to add this: if we weigh the things themselves, the progress, and the processes of human life only according to our own foresight or knowledge, we will certainly think many things happen by a certain accident and by luck <term>fortuna; the Roman personification of luck or chance</term>; but if we look to the Divine foresight, to which every single thing and even the smallest details have been foreseen from eternity, nothing happens by the power of Fortune. Instead, all things are referred back to the rule of Divine Providence—those very things which many impious people claim happen as if by chance, rashly, or without any Divine administration.

Have a little patience, if you please; I will give this explained to you by an example. A master of a household <term>Paterfamilias</term> sends out two of his servants—who are unaware of his intention—by different roads, but to the same place. Here, the meeting of one with the other is a matter of "luck" for them, but not for the Master.

# PRELUDE <note>original: "PRÆLUDIUM"</note>

In the beginning of the creation of the human race, God did not make one rich and another poor, but opened the same earth to all.

> (The entire human race arises from a similar origin) <note>original: "Omne genus hominum simili consurgit ab ortu." A line from the philosopher Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*, reminding the reader that all humans share a common birth regardless of social status.</note>
> By what agreement then, since that earth is common to all, do you possess so many acres of it,
> while not even a single clod of soil is available to me?

Therefore, it is necessary, by ascending back through the line of ancestry, to find the Author of injustice who amassed the mammon of unrighteousness. You say, "We shall by no means share our riches and resources with the poor; they are our inheritance and patrimony, which we shall use as we please." O worthless sons <note>original: "filii ficulnei," literally "sons of the fig tree," a Latin idiom for people who are brittle, useless, or of little value.</note>, how truly hollow is the imagination of Mortals! There is no need here for long guessing or lengthy investigation; the matter is plain: the munificent hand of God alone poured all these things out upon you. Whatever gifts are in you, whatever goods, they proceeded from His generous heart. You owe everything you are or have to His bounty, I say—and yet you still say they are yours? Why then do you not take them with you when you are soon to depart from here? Will it not be said to you:

> When the curtain of the Great Theater stands closed,
> When all mortals have played their parts, when finally the Antichrist <note>The author uses "Antichrist" here in a cosmic sense, representing the final act or the end of the world’s worldly drama.</note> has placed the fatal epilogue on the tragedy,
> *Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward?* <note>original: "Reddite rationem villicationis vestræ." A reference to the Parable of the Unjust Steward in the Gospel of Luke 16:2.</note>

Furthermore, grant me pardon, *readers of these early harvests of my meadow*, that I remain stuck here for so long, enticed by such great fertility of this most pleasant field (in which the Winged Farmer <note>original: "Aliger-Agricola." # PRELUDE

# MIXED PROSE AND VERSE
<note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM." A literary style that alternates between prose and poetry.</note>

...let us burst forth into small discourses in this manner, since no proclamation concerning the excellence of this Art can be so ample, no hymn so human, and no song so sublime that it is not surpassed by its immensity and excelled by its height. Truly, the unnavigable height of this <term>Amphitrite</term> <note>original: "Amphitrites." In Greek mythology, the goddess of the sea and wife of Poseidon; here used as a metaphor for the vast, deep ocean of Alchemical knowledge.</note> overcomes the narrowness of human intelligence and nearly the entire faculty of speech, so much so that it is far more sublime than the most excellent geniuses and the most eloquent tongues. Is this not truly that distinguished, incomprehensible book written in golden letters, full of the highest masteries, and filled with the deepest science without the slightest error? Is this not that Labyrinth twisting itself a thousand thousand times in circles and coils, which leads around and drives about those who have once entered? ->§. 16.<-

The poets, those sons of fables, spun from their brains the story that the Gods had heaped <term>Pandora</term> with all kinds of gifts and rewards because she had brought forth a celestial and divine offspring, as can be gathered well enough from her name, which sounds the same in the Greek tongue <note>original: "Argolicè."</note> as "all gifts." This is indeed fabulous and fictional, yet it is certain that <term>Ortho-chemistry</term> <note>original: "Ortho-chymia." ### PROSIMETRIC COMPOSITION
<note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM," a work composed in a mixture of prose and verse.</note>

Are all those in Boeotia <note>A region in Greece whose inhabitants were proverbially considered by Athenians to be dull or "swinish."</note> pigs? # MIXED PROSE AND VERSE <note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM"</note>

V 2

...I wish; for nothing is so incredible that it cannot be made probable through speaking, and nothing is so rough and unrefined that it does not shine through oratory and become, as it were, polished. Because I thought this way, I have acted even more boldly than those very men of whom I speak. **Paracelsus** is a friend to me, **Galen** a companion, and even **Aristotle** and **Hippocrates**; but truth is more beloved. I shall stand by their side only so long as they stand by the truth; I shall agree with them only as long as they agree with the truth and themselves. For **by whomsoever truth is spoken, it is from the Holy Spirit** <note>A famous medieval maxim, often attributed to Ambrosiaster, suggesting that all truth has a divine source regardless of who says it.</note>. Finally, you will have business with me only until some new star flies in from elsewhere—and may faith attend this omen, for I do not live as an empty prophet of things to come—and you, held by its novelty, run toward it as if to a new heavenly body. Nor is there any reason why I should pass this over, for such novelty once led and misled even **Demosthenes**, the prince of the Greeks.

For while he was heading to the school of **Plato**, he once saw a huge crowd of men in the Athenian marketplace listening greedily to a new philosopher, **Callisthenes**, to whom the people had rushed in a swarm due to an "itch for novelty." Demosthenes also approached and listened to him, and, captured by his chatter, he thereafter turned away in disgust from Plato, who nevertheless easily surpassed the other a thousand times over in the solidity of his doctrine. Thus even now, some who are wise in their own opinion are led and misled by novelty; they affect the allurements of speech, like the "Erasmian ladies or monkeys" <note>A likely reference to the satirical writings of Erasmus of Rotterdam, mocking those who mimic intellectual styles without understanding the substance.</note>, and do not pay attention to what tastes of true wisdom.

In these **Practical Lots** <note>original: "Pragmaticis Sortibus"; this likely refers to the title of the author's work or the specific divinatory system he is presenting</note> of mine, do not hunt for gilded eloquence or a decorated style, nor for discourses prepared with cleverness and polish. **The speech that serves the truth ought to be uncomposed and simple** <note>A sentiment famously expressed by the Stoic philosopher Seneca, arguing that truth does not need fancy packaging.</note>, without folds or pleats. Let my words not delight you, but benefit you. It is not my intention merely to stroke the ears or serve their allurements with theoretical and artificial pigments smelling of Cicero's desk <note>original: "Tulliana scrinia"; Marcus Tullius Cicero was the Roman gold standard for ornate oratory</note>, nor to overflow with mere grandiloquence. **Once the matter is understood, we should be flexible in the use of words.**

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

<summary>The author argues that while he respects great authorities like Aristotle and Paracelsus, he prioritizes truth above all, warning the reader not to be distracted by flashy "new" philosophies or ornate rhetorical styles.</summary>

# PRELUDE <note>original: "PRÆLUDIUM"</note>

> What I know is enough for me; I do not seek to be a **Pericles** <note>The famous Athenian statesman known for his powerful oratory.</note>,
> Nor an **Aeolides**, nor to bear the names of the **Neleids** <note>Referring to the descendants of Neleus, such as Nestor, who was famous for speech sweeter than honey.</note>,
> Those who generate bees from their eloquent veins and mouths,
> When they pour out melody and honeyed songs from themselves,
> And their words flash from their pouting lips,
> The polished hiss of thunderous **Persuasion** <note>original: "Suadæ", the Roman goddess of persuasion.</note>,
> Refined beauties to be mixed with **Hyblaean** honeycombs <note>Honey from Mount Hybla in Sicily was famous in antiquity for its superior quality.</note>:

Truly "goldenly" <note>An adverbial play on the "golden" speech he is about to reject.</note> and here as a *broker of eloquence*, let us not seek the little flowers of words; he who seeks the fruit of maturity despises the pleasantness of the fields. What use is a golden key if it does not open what we want? Therefore, in this midday light, all those who expect me to be a "buskined" <term>Orator</term> <note>A "buskined" orator refers to the high boots (cothurni) worn by tragic actors, implying a pompous or overly dramatic style.</note>, or a sacred <term>Preacher</term> <note>original: "Ecclesiasten"</note> rhetorizing from a more sublime place, are entirely in the dark. I shall strive to be plainly "flat-footed" <note>original: "planipes", referring to a mime actor who performed without the high boots of tragedy; here meaning a humble, direct style.</note> and more **Laconic** <note>Concise and blunt, like the ancient Spartans.</note> than **Asiatic** and redundant. I shall endeavor to act more through <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole, implying brevity.</note> than through paraphrase. I shall labor, I say, not only with short little verses (the kind that usually belong to the *dwellers of Elysium*) but also with signs, syllables, and indeed mere monosyllables, if it were possible to represent these things briefly, as if in a mirror—namely, to impart the truth to you, and the reality of the matter. Thus I shall be eager to gratify your minds: I shall discourse on the truth, I shall act plainly; for I have not been eloquent "since yesterday or the day before" <note>A biblical allusion to Moses’ speech in Exodus 4:10, where he claims he is not a man of words.</note>.

> Indeed, I shall not strive for this: that my pages should swell 
> With "bubbling trifles," or to adorn my papers with white-lead makeup:

To pursue the truth inwardly will be my aim; the hinge of the whole matter will turn on this. I believe you prefer a "flat-footed" plainness under a shabby hood <note>A reference to the humble clothing of a monk or simple scholar.</note>, rather than <term>philology</term> covered in gold under a fine gown.

# PROSIMETRIC <note>A literary style that mixes prose and verse (original: "PROSIMETRICUM").</note>

...from the blows of disputes, they offer no small grace to the wise; for daily, examples are seen in them of what *we* ought to avoid. Nevertheless, nearly the entire modern age stands as a defender of their most tasteless trifles—which is no wonder, since the World does not seek truth, but only its own masks. They act exactly as if someone were to fashion the character of **Hylas** <note>A youth in Greek mythology, a companion of Hercules, known for his beauty.</note> or **Hyacinthus** <note>A beautiful youth loved by the god Apollo.</note> through a most absurd eunuch-actor; and yet, I believe, the prey would not be snatched away by the Nymphs because of it, nor would **Apollo** <note>The Greek and Roman god of the sun, music, and prophecy.</note> renew the shade of the dead youth into a flower.
