# PRELUDE <note>original: "PRÆLUDIUM"</note>

...would not admit any disciple or listener who did not pledge himself to keep silence for a fixed time—usually five years, or at least two, at the teacher's discretion and pleasure, according to the estimated grasp and skill of each. To be silent, I say, and so strictly indeed that throughout that whole period of sworn silence, it was forbidden to inquire about what they poorly understood, or to speak or comment on what they had heard. Those assigned to that period were called "listening and silenced auditors."

->O man of exceptional, crafty cunning!<-

He, so to speak, fished for dolphins and whales with an iron hook—and caught them for certain—while meanwhile those other **word-grinders** <term>Tritologists</term> <note>From the Greek 'tritos' (worn down) and 'logos' (word); those who wear out language through trivial or repetitive analysis.</note> shout themselves hoarse, catching barely a few earthworms with a golden hook. This is because, enslaved to their senses like African hens <note>Guineafowl, which were noted by ancient writers for their loud, incessant cackling and lack of intelligence.</note>, they fix the blind eyes of their minds so stubbornly upon the noisy rattle of words that they never strive to grasp the sweetest juice of nature or the very truth of the matter. **Anacharsis** <note>A 6th-century BCE Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens and was known for his blunt, "barbarian" wisdom.</note>, the philosopher of Scythian stock, used to sing his mockery of the foolishness and absurdity of the **Greeks** <note>original: "Danaï"</note>:

> There are Great Greeks philosophizing with words,
> But babbling <note>original: "affaniantes"</note> in life, vices, and manners.

**Plato** likewise rebukes these same Greeks in the *Timaeus*, saying: *“You are always children, and no Greek is an old man.”* Both authors condemn their chatter and wordiness, because while they taught many things and handed down various precepts in magnificent and bombastic words, they carried out nothing—or at least very little—in practice. Yet how much more correctly and truly can this be said of the **Laureated Chair-holders** <note>Scholars who hold official academic positions or degrees; literally "those crowned with laurel in their professorial chairs."</note> who lack either one of these!

> But ah! Whither, O tongue, do you rush? One must say "nothing" <note>original: "mu," representing the Greek letter or the smallest sound.</note> about these men;
> This will not suit the strings [of my lyre]; where does the tongue stumble?
> Cease to tax the manners of the reigning Gods <note>Likely referring to high-ranking academics or powerful church authorities.</note>,
> And to measure great wealth <term>Aquifundia</term> <note>Vast estates or overflowing resources; a play on 'latifundia' (large estates).</note> by small tasks.

# PRELUDE <note>original: "PRÆLUDIUM"</note>

...not only the venerable antiquity of the first philosophers and the most evident monuments of ancient volumes, but even against the most eloquent experiments of the matter and irrefragable <note>irrefutable or undeniable</note> truth.

->By what art, being deceived, they frustrate the rest with the same;<-

For we all always prefer to believe rather than to inquire, and to be idle rather than to work; and indeed, the enemy of this truth is sometimes his own worst foe, for no other motive or cause than that he was so thoroughly imbued by the Teachers in the Academies. But later, weighing the matter more deeply and highly, and judging it from the very works of nature, I found myself miserably blinded <note>original: "implanatum"; literally "plastered over" or "beclouded," referring to being misled by superficial learning.</note>,

> For Error deceives with the splendor and shadow of science,
> So that it is beautiful to be pointed out with a finger, and for it to be said, *this is he!* <note>A reference to the Roman satirist Persius, mocking the vanity of being recognized as a "great scholar."</note>
> Thus study inflates the ego; hence I thought I knew many things;

And in truth, I was wandering in the densest shadows of ignorance, groping just as the blind feel along walls. In the likeness of a parrot <note>original: "psittaci"; used here to mock students who merely repeat what they hear without understanding.</note>—I speak from experience—I held nothing but some assertions:

->I held their Cathedral dogmas and naked words:<- <note>original: "Cathedrales"; referring to the *cathedra* or the professor's chair of authority from which academic dogmas were dictated.</note>

Although just *yet* I have nothing certain known or discovered: for as far as *Theology* is concerned, I am utterly ignorant of all things; as for *Philosophy*, I am skilled in very few; regarding *Mathematics* <note>original: "Mathesis"; in this period, this often encompassed the "Quadrivium": arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>, I am another ignoramus; in short, as for all other *Sciences and Arts*, I know nothing—to God be the praise, glory, and grace. For as much as concerns the *interpretation of the law*, otherwise right, which...

# PROSIMETRICUM <note>A literary work that mixes prose and verse.</note>

...your own women, without a doubt, know how to explain these things better than I, and they will inform you sufficiently. Furthermore, as far as *Alchemy* is concerned—otherwise known as the *Philosopher’s Stone*—bakers, ditch-diggers, or even cleaners of latrines <note>original: "latrinarum purgatores"</note> can fashion it more skillfully than I. If, therefore, I were to betake myself to the Abbot of the Clerics of Anticyra <note>Anticyra was a Greek city famous for hellebore, a plant used to treat madness; an "Abbot of Anticyra" is a mock title for a leader of fools or the insane.</note>, I would do nothing unworthy of my station; for where I should even begin, I do not know. In all things I hear that I am quite ingenious, but I must look through something nearly ten times before I am able to read it.

I myself, a little while ago, when I was reviewing the lineages of the philosophers, as it were, said that the greatest men were foolish, raving, and out of their minds. If none of them saw the truth concerning the *Matter of the philosophers* <term>Re philosophorum: the fundamental substance or "Great Work" sought by alchemists</term>, it is to be feared that it is nothing at all. For these things which I write are entirely fictional, scarcely worthy of the late-night toils of old women. Because of this, I have no doubt that it will seem a paradox to many that I (who have always been, and presently am, the "swine among asses" <note>A self-deprecating Latin idiom roughly meaning "the lowliest of the low" or "the odd one out."</note>) have proceeded to such a point of rashness and audacity. The same must be said regarding the matter at hand: it is certainly no small proof of stupidity to celebrate some philosopher—even if he were more philosophical than Hermes <note>original: "Hermete... philosophiorem" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "thrice-great" founder of Hermetic philosophy, often cited as the ultimate source of wisdom.</note>—or to proclaim a Commentator <note>term for a scholar who writes explanatory notes on classic texts, often used in medieval universities to refer to the philosopher Averroes.</note> even more famous than Caesar, if his soul is not imbued with true wisdom and clothed on every side with Christian virtues. Conversely, those "Narcissuses"—the well-dressed, the belted ones, the darlings of their parents—are often stupid, dull, useless as fungi, and even perverse, intractable, and unteachable. Hear a wonder!

A Little Lordling <note>original: "Dominellus"</note> and a Poor Fellow <note>original: "Pauperculus"</note> both enter a marketplace shop together. The former wears rich, studded, and fringed clothing; the latter is dressed in common, torn, and filthy rags. A calculation begins to be made regarding them: who carries more value? Regarding the Little Lordling, there is no doubt that he is judged to be as laden with gold and silver as his outward appearance and physical attire are beautiful. The Destitute Man <note>original: "Inopulum"</note>, however, is thought to bring nothing besides his patchwork rags and an old, worn-out cloak. When it comes down to business and each is searched separately, it is discovered that the public judgment was very far off. For he who was thought to be opulent is found to be poor and without coins, shining only as far as that exterior appearance he was flaunting. But the one who was counted among the beggars is found to have no patch on his poor clothing that is not lined with a silver shield-coin <note>original: "scutatum"</note> or stuffed with ducats of the purest gold. Ha! Who would have thought it?

Rightly, therefore, and with great charm, did that most illustrious star of moral philosophy, Seneca, say: *A sword is certainly not good because it has a gilded belt or a scabbard distinguished by gems, but because it has a sharp edge for cutting. What of it? Is not a steel sword often hidden in a rotten scabbard, and conversely, a rusty or leaden one in a jeweled one? Is not wisdom often found under a dirty cloak? Do we not see...*

*Therefore I say*, it is nothing other than a comedy of all mortals, a play exhibited in a theater, where many characters are indeed introduced, but all walk about transformed in costume. No one retains their true form or their natural state, <note>original: "eunuchiámque" — likely used here to mean a state of being stripped of one's external "manhood" or social potency, referring to the "naked" or unadorned self.</note> but each is dressed and adorned by the director according to the role. He knows how he must use each person, assigning to each their fitting character and mask <note>original: "persona" — in Roman theater, this specifically referred to the physical mask worn by actors to project their voice and character.</note> as the logic of the play requires. He makes one a source of wisdom (an old man) though he is young; he fashions another as a youth, though otherwise he is old. He adorns this one with gold, gems, ribbons, and precious clothes as if he were a rich man, though at times he is very poor. To another, he does the opposite, likening him to a beggar though he is otherwise wealthy. He introduces another as one wonderfully powerful, a Prince or a King, though the person himself is otherwise contemptible. Quite often in this grand play, someone is decorated with high honor,

->Who nevertheless is worthy of the name of no title.<-

Another is held in contempt who nevertheless would deserve every tribute of praise. God is that sole Dramatist <note>original: "Dramatistes" — the playwright or director who conceives the entire performance.</note> who brings us out onto this amphitheater of his. He knows what pertains to the play; he uses the labor of us all for his own work. He knows where he must destine each individual thing for his own glory. He is the only one who knows us all; he knows each person in their true form, whereas we can only know who anyone is once the story of our life is completed. Because as many as are in this play, no one has their genuine and proper form as long as the play lasts; no one can be distinguished—whether they be master or servant, rich or poor, young or old.

Is the eye not captivated by the sight of the heavenly arch, which is called a rainbow <term>iris: the personification of the rainbow in mythology, used here for the phenomenon itself</term>, which one concludes is colored, even though sound philosophy teaches that no color is actually present there? <note>This reflects the early scientific view that the rainbow's colors are "apparent" or "emphasized" by light rather than being inherent pigments in the sky.</note> Without doubt, the sun is much larger than the earth, and yet a rustic and barbarian man, who is ruled by sight alone, would say the opposite. “Yesterday I deceived the birds, but today you have deceived me, the artist.” <note>This refers to a famous anecdote from Pliny the Elder about the rival Greek painters Zeuxis and Parrhasius. Zeuxis painted grapes so realistically that birds pecked at them, but Parrhasius then painted a curtain so realistically that Zeuxis asked him to pull it aside to show the painting, thus deceiving the master artist himself.</note>

Therefore, as we have seen, our sight errs—specifically in its judgment of the mental talents of certain people. But if we also consult our hearing and command people to speak, we will soon recognize those who seemed wise and learned to us to be fools and dullards, and vice versa. Thus, when a wealthy man once sent his young son to **Socrates** so that he might inspect the boy's nature, the tutor said, *“Father has sent his son to you, O Socrates, so that you might see him.”* Then the **Athenian elder** <note>original: "senex Actæus." Actæus refers to Attica or Athens.</note> said to the boy, *“Speak, then, young man, so that I may see you,”* <note>original: "loquere ergo... adolescens, ut te videam"</note> as if secretly suggesting that a man's character does not shine forth from his face as much as from his speech—that is, it is discerned not so much by sight as by hearing.

> Although faith is seen to be always uncorrupted,
> Even when wounded by the biting needle of envy;
> And though malice is the customary companion and enemy of virtue,
> Through which celebrated honor is buried by foul poison;

As my **Messenger** <note>This "Messenger" (Nuntius) likely refers to a character in a contemporary play or a specific philosophical source the author is citing.</note> says eloquently and gracefully: *“Just as there is no fire without smoke, so there is no virtue without envy”*; and, *“just as a shadow follows those walking through the sun, so too does the madness of malice follow those walking the path of glory and virtue.”* Similarly, since envy is the handmaid of rising men and of mortal successes—and since not even **Jupiter** himself can please everyone, whether he brings rain or clear skies—it is finally a most difficult thing to provide work that is pleasing to an ungrateful World. These envious people are worthy of brotherly pity rather than anger, until they might eventually free themselves from the agonizing prison of their own malice, in which they are tortured by way of retaliation—let that be their rack! Truly, it is a rabid vice and an evil of the underworld! Oh, what a bloodstained beast! How much it is to be pitied: the heart that you invade, and the soul which you occupy and torment! 

Who then is the man, whose heart is otherwise wise, who would complain about envy if he happens to suffer it? For is anyone either more fortunate than the object of envy, or more unhappy than the envious person? Is there anything more praiseworthy, anything more worthy of eternal praise, than to perform such great wonders from which envy might arise in others?

Who *ever* envied a bad man? Who *never* envied a good man? Look—envy is the companion of virtue, which mostly follows—and indeed pursues—the Good! Although I would easily believe that not a few men, otherwise conspicuous for their learning, have refused to let their sleepless labors <term>vigilias</term> <note>original: "vigilias" - literally "watchings," referring to scholarly works produced by staying up late at night</note> come into the light for this reason alone: that they greatly feared and dreaded the insults of chatterers and the mouths of those who bark at them (considering today's infinite itch <term>cacoëthes</term> <note>original: "cacoëthes" - a term from the Roman satirist Juvenal meaning a malignant habit or "itch," specifically for slandering or writing</note> for slandering), which are accustomed to spare no writer, however wise. And indeed, not without reason; for there is truly no one who binds himself to more judgments than he who applies his mind to scholarly labor, especially in this age, which has become so accustomed to the delights of archaism that unless aphorisms are subtle, polished, refined, and most carefully cultivated, they are hardly sellable. Thus, he who is allowed to lie hidden and retreat into cover can deservedly triumph. Therefore, I had never decided to publish anything in print, especially since I am not unaware that in this kind of commentary many before me have worn themselves out in vain, whose books are carried around ridiculously. Furthermore, I was not unaware of this very "nosy" century <note>original: "nasutum hoc sæculum" - a play on the word "nasutus," meaning both having a large nose and being critically witty</note>, in which:

-> Even boys have the nose of a rhinoceros: <note>original: "Et pueri nasum Rhinocerotis habent" - a quote from the poet Martial (1.3.6), meaning even children have a sharp, mocking sense of criticism.</note> <-

Therefore, I thought it much safer to *toil* quietly at home than to *go* into public with disgrace; since, as human customs are now, no thing, no business, no work is undertaken for such just causes that there are not those present who would carp at it or pierce it with their slanders;

-> By Pollux, no one will go safer than Antimachus, nor Homer; <note>Antimachus of Colophon was a Greek poet often compared to Homer; the author implies even the greatest writers are not safe from criticism.</note> <-
-> And envious Fate <term>Parca</term> <note>One of the Parcae, or Fates, here personifying spiteful destiny</note> pinches even the great Gods. <-

He who intends to go into public takes upon himself as many censors <term>censores</term> <note>Official critics or evaluators of conduct and writing</note> against himself as he has readers; for *some* stir up complaints against him because he is long-winded; *others* because he is brief; *this one* because he brings nothing new but acts out an old play; *that one* because he departs from the common way of handling a subject; *another*...

### PRELUDE

[One] notes the style, *that one* the thread of speech, *another* critiques the text; *many* are indignant because the work proceeds in verse; *very many* cry out against "barbarous, obsolete, and foot-and-a-half-long words" <term>sesquipedalia verba</term> <note>original: "sesquipedalia verba" — a famous expression by the Roman poet Horace referring to long, pompous words that take up "a foot and a half" of space.</note> which they perhaps have not encountered before. In short, any commentator provides almost as many judgments against himself as words he explains.

For this reason, it has always been a matter of great fear for all wise men to release anything to the public; for doing so is like putting one's hand into a most scorching flame, exposing oneself to the tongues of those who would stab, and turning the arrows of every curse against oneself—especially if the matters under discussion are heavy and significant. Since the hidden treasure, which is sung of here in oracular style, almost transcends human understanding, I fear being seen as unfaithful to the truth <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> while I proceed to reveal its hidden mysteries so clearly and concisely; especially because I know it is necessary:

-> To choose subject matter that is equal to our strengths as writers, <-
-> and to weigh for a long time what our shoulders refuse to bear. <-
<note>original: "Sumere materiam, nostris, qui scribimus, æquam / Viribus, & pensare diu, quid ferre recusent" — another citation from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* advising authors to know their own limits.</note>

For it is the mark of an imprudent man to not know his own measure; *and furthermore*, I recall that everyone is deceived by their own writings and misses the errors; for just as even deformed children delight their parents and seem most beautiful to them, so too do harsh and unseemly verses thrill their creators and seem the best to them. From this it happens that, since they are pleased with their own work, they easily allow it to emerge into the public light. But the "benefit" they gain from this is that, where they falsely flattered themselves that they would acquire praise and the glory of a name, they instead bring upon themselves no small insult and disgrace; while their ignorance and stupidity, which was previously hidden, is now made manifest to the whole world.

-> Like a scabby baldness more worthy of a laugh, <-
-> Which stands naked, though previously it was clothed in hair. <-
-> The clever monkey facetiously mimics human form and gesture, <-
-> While it sits properly upon the ground. <-

# PROSIMETRICUM <note>A literary work that mixes prose and verse.</note>

> But the more he lifts himself up, the more he is seen
> ->to be an ape with a bare backside.<-
> <note>original: "Sed quantò ſe plùs effert, tantò magis ipſe / Conſpicitur culo Simius eſſe glabro." This was a common proverb in the Renaissance: the higher a monkey climbs, the more it exposes its unsightly parts. It serves as a warning against vanity.</note>
> Thus also the vainglorious, whom a great name has driven,
> ->the more conspicuous they are, the more ridiculous they become:<-
> For indeed, he who rashly undertakes things greater than himself,
> ->if he becomes conspicuous, he also becomes ridiculous:<-

Truly, I ask, whom would these things not terrify, even the strongest Achilles? <note>Achilles is used here as the archetype of the most fearless man.</note> And in truth, I thought these things should be weighed all the more firmly by me, as both the faculty of my talent and the comfort of my life are lesser, while there is now a greater abundance and richness of Treatises <term>Tractatuum</term> <note>Scholarly or systematic discussions of a subject.</note>, not only of ancient writers but also modern ones. Consequently, there is a more savage and prone playfulness, and a desire to reject everything; so much so that now, in the present appearance of this ulcerated age, he who publishes his works seems to do nothing more than spread a table for detractors and critics <term>obrectatoribus</term>, who tear apart and gnaw everything served—not with manners, I say, but with violent, gaping jaws <term>rictibus</term> and crooked teeth. They do this not only to what displeases them, but even to what greatly pleases them from time to time, like cats that are accustomed to growl all the more vehemently at someone the more elegant a morsel they feel has been offered to them.

Although I, for my part, have always judged that a wise man should care nothing, or at least very little, about such backbiters, but should always consider them of no value <term>floccipendendum</term> <note>original: "floccipendendum" — literally "to weigh as a tuft of wool," meaning to consider something worthless.</note>;

> For what the envious crowd has taken from me while alive,
> ->the trumpets will return a thousandfold with interest after death.<-
> The heralds of a name never sound during life,
> ->but those things are accustomed to rise up only after death.<-

Therefore, who would not attribute it to imprudence and faint-heartedness if someone were deterred from a work—otherwise painstaking and wonderfully desirable to many—due to fear of those who rebuke and detract? For, as Ecclesiastes <note>A book of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon.</note> says: *he who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap.*

> You wait like a peasant for the river to flow past; but it glides on,

Nor is there any reason why I should greatly fear the furrowed brows and censures of the "Aristarchuses" and Critics <term>Aristarchorum</term> <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famous library scholar in Alexandria known for his rigorous—and often harsh—criticism of Homer. In this, I would undoubtedly be acting more justly and reasonably than Virgil, that easily first among the Latin Epic poets. After he had produced that world-famous and scarcely ever sufficiently praised glory of the *Aeneid*, he was so displeased with his own work that when, oppressed by illness, he saw death approaching, he earnestly and stubbornly begged his dearest friends to destroy the work and commit it to be swallowed by the flames. He judged it unworthy to be presented to the eyes of the Wise. Therefore, let it be permitted for me, with a thousand times more justification, to sing:

# PROSIMETRICUM

[...from Hermo]genes I accepted it, so that I would not go forth into the market without merchandise, nor leave the tavern without paying my share <term>asymbolus</term> <note>original: "asymbolúsque." From the Greek *asymbolos*, referring to someone who attends a social gathering or feast without contributing their portion of the cost.</note>. I do this to show by my own example that in great matters, the intention alone is usually enough. Whether or not I have achieved what I intended, I leave to the conscience, time, and experience of each reader; nevertheless, I have played my part.

> But if strength should fail, our boldness was
> ->a thing of praise; for in great things, to have willed is enough.<-
> <note>original: "Quod si defuerint vires, audacia nobis / Laus fuit, in magnis nam voluisse sat est." A quote from the Roman poet Propertius (2.10.5-6), a common defense for authors attempting ambitious projects.</note>

For if it is a great thing to understand individual disciplines <term>disciplinas</term> <note>Referring to the various branches of knowledge or the liberal arts.</note>, how much greater is it to understand them all? This is necessary for those who have set themselves the goal of finding the truth, and who must speak both against and on behalf of all philosophers <term>philosophos</term>. I do not claim to have attained the ability for such a vast and difficult thing, but I profess to have pursued it. Although I knew myself to be many miles <term>parasangis</term> <note>original: "parasangis." A Persian unit of distance (roughly 3-4 miles). The author uses it metaphorically to say he is "far off" from being equal to the task.</note> unequal to this task, I nevertheless preferred to be exposed to the display and mockery of all, and to commit myself to the theater of the world and the danger of rash judgments, rather than deny the labor of my messenger Mercury <term>Paraphrastæ Mercurio</term> <note>Mercury was the god of eloquence and interpretation. A "Paraphrast" is one who clarifies a text. The author refers to his own interpretive writing as his "Mercury."</note> in such a useful and religious purpose. Having resolved to risk the dice of fear rather than hang longer in suspense between hope and fear.

And although once again the current condition of this degenerate age could easily deter anyone from such an undertaking—an age in which the minds of men are so idle and bitter <note>original: "malè feriati & exacerbati." Literally "badly holiday-making," describing people who use their leisure time for spite or destructive criticism.</note> that, if possible, they would abolish all effort and use from our midst—therefore (unless I divine wrongly) there will be hundreds <note>original: "sexcenti," literally "six hundred," a standard Latin idiom for an indefinitely large number.</note> who will interpret *this fatal task of mine* as a sign of foolishness, or others as impudent pride. They will wonder how I, who cannot present myself through great studies, practices, or the talents of my station, have dared to attempt such an arduous thing. This is especially true in that kind of Art <term>Artis</term> <note>In this context, "The Art" usually refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work" of Hermetic philosophy.</note> in which other men, so illustrious and gifted with such experience and learning, have always worked with the greatest diligence; and in which many others, swept away by the shipwrecked <term>navifragâ</term> desperation of their own genius, have miserably stuck in the water.

# P R Æ L U D I U M
<note>Prelude</note>

Yet this is the one thing by which I hope to be able to defend that boldness of mine—or as the envious might call it, my [rashness]—both before God (by whose unspeakable grace and kindness toward me I have recorded these things, and by which they have been brought to a successful conclusion <term>colophonem</term> <note>original: "colophonem." Historically, a "colophon" refers to the finishing stroke or the completion of a work.</note>, and will continue to be) and before myself: namely, that I have been devoted not so much to catching the breeze of favor, and much less of human honor—since I hide both my head and my body—but rather to the study of a fated genius and public utility, and moved solely by the motive of uprooting the truth itself. It is for this reason that I have entered this labyrinth entangled with a thousand windings <term>mæandris</term> <note>A reference to the Meander River, used metaphorically for complex or circuitous paths.</note> and errors, and this undared and treacherous sea, which is almost unsearchable even with the longest plummet <term>bolide</term> <note>original: "bolide." A sounding lead or plummet used by sailors to measure the depth of water.</note> of reason; indeed, it is the most hidden and veiled mystery of all the earthly <term>sublunarium</term> <note>original: "sublunarium." Literally "below the moon," referring to the changing, corruptible world of Earth in the Aristotelian cosmos.</note> secrets of God.

From this, surely, for anyone who weighs the matter a little more fairly, it should not be criticized, but rather greatly wondered at, how I—still a stranger in this work, whatever it may be, with equal daring and fear, without means or money on the journey, and having no book or companion—have brought it to a port more truly desired than hoped for, in the worst of times, when the burdens of extreme necessity and the most diverse cares of obtaining food and clothing extort everything. I have done so with the All-Knowing Leader as my guide, who was the author of this present web <note>The author uses the metaphor of weaving a textile ("tela") to describe his writing.</note>, and who will, I hope, happily direct the mind (easily conscious of its own weakness) and the hand itself even to the end:

> In many ways I have been led astray, by disease, imprisonment, and poverty:
> Then fear drives all wisdom out of my heart;
> *Mice, lice, and dormice, daily in my dreams*
> *Threaten wretched punishments and evils for my life;*
> There is no one of such firm character and great confidence
> Who would not shrink back with fearful blood and waste away with dread.

From which it is now clearly evident, by Hercules, that the conditions of fortune have not smiled enough upon these Symbols and their Symbol-Writer <term>Symbolographóque</term>, and therefore not

### PROSIMETRICUM
<note>A work composed in a mixture of prose and verse.</note>

...not rarely have I myself been of the opinion—perhaps because God did not wish these things to come out into the public—that I should often resolve to turn my mind entirely away from their publication. Indeed, I do not know why the outcome of my fate has nonetheless not matched my proposal; but if by chance you, on account of my midnight labors <term>lucubrationes</term> <note>original: "lucubrarum" [sic, lucubrationum]. This refers to scholarly work done by lamplight late at night.</note>,

> Shall be my readers, and not burdened in the least
> To have offered me your right hands and given your coins,
> I shall bind you, I shall praise you, and I shall bless you.
> <note>The author here adapts a playful and somewhat aggressive Roman poetic style to address his patrons and readers.</note>

That famous Thales of Miletus (who, because of the outstanding sharpness of his intellect, was once the first in Greece to be greeted with the title of "Sage") when he learned that Pherecydes of Syros—a man of no common learning—intended to discourse upon the sacred mysteries before a gathered assembly, signaled to him in writing that it seemed better to him if he kept those difficult matters at home. He suggested that, having called aside only his companions of a fairer judgment and more mature refinement, he should propose them for discussion; for those subtle and sublime concepts would bring no value, or certainly a very meager one, to the grasp of the thick-headed and unskilled multitude. 

While I was meditating on this excellent lesson from Thales, directed to *men girt for action* <note>original: "viri accincti," a metaphor for those prepared for difficult labor or spiritual struggle.</note>, I know not what urge came often to my mind and plucked at my ear regarding that most profound part of the Hermetic Art which treats the *Philosopher’s Stone* <note>original: "Lapide Philosophico."</note>. It warned me that a burden of this kind, once taken upon the shoulders, ought not to be rashly scattered among the common folk, but rather that it would be more well-advised to review it in a familiar gathering of learned men.

By my faith, I would truly be pleased if the matter could be handled so: but where, I pray, could you find the places where those mystic things regarding the *heavy and pregnant Galena of the philosophers* <note>original: "gravi prægnantíque philoſophorum Galenâ." Galena is a lead ore; in alchemy, it often refers to the "raw material" from which the secret essence is extracted.</note> are not hidden? For although there is almost no region of the world, nor any city, that does not swarm with at least some people devoted to the "Love of Magic" <term>Philomagia</term> <note>A term coined to describe the pursuit of occult or divine wisdom.</note>, who, relying on the whims of their own minds, dare even to promise themselves—with wondrous boasting and contentiousness—a "cyclopedic" or all-encompassing knowledge of this mastery; yet today, everyone is so pleased with their own inventions...

### PRELUDE

Nevertheless, if you see how those people progress and how they act, when you have thoroughly examined the matter, you will undoubtedly find that they are not only ignorant of what constitutes the **orthophysical** <term>orthophysica</term> <note>A term derived from Greek, meaning "naturally correct" or "according to the true laws of nature." The author is arguing that many seekers use materials that defy natural laws.</note> matter of this **Secret** <note>original: "Secretum." In this context, the "Secret" refers to the Great Work of Alchemy—the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, as well as the knowledge necessary for directing and perfecting it, and finally the proper method of forming it; but furthermore, you will see that they adopt things for themselves which are alien and foreign to the business of constructing the Stone, and indeed too contrary to it. From this it happens that, at last, the longer and more expensively they have been intent upon the work, the more truly does that fate happen to them which a certain more deceptive writer among us divined would befall them: namely, that instead of a *Magiolith* they find a *moriolith*. <note>original: "Magiolitho... moriolithum." This is a clever pun. Magiolith (Stone of the Magi/Wisemen) is contrasted with *moriolith* (Stone of Fools), from the Greek *moria* meaning folly.</note> With such brains, then, I ask you: *who would reason freely and willingly on this matter?*

Wherefore, *Brothers inclined toward the art*, I have judged that my candid, laconic poetry would be more laborious for me (given their fantastical leisure), but more pleasing and far more useful for you. For unless they abstain entirely, they will at least be warned here about revoking their poorly instituted work; *commonly, it is said that it is better to run back than to run badly.* <note>original: "vulgò, ſatiùs eſt, dicitur, recurrere, quàm currere malè." This is a Latin proverb suggesting it is better to start over than to continue on a wrong path.</note> And so, I consider again with myself that it is not enough to know what you know, but that it also pertains to the public utility to reveal through writing what is in the public interest, for the public, and publicly. Away with you then, away from here, you deceitful and proud ones! We do not want eagles—which fly sublimely at the borders of the sun—but rather birds, birds that nest low, on the roof, and often on the ground. <note>The author uses "eagles" as a metaphor for those with overly lofty, unrealistic, or arrogant ambitions, preferring "birds that nest low"—humble, grounded seekers of truth.</note> To such people I whisper these things not in *meter*, but as if by voice and with a certain secret *chalk* <note>original: "cretâ." Literally "chalk," but often used metaphorically for a mark, a shorthand, or a secret sign of distinction.</note>; and so that they may be "tongueless" in retaining these things, I seal their mouths by the religion of a most holy oath. These *Initiated Brothers*, when they hold these things with us, shall also hold with us the duty to sing immortal thanks for such a great privilege to the Eternal and Unborn God. But now, so that I may purge myself of all envy, I shall set forth the opinions of the Ancients concerning the **Discovery of the Gods** <note>original: "Invento Deorum." A high-flown alchemical term for the Stone, suggesting it is a divine revelation or a substance used by the gods.</note>, at which point all seem to be summoned so that they may judge which of them is true:

<header>-> MIXED PROSE AND VERSE <-</header>

<note>original: "Prosimetricum." A literary form combining prose and poetic meter, often used in antiquity and the Renaissance for satirical or philosophical works.</note>

> Begin now to forge verses upon the deep lathe,
> And come into your role, Little Poet.

Then at last the **Lyceum** <note>original: "Lyceum." The school founded by Aristotle, used here to represent the assembly of philosophers and scholars.</note> will seem bold to me: if either everyone agrees, or if someone is found who has discovered what is true; and so I might delight to cry out, as **Statius** does in his *The Young Friends* <note>original: "Statius in synephebis." Referring to Caecilius Statius, a Roman comic poet. The "Synephebi" (The Young Friends) was one of his famous plays.</note>: "O gods of all my fellow youths! > *A prostitute refuses to take money from a lover who is a friend.*

But rather, I cry out so that they may be present, that they may learn, and that they may notice what must be thought concerning the **Invention of the Immortal Philosophers**, and concerning the sublime mastery of the **magolith** <term>magolith</term> <note>A term coined from "magus" (wise man/magician) and "lithos" (stone), referring to the Philosopher's Stone. For all these things must be referred back to this inscription concerning the ***Chemical Winnowing Fan*** <note>original: "Chymica vanno." This likely refers to a process of "sifting" the true alchemical secrets from the false, or perhaps a specific contemporary work with that title.</note>. Truly, the great dissension of the most learned men regarding this most important matter forces even those who think they hold some certainty to doubt. Come then, **Men most just toward the art**, see what aphorisms of the Adepts await our **love of magic** <term>philomagiam</term>,

> I shall not relate these things to be sung in the humble buskin,
> I am compelled to set out on a great journey to learned Athens,
> So that the longer path may strip me of every punishment;
> Let us gird ourselves to visit the ancestors of ancient Janus.
<note>The "humble buskin" refers to the low shoes of comic actors; the author is stating his work is high "tragedy" or serious philosophy. Janus, the two-faced god of beginnings, often symbolizes the dual nature of the alchemical "First Matter."</note>

Let us survey the sacred tapestries themselves, the greatest of secrets, which surpasses all hidden things, and than which nothing is more secret in nature itself. Let us taste that toward which you strive and which you intend. I shall draw back the shadows with which the vision of mortals is clouded, and by which nature protects herself from the sight of the profane; and I shall demonstrate the Goddess herself—namely, that most adorned **Nymph**, and her bedchamber, and **Diana** naked without her robe. I have no doubt that when she appears to you uncovered, she will immediately provoke incredible love for herself. Now, therefore, let it be the final time to approach that which we have established.

<header>PRELUDE</header>

...I shall bestow [most beneficent] gifts, so that we all—if we cannot do so with a worthy song, then at least with such praise as is permitted—may as suppliants worship the incomprehensible power of God and the unsurpassable loftiness of the Divinity. (For unless the weakness of the human mind is illuminated by the radiance of divine light, it would very easily be led away into the most destructive windings of ambiguities and the bypasses of errors). I indeed, bowed and prostrate, adore and kneel before this power, not denying my own fear, trembling as I sail across such an Ocean of secrets in the humble and flimsy skiff of my small talent; for in such a vast and swirling voyage, even the most clear-sighted captain has cause to dread a shipwreck. Truly, in this matter, even the wisest men talk nonsense, nor can they look upon the unexplored center of things with steady eyes; for it is an abyss in which reason is swallowed, a pit in which every human effort is spun around, and a sea in which all human genius is blinded and risks total wreck.

Therefore, lest we wander astray by some erratic star and be trapped by the shallows and narrows of the quicksands, we must frequently look back to the North Star <note>original: "Cynosura." Literally the constellation Ursa Minor, used here as a metaphor for a guiding light.</note> of divine light—that teacher of Angels, and the eternal and infinite Word. Thus, where the torch of human reason fails or is shrouded in darkness, that Word, acting as mistress and pilot, may direct the course of our navigation, reveal to us its hidden chests of treasures, and finally bring to completion the work of its powerful right hand. We must do this so that the sparkling brand of so great a mystery, suddenly striking the weak eyes of our mind, does not blind us with excessive splendor. If divine help must be implored in the smallest of matters, what then ought we to do in matters so arduous and great? 

Alfonsus <note>Likely referring to a Latinized version of an Arabic authority or King Alfonso X of Castile, to whom many medieval alchemical and astronomical works were attributed.</note>, that most sagacious Arabian magus, at the beginning of his book of more occult philosophy titled *The Key of Wisdom* <note>original: "Clavis sapientiæ."</note>, begins thus: *Let us first praise God, who is the inspector of all things, nor is there anything that remains hidden from Him; for He is bound to His creatures through His word, and yet separate from them, insofar as He transcends them.* Similarly, others who have dared to treat the **physico-chemical Phoenix** <term>physico-chemical Phoenix</term> <note>A poetic and alchemical metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone, representing the process of death and rebirth (purification and perfection) of matter.</note> begin: *To God, my son, to God; turn your heart and mind to Him rather than to the art itself: for the art is the highest gift of God, and He grants it to whomever He pleases.*

<summary>The author humbles himself before the "Ocean" of divine secrets, arguing that human reason alone is insufficient for alchemy without divine guidance. He cites the "Arabian magus" Alfonsus to emphasize that the Great Work is a gift from God rather than a mere technical skill.</summary>

How vain are the comforts and consolation here, how frequent the tribulation, and how manifold the restlessness among men—how long and bitter a delay from the nest of my eternal mansion!

O my God, when at last will You glue me, as I languish, with the glue of Your magnetic grace, so that I may never be moved! When will You join me to Yourself with pathetic and <term>adamantine</term> <note>meaning unbreakable or diamond-like</note> chains? When, intoxicated by the richness of Your house and having drunk from the torrent of Your pleasure, shall I be in Your court...

# PRELUDE

...heavenly, in that most blessed home of Your Saints, for eternal ages, it will no longer be said of me, mournfully and shamefully, "he clung to one of the citizens of that region" <note>A reference to the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:15, who in his desperation "clung" to a foreigner to feed swine.</note>, but rather "he clung to God, and is one spirit" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 6:17.</note>? Behold a **duck-like clinging** <note>original: "anaticam." Likely a playful or technical reference to the way a duck’s feathers or a specific adhesive bond works</note>, a most sublime union, and beyond the *likeness of nature* <term>homoeosim</term>! It is the union of rusty iron with the <term>orthochymico</term> <note>purely alchemical</note>, with the <term>obryzo</term> <note>pure or fine gold</note>, with gold seven-times refined; the union of a man of ash and dust with God! O ecstatic *metamorphosis*, more ineffably wonderful and better than all Ovidian transformations, and even a thousand *Philosophers' Stones*! 

Alas, what a <term>cacophony</term> and *pause* <note>original: "diapsalma," a musical term from the Psalms often meaning a meditative pause or a change in tone</note> my hoarse strings produce! Ah Lord, it is You, You alone whom my drum proclaims:

->In place of Philinna <note>A name from classical Greek poetry representing a beautiful beloved</note>, lie alone upon my breast.<-

Pile up, heap up, pour in, O Jesus, at this **crossroads**, in this **point of stillness** <term>punctistitio</term> of such a disparate eternity and of so unequal a wheel; whatever evils you will, I will bear them as I am able; for I am prepared for lashes. # PROSIMETRIC

> O shade-bringing Jesus, oh sweet breath of life, <note>original: "Umbrifer ô Jesu, vah dulcis halese perese." The terms "halese perese" appear to be Hellenized mystical epithets for breath or spirit.</note>
> Never depart from my mind or from the path of my heart!
> I will fly to You, the Rock, whenever I am hunted by the kite, <note>A kite is a bird of prey; here it symbolizes the devil or worldly temptations.</note>
> You who echo perpetual help to all, Amen.

Now therefore, since the radiance of the divine torch has sufficiently scattered the Cimmerian <note>A reference to the Cimmerians of myth, who lived in perpetual mist and darkness.</note> darkness of ignorance and of minds, as well as the misty little shadows of the eyes, enter through the open gates! Do so that you may be able to take your pleasure with the Nymph of the World—the foundation and support of all nature—once the veils are removed and the hymen broken, just as if you were with an unclothed Diana. At the sight of her most charming face, let the minds of all soften, and let them be set on fire by the isthmus of her love. If they drink from this water, or drink from her well-watered veins, let them thirst again, and let them be continually held by the **thirst of dropsy**, <note>Hydropsy or dropsy is a medical condition causing swelling and unquenchable thirst; here it is used as a spiritual metaphor for a soul that can never get enough of the Divine.</note>

> Just as those whose bellies have swollen from dire waters,
> They always thirst the more, the more they have drunk:

Draw these waters for yourselves, you thirsty ones; overflow with them and settle your thirst, for they are the best and most healthful. These are those waters of **Father Pelops**, <note>original: "Patris Pelopis." This is a highly unusual classical allusion, likely linking the "ivory shoulder" of the resurrected Pelops to alchemical purity or the "white" stage of the Great Work.</note> to which I invite the gasping ones, so that they may come and buy freely, without silver and without any exchange. A sonorous voice indeed, and one pleasing to the ears of those practicing philosophy! O inexhaustible fountain of riches for those thirsting for truth and justice, ah, a ready asylum for the anxieties of the shipwrecked! 

My predecessors wished to interpret these things only for their own close friends, and desired to explain nothing to the common multitude. I, however, will offer the theorems of sublime <term>Aurigraphy</term> <note>Gold-writing; the art of recording divine or alchemical truths.</note> to everyone here, and that for free. Indeed, from the innermost recess of my heart, I most liberally offer up this concise *harvest of the metric field*, and the first-fruits of my produce—those brought forth before the lamp of **Cleanthes** <note>A Stoic philosopher who worked as a water-carrier by night so he could study philosophy by day; his lamp symbolizes diligent, late-night study.</note> and assigned to the press by the **Immortal Adepts**. I do not think I could have undertaken anything more excellent than this; if I knew of anything more worthy, I would bring it all into the light and share it to be published by the printing presses.

> But my muse is unrefined; we sing what odes we can,
> The bird that chatters unlearnedly often restores itself.

# PRELUDE

->I shall not plow the foamy sea with a ship’s keel,<-
->All our rest lies in a narrow river.<-
->For I am tender and small, dull in mind and by birth,<-
->The *poor wretch* has no gifts, except those he has happened upon.<-

Use me meanwhile as a supplemental Commentator, I who have undertaken to review for you the acts of the assembly of the *Silent Ones* <note>original: "Silentûm." This refers to initiates of the mystery traditions or alchemists who are sworn to silence regarding their secrets.</note> and their entire deeds; for this *Sibylline* <note>Referring to the Sibyls, the ancient prophetesses of the Greco-Roman world.</note> shrine reveals their holy decrees. And yet, we have already advanced once and for all quite enough—and more than enough—into this great *forest of the prelude*. The retreat must be sounded, and the matter must be brought "to the navel," <note>original: "ad umbilicum ducenda." An ancient Roman idiom meaning to reach the end of a book or scroll, which was wound around a central stick called an umbilicus.</note> as it is commonly said: *labors completed are pleasant*. Nor was Euripides wrong—I shall conclude in English <note>original: "latinè." The author says he will conclude the thought in Latin, though the source was originally Greek.</note> if I can—for you all know this Greek <note>original: "Argolicam." Referring to Argos, a city in Greece; used here to mean the Greek language.</note> sentiment: *The memory of past labors is sweet.* <note>original: "Suavis est laborum præteritorum memoria." # The Pathways & Meadows of ELYSIUM.

1. That is, the Fields; for just as a **field** <note>original: *campus*</note> obtained its name from **taking** <note>original: *capiendo*</note>, because it easily **takes** <note>original: *capiat*</note> a remarkable harvest of animals or other things; so also a **meadow** <note>original: *pratum*</note> comes from **preparing** <note>original: *parando*</note>, because it is certainly **prepared** <note>original: *paratum*</note> for the taking of fruit, in which, specifically, only a scythe is needed to gather it.

2. That is, Full and swollen with gold, etc. See more extensively below in the *Monuments of Deiphobe* <note>Deiphobe is the name of the Cumaean Sibyl who guided Aeneas</note>, in the seventh Gloss.

3. That is, Middle, many, mature, etc. Otherwise and more commonly called **the time of reclining** <note>original: *concubia*</note>, because almost everyone **lies down** <note>original: *cubent*</note> then; or **the time of silence** <note>original: *conticinium*</note>, because **all things** <note>original: *cuncta*</note> are then **silent** <note>original: *taceant*</note>. However, it seems to me that the phrase **dead of night** <note>original: *Nox intempesta*</note> is a contraction of **unseasonable** <note>original: *intempestiva*</note>, perhaps because that part of the night is **unseasonable**, that is, inconvenient for conducting small affairs.

4. That is, a Good voice, or more rightly an **honest voice** <note>original: *proba vox*</note>, as if **prohibiting** <note>original: *prohibens*</note> one from wandering into error.

5. That is, Constant, everlasting, etc. For just as **everlasting** <note>original: *sempiternus*</note> is composed of **always** <note>original: *semper*</note> and **eternal** <note>original: *æternus*</note>, as if it were **age-enduring** <note>original: *æviternus*</note>; so also **perennial** <note>original: *perennis*</note> comes from **through** <note>original: *per* and **year** <note>original: *annus*</note>, with the *a* changed to an *e*, as if **lasting through all years**.

6. Here it means, bringing Consolation and assistance, because **safety** <note>original: *salus*</note> is taken to mean a remedy, a healing, etc.

7. In which, clearly, the **Golden Fleece of the Phryxian Ram** is guarded by an ever-watchful dragon; the word for **grove** <note>original: *luco*</note> comes from **to shine** <note>original: *luceo*</note>—certainly not by antiphrasis <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</note> because it shines the least (as is commonly believed), but more truly because of the frequent **lights** <note>original: *lumina*</note> of the sacrifices which are performed at night in this grove of **Mars**. He is so named because he presides over the **males** <note>original: *maribus*</note> making offerings there; poetically he is called *Mavors*, because he **turns great things** <note>original: *magna vertat*</note>, etc.

8. That is, Immortal, bringing the scent of nard, always accompanying, etc. For a **shadow** <note>original: *umbra*</note> follows the body whether we wish it or not; it is named as if it were **rain** <note>original: *imber*</note>, because all shadows are "shingled" <note>original: *imbricæ*</note> or **rain-bearing** <note>original: *imbriferæ*</note>, that is, moist, smoky, etc.

9. It is most worthy of consideration what the word **Orcus** <note>a name for the Underworld or the god of the dead</note> signifies here and elsewhere; it is named (at least according to me, the commentator) surely not from **urging** <note>original: *urgendo*</note> because it urges us toward death, but rather as if it were a **Shady Garden** <note>original: *Hortus opacus*</note>, because it is surely the **beginning** <note>original: *orsus*</note> and **origin** <note>original: *ortus*</note> of all things.

10. That is, Triumphal, from the verb **to rejoice** <note>original: *ovo, as*</note>, which means to be glad, and to demonstrate that gladness by shouting or singing; from this comes the <term>ovation</term> <note>a smaller triumph granted to Roman generals</note>, which is a lesser triumph. In this rite, **sheep** <note>original: *ovibus*</note> were sacrificed on the Capitoline Hill, just as **bulls** were in the greater triumphs. It is so named as if it were an *ohatio*, from the interjection of one exulting, "**Ohe!**" Or perhaps we can etymologize it more correctly by noting that the verb *ovo* is derived from the voice of those who crowd the side of the one **rejoicing** <note>original: *ovantis*</note>; for those people, full of cheer, are accustomed to cry out a doubled "**Oo**," from which (by interposing the consonant *v*) I believe the verb *ovo* resulted, with the first syllable short.

11. Poetically used here for heaven, just as previously in the *Choir of Philosophers*; it is named as if it were <note>original Greek: *ὅλος λαμπρὸς*</note> **entirely bright**, that is, total and shining on all sides, because it possesses a clear sun and is never darkened by any clouds.

Since then, I remember having heard—among not a few men, even those otherwise distinguished by learning—similar mouth-filth <note>original: *orisulgetra*; a rare, colorful term for foul or obscene language</note> erupted time and again, and indeed with much more abundance, driven by I know not what roar of "free speech" <term>parrhesia</term> <note>From the Greek *parrhesia*, meaning boldness or frankness of speech; here used sarcastically to describe reckless insults.</note>. At first, as I have said before, I decided to strike out openly and dash a balanced fist immediately into their faces to knock every tooth from their gums. I say my rage was so renewed and broke out so fiercely that I soon almost wished most of those devils utterly abolished and deprived of light; and if the indulgence of laws or my own strength had permitted, look! I would have already extirpated them with these very hands. I would have immediately torn the tongues from their heads, and having snatched a knife from my bag, I would have brained them and extinguished them. Indeed, if that entire dreg of insulters and mockers had possessed but a single neck, I would have beheaded them and cut their throats at a single stroke in one glance:

> *But because the anger of one is vain and without strength,*
> *it is difficult and hard for one to restrain many:*
> *Light is the vengeance which a small arm can deliver;*

And so I was merely carrying words into the wind and casting my voice in vain, acting like a common scold <note>original: *fœminando*; literally "acting as a woman," a period-specific trope suggesting that the author's verbal venting was powerless or shrill compared to the action he desired.</note> and prattling those things with the tongue of an old woman.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

> *(Why should I, in my madness, hope for these Sisyphean successes?*
> *Successes which no day grants me, nor ever will)* <note>The author uses the myth of Sisyphus—condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever—to describe his exhausting and seemingly futile struggle to restore the reputation of alchemy.</note>

I believed that they should be demanded, pleaded with, and disturbed by every shout, word, and deed possible—those who seek to erase, denounce, and annihilate the works of these insulted men <note>original: *carinatorum*; likely referring to those who have been "keeled" or reviled by critics</note> and to consign such great talents of our assembly to oblivion. If they were willing and able, whether they are still present among us or are now among the Silent Ones <note>The dead.</note> themselves:

> *Anyone, whether Living or at Rest, must be urged,*
> *Let my troubled mind break forth in every direction,*
> *From which I might be able to soothe my soul with avenging punishments.*

But where should I first voice these complaints of mine? Whom should I disturb? Before whom should I plead this twisted case? Should I go to the common people and the rabble? But their tongues are so unrefined <note>original: *lima*; literally "a file," here implying a lack of intellectual polish</note> regarding this matter that most of them absolutely refuse to know, or scarcely know by name, **Alchemy** <term>Chymiam</term>—even though they should have drunk its special and noble privilege like milk from their mothers’ breasts. Or if they do know of it, they think its students are barely worthy of their bread or the light of the Sun <note>original: *Phœbóque*; referring to Phoebus Apollo, the sun god and patron of light/truth.</note>.

Should I turn to you, O Learned Men and Doctors, you chair-holders and hair-splitters? For most of you—trapped as you are in those six hundred useless scholastic repetitions <note>original: *battologiis*; a term for vain, wearying repetition in speech.</note> and false arguments—the very shadow of **True Magic** <term>Orthomagiam</term> has never even occurred. You fail to see that it is not only the storehouse <term>myrothecium</term> <note>From the Greek for a casket of perfumes or ointments; a metaphor for a refined collection of knowledge.</note> of human wisdom and all profound and hidden literature, but that it is also the "metropolis"—that is, the workshop of all arts and all wonders. It was this Magic which long ago made that wise Athens <note>Metaphorically referring to the intellectual center of the world.</note>, the mother and nurse of most disciplines and arts—the first true University of the Universe, I say—to bloom so honorably.

But truly, how many are there who see these things? Alas! Our current "Iron Age" has fallen too far from that "Golden Age." It has fallen so far that whole arts and simple sciences have degenerated into patchwork rags and useless offshoots; while the elephant is cast out, the gnat is strained; <note>A play on the biblical proverb (Matthew 23:24) about straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel/elephant; here it suggests missing the great truths while obsessing over trifles.</note> and with limbs out of joint, people everywhere argue over "the shadow of Apuleius’s ass" <note>A proverbial expression for arguing over nothing, referencing Lucius Apuleius, the author of the 2nd-century Roman novel *The Golden Ass*.</note>.

### THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES.

In a former age, the sharper wits of men were exhausted by the most diligent investigation of hidden things and the most excellent parts of secret doctrine and natural mysteries. Through these, they served as a defense for all their subjects, both in times of war and in times of peace <note>original: *tum sagi, tum togæ*; literally "both of the military cloak and of the toga," a common idiom for war and civil life</note>. In our modern age, however, men perversely cultivate and polish the worthless <note>original: *ficulneas*; literally "of a fig-tree," an idiom for something brittle, useless, or of little value</note> fantasies of lawsuits and useless insanities. By these means, that profitable and more valuable **Philomagia** <term>Philomagia: a term combining "love" and "magic," used here to describe the sacred art of alchemy or divine wisdom</term> of the Ancients has been unjustly emptied of its substance. The Senate of the Ancestral Sages used to mark those nobler Muses with white chalk <note>An ancient custom of marking lucky or favorable days and things with white stone or chalk</note>; for their sake, they threw themselves into the most taxing clouds of troubles, so that by possessing those arts, they might make themselves and their fatherland more famous. In our time, however, not only does mockery and distortion of this Art increase, but even violence and abhorrence rave against such a fruitful berry and the very peak of mystical knowledge. Should I then finally approach the lovers of these arts themselves? Should I go to Kings, Princes, and Nobles? Today this one, tomorrow that one, the day after another—until finally, one humble little man has addressed them all in order?

> Would you, my bashful little face, have enough daring
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To speak, little eye, under the steady gaze of a King?
> Alas! A task so immense is terrifying for a small man,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Greater even than the hands of Hercules!
> Shall those who bark at us and those who oppress the treasurers of wonders
> mock and hiss with impunity at the beehive
> flowing with the honey of all-round mysteries,
> using their threads and such sharp-toothed arrows?
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shall that man hurl his jeers at me with impunity?
> This one his mocks? Shall he provoke the Academy <note>original: *Lyceum*; the school of Aristotle, here representing higher learning</note> with his mouth?
> Or the three-fold tricksters of the Theater with their wit and satires?
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And that infamous little book written with slanted bile?
> Not so, not so; the tongue that has spoken so rabidly
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shall be harmed by that same rage of a blasphemous tongue.

I have therefore thought and approved that our **Philomagi** <gloss>Lovers of Magic/Sages</gloss> who now dwell in Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld; here meaning the dead</note> should be appealed to and courted with wails, tears, laments, offerings, and atonements, in whatever way I might most conveniently. My goal is that they, being now **Indigites** <term>Indigites: deified ancestral spirits or local patron deities</term>, might inform and imbue the **Philomathas** <gloss>Lovers of Learning</gloss> who are still working,

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

With sealed oracles, prophecies, and visions—sent even in an extraordinary and truly unexpected manner, but also on account of unforeseen and unheard-of injuries—dispatched to them from the Shadowy Realm <note>original: *ex Opaco*; likely referring to the Underworld or the hidden realm of the dead</note>, in the event that perhaps the wavering alchemists <term>homotechni: literally "fellow-craftsmen," used here for practitioners of the alchemical art</term> (since philosophers no longer use our ether, but act as overseers to bring the matter of the Arch-Magus Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> to its summation against the slanderers of so many and such distinguished men, who insult that Queen of Sciences, Alchemy <term>Spagiria: the alchemical art of separating and recombining elements, often for medicinal use</term>, with such unrefined and savage lips of petty scribblers) might even now, at last, be able to waver and triumph together in their inauguration. And so, bowing down upon my knees, I began to entreat the still uncertain Deity:

> I begin to weave these threads; you, O Gods, feel my complaints,
> The supports of my weeping and the laws of my fear.
> After a thousand jokes, bless the funeral pyres among the stars,
> And after a thousand torches, O Orcus <note>The Roman god of the Underworld</note>, receive my prayers.

### §. 3.

Thus I began now to devote myself to Jove, to hammer away, to pour out my vows, and to weary the inhabitants of Elysium <note>the "Elysiicolas," or the blessed dead</note> with dense cries and wailings. I labored day and night to produce applause and lamentation for our Ancestors—to the Platos, the Bacons, the Gebers, the Rhazes, the Rosariuses, the Avicennas <note>These are the great authorities of medieval and Renaissance science and alchemy: Roger Bacon, Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), Rhazes (al-Razi), and Avicenna (Ibn Sina)</note>, and equally to Morienus, that most sagacious patron of these festive works from long ago. I called upon the Elder <note>original: *Seniorem*; referring to Senior Zadith</note>, the presenter of the twin birds, Zadith son of Hamuel <note>Ibn Umail, an Arabic alchemist whose work "The Silvery Water and the Starry Earth" was highly influential</note>—alas!—who was once entirely devoted to this Art. I prayed that if any of them, or (as I would have preferred) all of them in harmony together, would deign to look back upon their own, they might stand by the Truth (which they held so holily while living) which is now slipping further and further away in their absence.

> But you, O merciful Ruler of Nature <note>original: *Physiarcha*</note>! and you blessed souls
> Of the ethereal regions, I pray you, take pity on us,
> Hear my just prayers, and lend a kind ear
> To me; thus do I seek you, thus do I surround you with my vows:

Though struck a little, I nonetheless hastened my pace,
But as I came toward the very curtains of the Underworld <note>original: *averni*; Avernus was a volcanic crater in Italy traditionally regarded as the entrance to the realm of the dead</note>,
An image of a mournful Art appeared to me,
Snowy, radiating light, and most solemn in her whole countenance,
Changing <note>original: *Vertumnans*; referring to Vertumnus, the Roman god of seasons, change, and transformations</note> her **dark colors** with a gold-bearing brow,
With painted hair, she stood there in the shape of a peacock,
And spoke with a mixture of fear and hope;
"To tempt further is a sin, to press on is forbidden:
For thus far only is it permitted; leave, mortal man,
It is possible to go only to a certain point; not a bit further <note>original: *ne gry*; a classical idiom meaning "not even the smallest possible amount"</note> is granted."

Furthermore, at that second sight, such an obscene omen appeared there, a portent which I can equate to nothing described by any of the monster-slayers (not even in a shadow): for it had a seven-angled head, receding and bald, with a protruding snout <note>original: *broncum*; a term for a misshapen or projecting jaw</note>, eaten away and burnt by decay and mange, curved, bent, pointed, and sharp; the face fell all the way to the navel, protected by a chin so sharp we could have scraped calf-hooves on it. The nose was upturned, eagle-like, and hooked like the trunk of an elephant. The mouth was full-cheeked, turned backward, slanted, distorted, and viper-like. The teeth were like a boar's, protruding and very long, like those whitened stakes upon which we are accustomed to stretch linens when they are bleached in the sun. The eyes were like those of a Cyclops, pitch-black. The ears were like a wild ass's <note>original: *onagrinæ*</note>, drooping and deaf. The neck was cramped, like a cuckoo's, and as black as pitch though shaped like a swan's. The beard was thick and woolly <note>original: *bætica*; a reference to the Baetica region of Spain, famous for its high-quality wool</note>, goat-like, a foot long,
Filthy, stringy, and bristling with thorny thickets.

The nostrils were curved back, poisonous, hawk-like, breathing out a foul vapor <note>original: *mephitim*; a noxious, suffocating gas associated with volcanic vents</note>, exhaling asphalt, and smelling of the Lake of Ampsanctus <note>original: *Amſanctum*; a site in Italy famous for its deadly volcanic gases</note>. The face was pimply, corpse-like, warty—plainly like Aesop <note>The famous fabulist was traditionally described as being physically deformed</note>, Thersites <note>In Homer's *Iliad*, the ugliest and most foul-mouthed of the Greek soldiers</note>, or Marcolphus <note>A coarse, ugly, but witty figure from medieval popular literature</note>, and spherical in the manner of a hunting dog; the skin was decayed and rough; finally, the whole body was shaggy, womanish, full of notches and thick joints, and wild with crocodile-like hair:

->A bearded monster, goatish, hairy, a father-killer.<-

And do you see? While I grow pale at the sight, and through the windows in the open countryside, I secretly turn my gaze;

Already then, according to my vow, I seemed to cast my sharp gaze upon one nearby, remarkable shadow among the many of all those **Phantom-Fighters** <note>original: *Fugillatorum*; likely referring to fleeting, spectral figures or those who shadow-box with the void</note>, exceedingly notable in her whole face and dress, and more refined than the rest;

> Of these, one who was closer to my sight
> Seemed to speak: "Oh! Move your feet, rather follow behind
> And fix yourself at my side. What mournful thing has happened
> On earth? Or what harm have you suffered, that you ponder
> So many things anxiously? Boldly entrust your complaints
> To our ears; this day, I promise, will bring a remedy
> To your affairs and prayers. *I shall grant you the bountiful Underworld* <note>original: *almum tibi largiar Orcum*; Orcus is the Roman god of the underworld, here implying the speaker will grant the narrator access to its secrets</note>,
> In which you will learn all the mysteries of the world."
> She sings these responses; I am enticed, stupefied by the
> Favorable omen, and I felt the premonitions of a step in fortune:

For she struck in me a spark of divinity, and soon a sense of reverence. Her entire leggings, loose, suspended her feet—clad in rustic boots—humanely above the ground; her body was covered by a clean and long, wrinkled **Canusian garment** <note>original: *canusinâ*; Canusium was an ancient Italian city famous for its fine, reddish-brown wool</note>. Her bound hair shaded—or rather, did not shade—on one side the broad and smooth surface of her forehead, and on the other side her exposed ears and her **eyed-shoulders** <note>original: *scapulas oculatas*; a surreal or visionary detail suggesting the figure sees in all directions</note> with her semi-naked neck. And so, thus dressed in Canusian wool, wearing sandals <note>original: *baxeata*</note>, a traveler's hat <note>original: *petasata*</note>, wooden shoes <note>original: *sculponeata*</note>, and fastened with thongs <note>original: *corrigiata*</note>, she represented a traveler, tucked up, equipped, already **in battle-array** <note>original: *endo-procinctu*; an archaic Latin term for being prepared for immediate action</note>, and as if prepared to go and return, to undertake my petition for herself, and through the depicted **Emerald Way** <note>original: *viam Smaragdinam*; likely a reference to the alchemical 'Emerald Tablet' or a path of hidden wisdom</note> to perform the same task for those **Adept inhabitants of Elysium** <note>original: *Elysiicolas illos Adeptos*; refers to those who have achieved spiritual perfection and dwell in the blessed afterlife</note>. "I beg you indeed," I seemed to ask, "tell me please once and for all, of what country, or from what house or tribe are you? Are you from above or from below?" (If I heard correctly and remember rightly) the rest of the wandering and roaming crowd of Shadows called him by that name.

->§. 6.<-

To which name, **Cerdo** <note>original: *Cerdoo*; likely derived from the Greek *kerdos*, meaning profit or gain, an epithet of Mercury as the patron of tradesmen and craft</note>, the auguries and prophecies of the Pagans claim the power of discourse and proper speech, as he was the one who first set forth the alphabet. Hence, long ago in Athens, in a certain portico—where among other temples of the Gods there was also a gymnasium which they called "Mercury's"—it is said that he, having invented the arts, imbued others with them with the greatest zeal so that they might be passed down to posterity. He was known not only for leading the souls of the dead to the Underworld and offering them to **Charon** <note>The mythological ferryman who carries souls across the river Styx</note> to be transported, but indeed most especially for moving among the Gods above as an interpreter of the Divine;

> The son of Atlas <note>original: *Atlantiades*; a title for Mercury, grandson of the Titan Atlas</note> is said to be the messenger
> Of great Jove and the Gods, the venerable trainer
> Of the sacred wrestling-ground, a Deity common
> To both the infernal and the heavenly realms;
> Who alone holds the right to pass through both thresholds,
> And completes all dealings between the twin worlds;
> He himself leads the pious souls to *joyful shores*,
> And with his **golden rod** <note>original: *aurato vimine*; referring to the Caduceus, Mercury's staff</note> he gathers the light-footed crowd,
> Welcome to the princes of heaven and to dark **Avernus** <note>original: *averni*; a volcanic crater lake near Naples, anciently believed to be the entrance to the Underworld</note>:
> He himself, the father and kinsman of Atlas, devotee of the lyre,
> Skilled in whatever he could hide with a thief's sleight of hand,
> Tore away the rustic gestures of men through speech;
> With him as the clever instructor and cunning master,
> Noble **Amphion** <note>In Greek mythology, the son of Zeus who built the walls of Thebes by playing his lyre</note>, founder of the city of Thebes,
> Was able to lead Hyrcanian tigers and companion lionesses
> Along with the woods, and delay swift rivers,
> And with his **tortoise-shell lyre** <note>original: *chely*; from the Greek *chelys*, the tortoise-shell from which Mercury fashioned the first lyre</note> soothe the guardian of **Dis’s altar** <note>original: *custodem Ditis acerræ*; referring to Cerberus, the multi-headed hound of Pluto/Dis</note>,
> Though a hundred serpents armed the beast’s head,
> And a foul stench, rot, and gore flowed from its mouth;
> Bending whole fields along with stiff mountains,
> And reviving crags and stones with his **Aonian lyre** <note>original: *Aoniâ lyrâ*; Aonia was a region of Boeotia sacred to the Muses</note>,
> He moved vast rocks with his echoing shell.

And I observed that the Doctors of the Church easily agreed to his support of weighty and serious matters (specifically from his long-standing mission of laws and letters to the Egyptians). Furthermore, I noted that the name itself should be counted among the most favorable omens of the heathens, which promise a more successful outcome. This is because the name is considered just as lucky for all those who turn themselves toward marketplaces, business, and contracts, as it is utterly unwelcome to the "Prince of Darkness" <note>original: *tenebrarchæ*; literally 'ruler of shadows,' referring to the devil</note> and his henchmen. For on the day of this name—which was the fourth day from the creation of the world—God made two great lights: the **greater light** <note>original: *luminare majus*; the Sun</note> to rule the day, and the **lesser light** <note>original: *luminare minus*; the Moon</note> to rule the night and the stars. For that reason, I was of the opinion that a most prosperous and best omen could be established from this, by which the sun, moon, and stars are said to have been produced; for these are the origins of all joy and gladness, as much for metals and stones as for fruits. Thus, I believed that this **Tryphon** <note>In this context, a name for the guide acting as a patron of business and "Sacred Art" (alchemy)</note> would be the most suitable advocate for the affairs of this **sacred and open Art**, which has been so greatly muddied, to those *Ambrosian* patrons. Indeed, it was not hidden from me that this multilingual, **poetic Merlin**, most famous throughout the whole circuit of the sun—especially because of his recent wandering into the *World-Opaque-on-All-Sides* <note>original: *Undiqueopacum Orbem*; a poetic name for the realm of shadows or the Underworld</note> and his happy return from the same—was meditating on another journey into those same Acherusian <note>Referring to Acheron, a river in the Underworld</note> realms of Dis:

->For into what caves did he not go with his swift foot?<-
