Moreover, serious and industrious men would hardly praise the choice, because he was a charming fellow, and excessively like a character of Plautus <note>original: *Plautinus*; referring to the Roman playwright Plautus, known for his broad, low-brow comedy</note>, even in serious matters as often happens. I judged him to be the least suitable person to be trusted with such great and momentous affairs. Therefore, I refused to beg for his help, thinking instead of another of better trust and more well-known religious devotion—just like the Athenians, who rightly wished that great things discovered by a little fool should not be proclaimed by the fool himself, but rather by Aristides <note>Aristides "the Just," an Athenian statesman celebrated for his integrity</note>.

And there, Apuleius of Madaura <note>a 2nd-century philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*</note> came into view before my eyes, the very model of ***our Magical and Mimic Art***. He was a most diligent man who, because of the discipline he learned and taught at Athens, was given the title of "the Platonist." To him, my tablets could certainly be safely delegated to those *Silent Shadows*, and conversely, messages from the *Shadows* could be brought back to me, a *Mortal*. He was a man clearly most well-versed in law, always most faithful to his own interests and the public good, studious, and especially experienced in handling business—even secret matters. Having first been imbued with studies in Carthage during his boyhood and in Athens during his youth, he later went to Rome; there, on account of his singular prudence and sharp judgment, he attained the highest honors without rejection. The monuments of his own hand’s writings also testify that he can give the most evident signs of his return from the Ever-Shadowed World <note>original: *Undiqueumbroso Mundo*; a poetic term for the underworld</note>. Furthermore, Saint Augustine records that this man, because of his integrity of life and special sanctity, was elevated to the priesthood in the province of Africa.

But because I did not know well enough whether he was also entirely included in the fellowship of those good spirits <note>original: *Eudæmonum*; from the Greek *eudaimon*, referring here to benevolent spirits or "good demons" in the Platonic sense</note> on the right hand, or if perhaps he had been commanded by Rhadamanthus <note>one of the judges of the dead in Greek mythology</note>:

->To turn leftward toward the proscribed heap;<-

This was especially because of that abominable and most wicked stain with which he was heavily accused during his life—namely, the black arts <note>original: *nigrarum artium*; magic</note> by which he supposedly enticed the widow **Pudentilla**, now his wife, into loving him, and removed his own stepson **Pontianus** from the world. However, it was strictly necessary that the tablets of sharp tongues be delivered into the very hands of our Mardonius, and my affairs [could] not [suffer] a long delay...

> Ignorant of from where and why you come, and what it shadows forth,
> That these tablets from the mortal world should reach them:
> For you, conscious of the biting cause and revealing it,
> First clearing each detail in the noble custom,
> Then narrating your contents in order,

I delivered, I say, to Mercury the entire transcript and the little bundle of satirical pages to be carried most timely to my former fellow-craftsmen <note>original: *homotechnos*; colleagues in the same art or profession</note>. This bundle was *light indeed in physical bulk, but immense in the weight of its contents*. I did this not because I believed (as is the judgment of some) that there are:

> No ghosts <note>original: *Lemures*; restless or malevolent spirits of the dead</note>, nor subterranean kingdoms,
> Nor the river Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note> licked by men, nor wandering spirits <note>original: *Manes*; the souls of deceased loved ones</note>;

Not in the least; for those spirits exist, they certainly do, and I am certain of their existence through heavenly instruction. Rather, I sent these papers so that, moved by this great and anxious zeal of mine for resisting injury and assisting justice, they might more and more pity and help me; *The Gods favor those who try*, and *Fortune presses the timid, but fears the brave.*

And indeed, I seemed to have predestined everything in a foreign tongue <note>original: *barbarè*; likely referring to a non-Latin language or a specialized alchemical code</note>, both so that the First Wise Man <note>original: *Protosophus*</note> might better grasp those sharp reproaches of biting tongues and that they might be read to the whole Senate in that idiom in which Golden Magic <note>original: *Aurea Magia*</note> mostly operates; and also so that all might cry out with one voice what work is primarily needed here. I hoped that those Greater Lovers of Magic <note>original: *Philomagi*</note>, the dead speaking to the mortals, might likewise not find it burdensome to transcribe their individual conclusions or decrees into the Roman tongue <note>Latin</note>, as soon as my Aethalides <note>In Greek mythology, a son of Mercury who was allowed to retain his memory even in Hades and travel between worlds</note>—that auxiliary and administrative spirit—might attempt a return from that sanctuary of the Fortunate Isles into our world. This return would be by the Sapphire path, where messengers of these kinds of little books are accustomed to come and go, for the sake of those who sought useful words and wrote most upright discourses full of truth. Whence and why you come, though they are ignorant, and what you overshadow—
Those tablets destined to come to the mortal world:
For you, aware of the biting cause and revealing it,
Clarifying each detail first in the noble fashion,
Then narrating your contents in order,
Shall be fixed by a golden thread in the midst of the hall to be viewed.

I handed over, I say, the whole transcript and the bundle of satirical pages to <term>Mercury<note>The Roman messenger god, here serving as a spiritual bridge between the living and the dead.</note></term> to be carried most opportunely to my fellow-craftsmen of the past, *light in bulk indeed, but immense in the weight of its contents* <note>original: *inanem illam quidem mole, verùm rerum pondere immanem*</note>; not because I believed (as some might judge):

> That there are no ghosts at all, nor subterranean kingdoms,
> Nor the spirits of men licking the river <term>Lethe<note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note></term> as they wander;

Not in the least! For those spirits exist—they certainly exist—and I am certain of their existence, having been instructed from above. I sent these papers so that, moved by my great and anxious zeal to resist injury and assist justice, they might pity me and help more and more; *for the Gods favor those who strive* <note>original: *Dii conantibus favorabiles*</note>.

-> *Fortune presses upon the timid, but respects the brave.* <-
<note>original: *Preſſatur timidos, fortes fortuna veretur*</note>

And I seemed to have prepared everything in a foreign tongue <note>original: *barbarè*; likely referring to a specialized magical language or "Enochian" style script</note>, both so that the <term>Master of Wisdom<note>original: *Protoſophus*; a title for a supreme sage or spiritual leader.</note></term> might better grasp those sharp insults of the biting tongues and so they might be read to the whole Senate of spirits in that idiom in which Golden Magic mostly operates. I also did this so that all might cry out with one voice what work is primarily needed here, and that those <term>Greater Friends of Magic<note>original: *Philomagi Majores*; likely referring to deceased masters of the occult arts.</note></term> might not find it burdensome to likewise transcribe their individual decrees to the Lesser Friends of Magic—the dead to the mortals—into Latin <note>original: *Romanè*</note>, as soon as my <term>Aethalides<note>In mythology, a son of Hermes who was granted an unfailing memory and the ability to travel between the lands of the living and the dead.</note></term> (that auxiliary and administrative spirit) might attempt a return from that sanctuary of the Fortunate Isles into our world. He travels via the Sapphire path, by which messengers of such little books are accustomed to go and return. Such, then, were the mockeries, yawns, and wit of those crooked railers against the sons of Wisdom.

...or that "Gold-making Powder" <note>original: *Pulvisculum Aurificum*; also known as the Powder of Projection, a substance alchemists claimed could transform base metals into gold.</note>, by the casting of which all the inferior metals might most swiftly migrate into the most perfect and purest gold. These field-wandering "Ash-blowers," <note>original: *Ciniflones*; a derogatory term for alchemists, originally referring to slaves who heated hair-curling irons in ashes.</note> these Chemists, Sellers of Smoke, Fraud-makers, and Soot-eaters, are stuck in the water and fishing in the air—or perhaps they are shooting at the heavens. They endure eternal fevers of the mind along with Priscian and Aelius <note>Famous Roman grammarians; the author suggests the alchemists waste their lives obsessing over the "grammar" of old, cryptic texts rather than reality.</note>. Indeed, they occupy and exhaust themselves day and night seeking *wool from a donkey* or acting like *Atlas carrying the sky*, all so they might know the nature of the "triads" <note>original: *terniones*; likely referring to the alchemical trinity of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> in the underworld. Yet, miserably, every one of them is deceived and deceives others; they babble, they act like fools—proclaim it from the rooftops!

> I could never distinguish all their nonsense,
> O Almighty Father! May Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant of myth; the author prays for hyper-vigilance against these frauds.</note> watch over me:

Are these the sources of those mystical "God-magicians" and the brothers of the *Rosy Cross*? <note>original: *Rosaceæ crucis*; the Rosicrucians, a secret society of doctors and sages that caused a sensation in Europe in the early 17th century.</note> What has a dog to do with a bath? <note>A proverb for something completely irrelevant or out of place.</note> Furthermore, what kind of "god-magic" do those men cultivate, who pile mountain upon mountain only to cast you down from Olympus? What kind of mysteries, I ask, are sought by those who track down "holidays of truth" <note>original: *ferias veriùs*; likely a jab at the Rosicrucian claim to be ushering in a new age of enlightenment.</note> while adding oil to the fire?

This is because these foolish-talkers perpetually promise "Thessalian mares" and "mountains of gold" with only their bombastic words and dogmas. In truth, it is all "wonderful things about a lentil" <note>A proverb for making a huge fuss over something tiny or worthless.</note> and made of smoke. They are beautiful in title only; they are empty boxes and cowardly horses adorned with fine trappings. As the saying goes: *Here is Rhodes, here is the leap!* <note>original: *hic Rhodus, hic saltus*; a famous challenge from Aesop’s fables: don't brag about what you did elsewhere, prove it here and now.</note>

->With the time of life finally worn away along with their wishes,<-
->And their money consumed in empty breaths of wind,<-
->I have found this much of truth: I know nothing, I have nothing.<-

Smoke-sellers <note>original: *Fumivenduli*; those who sell "smoke," or empty promises of influence or secrets.</note>, Hearth-dwellers, Oven-tenders, Nonsense-talkers, Law-breakers, and Purse-cleaners—they try to adapt the tiny spoils of Pygmies into Colossal proportions. ->They seek to possess difficult trifles,<-
->For labor spent on foolishness is stupid.<- <note>A quote from the Roman poet Martial (2.86.9-10), mocking those who work hard at things that don't matter.</note>

### MAGICAL NIGHTS

...or that **Gold-making Powder**, by whose application all lesser metals might most swiftly be transformed into the most perfect and purest gold. These are certainly seductive and well-worn sayings! But it is all just ancient Paphian paper <note>original: *palæpaphia papyrus*; likely referring to old, fraudulent scrolls from the temple of Aphrodite at Paphos, known for deceit.</note>, as easily swallowed as a fox eats a pear!

> Even if the god Nereus <note>The Old Man of the Sea; here used to mean the ocean itself.</note> were made entirely of quicksilver,
> It could turn that whole, wide-wandering sea into gold;

This is incredible, even if Cato <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, the Roman symbol of absolute integrity and truth.</note> himself were to preach it to me. Bah, you gluttons and boasters! What an exaggeration—by Hercules, an exaggeration more exaggerated than all the poets put together!

> O, the foolish labors of men, O, the false brains!
> That they promise anyone the wealth of Croesus;
> But how much wealth is actually stoned to death <note>The author makes a pun on *lapidatur* (stoned/squandered) and the *Lapis* (the Philosopher’s Stone).</note>
> By these fools blowing on the deceptive Stone's lying shadows!

These field-wandering **Ash-blowers** <term>Ciniflones: originally slaves who heated hair-curling irons; here used as a derogatory term for alchemists hunched over their bellows.</term>, **Smoke-sellers**, **Fakers**, and **Soot-eaters** are stuck in the water and fishing in the air—or rather, they are shooting at the heavens. They endure eternal mental fevers alongside Priscian and Aelius <note>Famous Roman grammarians; the author suggests alchemists suffer the same tedious, soul-crushing labor as pedantic teachers.</note>, for they are occupied and exhausted day and night. They seek wool from a donkey <note>A Greek proverb for attempting the impossible.</note> and act like Atlas carrying the sky, all so they might know the "triads" of the underworld. Yet, wretchedly, every one of them is deceived and deceives others; they tell fables, they play the fool—oh, Hosanna!

> Though I had a thousand mouths and a thousand tongues,
> I could never list all of their nonsensical trifles.
> O, Almighty Father! May Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant of myth; a plea for constant vigilance against scams.</note> keep watch over me:

And what of those mystical **God-magicians** <note>original: *Theomagi*; those claiming to perform miracles through divine power.</note> and the **Brothers of the Rosy Cross**? What does a dog have to do with a bath? <note>original: *quid cani ac balneo?*; a proverb for something completely out of place.</note> What kind of "divine magic" do those men cultivate, who pile mountains upon mountains just to tumble You out of Olympus? What kind of mysteries, I ask, do they seek—they who hunt for "festivals of truth" while only adding oil to the fire!

# SIBYLLINE ORACLES

> What sort of comrades you are, the fool stands as witness;
> My unshorn father <note>original: *intonsus genitor*; a classical epithet for the god Apollo, the patron of prophecy and truth.</note> knows it, he who is unpolished at all hours;
> A student of measly scraps and bits of porridge,
> Of whose pigsty you are the initiates <term>Mystae: initiates into secret religious mysteries</term>, and what sort of "God-believers" <term>Theistae: here used ironically to suggest they worship their own delusions</term> you truly are.

**Blabbermouths**, **Swindlers**, **Schemers**, buffoons, street-wanderers, and wind-bags! With only their bubbling and talkative discourses, they claim to be richer than **Croesus** <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia.</note> himself; but in reality, they are poorer than **Irus** <note>The archetypal beggar from Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note>. They claim to have all the Indian gold mines at their own homes, while in truth any one of them is nearly forced to sell his very soul because of his poverty. And so, having nothing, they are "smoother than a leek" <note>original: *Liberide glabriores*; a proverb for someone who has been stripped of everything, like a peeled stalk.</note>. Their extreme destitution and calamity are truly to be pitied—but oh, such frauds! Such intolerable deceptions!

> The horse desires the plow-handle, the lazy ox wants the saddle;
> Let every man, I pray, practice the craft he knows best <note>A famous quote from Horace (Epistles 1.14), suggesting these men should stick to honest labor rather than alchemy.</note>.

**Vagabonds**, **Begging-charlatans**, **Pleasure-seekers**, **Wanderers**, **Bankrupts**, and **Smooth-talkers**—they put on the mask of **Chares** <note>An Athenian general known for making grand promises he could not keep.</note> and play the part of **Antigonus**, the King of the Macedonians, nicknamed **Doson** <note>From the Greek *Δώσων*, meaning "the one who will give." He was a king who promised much but never delivered.</note>. This is because these babblers constantly promise "Thessalian mares" <note>A proverb for something excellent and rare.</note> and mountains of gold with nothing but their bombastic words and dogmas; but in truth, they offer only "wonders made of lentils and smoke." They are impressive in title only: empty jars and cowardly horses decked out in fine harnesses. Here is Rhodes, here is where you must leap! <note>original: *hic Rhodus, hic saltus*; a famous proverb from Aesop’s fables, meaning: "Don't tell me what you can do elsewhere; prove it here and now."</note>

> At last, with the time of life worn away by vain wishes,
> And wealth consumed by empty winds,
> I have discovered this one truth: *I know nothing, I have nothing*.

**Smoke-sellers**, **Hearth-huggers**, **Oven-tenders**, **Nonsense-babblers**, **Law-breakers**, and **Purse-drainers**—they weary themselves with useless and futile labor, trying to fit Colossal statues onto the tiny offerings of Pygmies <note>original: *Pygmæorum Acrothinia Colossa*; an image of absurd disproportion, trying to claim world-changing results from worthless trifles.</note>. We might say of them, quite wittily, that they are insane:

> They seek to possess difficult trifles,
> For the labor spent on foolish things is itself a folly <note>A quote from the poet Martial (2.86).</note>.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

The goat has not yet given birth even once, while the young kids play everywhere upon the roofs—oh, what **Azanaean evils**! <note>original: *Azanæa mala*; a Greek proverb referring to misfortunes that are "parched" or barren, much like the unproductive efforts of the alchemists.</note> Behold how the fire-dogs, the curve-footed ones, and **Plato’s lice** <note>A derogatory classical joke referring to pedantic or parasitic students who cling to a master’s coattails.</note> hold to a rough and rugged path! How fruitless is their entire life of staying awake! How they move every foot without any certainty, facing the constant peril of a precipice!

**Triflers**, **Boasters**, **Griffin-sophists** <term>Gryphosophistæ: a mock-scholarly title suggesting a hybrid of monstrous nonsense and fake wisdom</term>, foolish-talkers, study-suckers, and sulfur-smearers! Ignorant of all refined speech, they peddle themselves as being so excellent and distinguished in learning that they believe they are not required to yield—even in the smallest matter (by their own persuasion)—to the Ancients. They claim to know the **Mystic God-Magicians** <term>Theomagos: practitioners of divine or sacred magic</term> so exactly (even if they have never actually seen them) that, although they are shameful idiots, asses, swine, magpies, and daws, they do not feel ashamed to contend and debate with veteran **Goddesses of Wisdom**, **Nightingales**, and **Swans** <note>Metaphors for true philosophers and eloquent scholars.</note>. Indeed, they dogmatize so many methods, so many wonders daily, and so many new, unheard-of, and unusual things, that they seem to obscure Antiquity itself (of which they wish to be called the guardians). They immediately claim to understand authors of more hidden and elegant reputation without having read them—barely knowing how to sound out a word or two in **Latin** <note>original: *Romanè*; literally "in the Roman fashion."</note> without hallucinating. They are taught only by that arch-trifler **Paracelsus** <note>A famous and controversial 16th-century physician and alchemist known for challenging traditional medical authority.</note>, the sorcerer, impostor, charlatan, quack-doctor, prince of entanglements, and architect of riddles—*hated by both heaven and earth*;

->If Bavius itches to write a song, does it not burn Mevius?<- <note>A reference to two notoriously bad poets from Roman literature; the sense is that one fool's actions irritate or excite another.</note>
->The scoundrels who wooed Penelope, and the subjects of Alcinous.<- <note>Reference to the lazy, gluttonous hangers-on from Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note>

### §. 10.

**The mad-brained teachers of error**, the **followers of Hermes**, the **Snarlers**, **Assailants**, and **Mimes**, having broken the chain with which the **Ruler of the World** <note>original: *Cosmarcha*; likely referring to the devil or a worldly tyrant who supposedly keeps order.</note> once bound them, have each retreated to the luxurious side of the world so that they might fleece men of their silver with a thousand tricks and artifices. The greater part of these men claim to possess *this year's harvest* and *chicken's milk* <note>Proverbial for something impossible or an unattainable, imaginary luxury.</note>, or they *possess the horse of Sejanus* <note>original: *equum Seianum*; a Roman proverb for a possession that brings total ruin to its owner.</note>; but instead, by blinding the roosters, they weave ropes out of sand, or pluck the hair from a bald man. While they are busy sniffing out the **Philosopher’s Stone**, they perpetually stumble over the stone of the foolish. They are followed by those who wander among the common folk, whose breeches and purses are full of holes like a sieve. Others...

<summary>The author mocks the intellectual arrogance of pseudo-alchemists who claim to surpass the Ancients despite their lack of education. He specifically targets the followers of Paracelsus, describing them as delusional swindlers who chase impossible goals like the Philosopher's Stone while remaining in poverty.</summary>

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES

...their possessions, sons, hearths, daughters and altars, and they have deserted the pleasant fields of the fatherland of wisdom for the sake of an idle leisure.

There are some who are even voluntarily poor, as it were, because they can receive nothing from anywhere, or because no one is willing to give them anything. *Many* likewise are Counts, Barons, and Heroes by origin; who, the more distinguished they are by birth, always consider themselves to be all the more knowledgeable. Nor are there lacking those who are called baptized Saracens or Jews, though they are somehow more deceitful than those who are unbaptized. These are the ones who have evidently learned through the **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: A Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition often co-opted by Renaissance occultists</term> to kill **Mercury** <term>Mercury: In alchemy, "mortifying" mercury refers to the process of changing its physical state, usually by "fixing" it with acids or heat</term> in many ways, to bring it back to life, and to keep it from coming back to life. Similarly, they learn to prepare all kinds of wolfsbane <note>original: *aconita*</note> in a thousand ways, so that they might lead to [cures for] all diseases and an infinite number of ailments. They claim the Hebrew language as the origin of all arts, and they preserve the most expensive and secret mysteries of public affairs, and they prove themselves to be inspired with foreknowledge of things to come. They frequently quote their Rabbis, the **Talmud** <term>Talmud: The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</term>, and the **harp of Nabolohu** <note>original: *nablúmque Nabolohu*; this appears to be a satirical or garbled reference to a mystical instrument or a pseudo-Hebrew term intended to mock the pretentiousness of the charlatans</note> with the little shrine of Solomon; hence they are no less able to speak of future things than of past and present ones. *Aha!* What loose brooms and **Abderite minds**! <note>original: *mentéſque Abderiticas*; referring to the city of Abdera, which was proverbially known in antiquity for the stupidity or madness of its inhabitants.</note>

Finally, there are those who make a show of religion, wearing monkish hoods and wandering through towns barefoot; they feign the life of a hermit with hidden hypocrisy, to whom God has revealed His secrets as if to little children. O sheep in clothing, but foxes in action! *Aha!* You "all-holy" Dianas! *Bah!* You gallows-birds and **forum-haunters**! <note>original: *ulmitribas ſubroftrarióſque*; *ulmitriba* refers to one beaten with elm rods (a slave), and *subrostrarius* to those loitering near the public platforms to gossip or deceive.</note> Will the evening of those skeptics and **lamp-living thieves** <note>original: *lychnobiorúmque Laronum*; those who live by the lamp, i.e., work at night or in secret</note>, who seek their food from the flame, finally come at last? Their prince is the arch-alchemist **Evil Demon** <note>original: *cacodæmon*</note>, the overseer of the night, who always shines through the smoke; for the arch-novice only dances with other novices; "the old man is looking for the old woman," <note>original: *caſcus cacabat caſcam*; an archaic and proverbial Latin phrase used to denote antiquated nonsense.</note>

->Bring cups with you, if you wish to recline with me,<-
->I shall provide the fat head of a crowned little donkey as a side dish,<-
->Which the elegant foster-children of **Phlegethon** and **Dis** shall eat.<-
<note>Phlegethon is the river of fire in the underworld; Dis is a name for Pluto, the god of the dead. The author implies these charlatans are dining with the damned.</note>

Deceivers, Boasters, **Icarists** <note>referring to Icarus; those who fly too high on wings of pride only to fall</note>, Pot-followers, Traces of Idleness, and World-destroyers—being made of the same plaster, they infect everyone.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

-> All have the same appearance: long and uncombed hair, <-
-> and only combed today for the sake of treats; <-
-> this one is the son of a shaggy shepherd, that one of an ox-herd. <-

They never have more than a single glove in their hand; a little pouch somehow hangs miserably from one side, which they do not put on immediately when leaving home, as is the custom, but only after they have already strolled for several furlongs <note>original: *stadia*</note>. Meanwhile, they are constantly straddling about, biting their nails, hissing and buzzing to themselves. Quarry-workers <note>likely meaning they labor intensely over nothing</note>, O fools and loungers <note>original: *blaces ac Phæaces*</note>, and fanatical men! Furthermore, such people are often seen as *gold-seekers*—or rather, I should say, *gold-wasters*—with a shirt in the back, remarkably dyed in Tyrian purple, hanging a good cubit <note>original: *ulna*</note> and a half out of their trousers;

-> Unless you believe me, I do not swear to you, because we have seen it ourselves, <-
-> yet I conclude that sometimes it can happen this way. <-

Grooms, simpletons, **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Here used pejoratively for those claiming secret mystical knowledge to find gold</term>, players, dwellers in hiding-places, sellers of nonsense <note>original: *lirivenduli*</note>, conspicuous with peacock feathers, like the little crow ridiculous in another’s plumes; they fly in acres and in flocks like cranes; they devour in their own way like swine; according to the rite of monkeys, with wanton and tasteless movements and rustic leaps, they caper and gesticulate. They are also like dogs: in broad daylight, they urinate on every post and foul every corner—truly, they are imitators of **Diogenes the Cynic** <term>Diogenes the Cynic: An ancient Greek philosopher who lived in a tub and rejected social norms, often behaving like a dog to show his contempt for "civilized" hypocrisy</term>. O sheep-like manners! O Arcadic actors! Bah, mackerel <note>original: *scombros*—referring to the fish, used here to suggest something cheap or meant for the trash</note>!

-> Ah, Samian *manners*, O circumstances, O *foolish* hearts <note>The author puns on the Latin *mores* (manners) and *mora* (foolishness/fools)</note>! <-
-> Then I shall often be carried on a decorated horse, <-
-> and daily I shall drag out a pleasant life on nectar. <-
-> Is it a beautiful thing, or one suited to the coming days of Kings? <-
-> To be able to set out anywhere with a gold-clinking purse, <-
-> to pretend to be **Croesus** <term>Croesus: A king of Lydia legendary for his immense wealth</term> one moment, and then to lie about being **Irus** <term>Irus: The beggar from Homer's Odyssey, used as a symbol of extreme poverty</term> the next, <-
-> and then to hold a beautiful **Corinna** <term>Corinna: A common name for a mistress in Roman love poetry</term> in one's embrace? <-
-> But the grief is that you all have the House of Art, <-
-> yet there are no doves in that same home; <-
-> the donkey is witness to what sort of **Arcadians** <term>Arcadians: Traditionally simple shepherds, but here implying they are rustic fools or "asses"</term> you are! <-

<summary>The author ridicules alchemists as unkempt, boorish frauds who mimic the behavior of animals and ancient beggars while dreaming of impossible wealth and luxury. He concludes that despite their claims to possess the "House of Art," their actual lives are devoid of the peace or success they promise.</summary>

### §. II.

Oh, wagons full of stinging tongues! Bah, famous titles—false and false again! Oh, the slanders, the sneers, the sarcasms, and the whole wantonness of their raving! They are double-beasts, triple-barbarians!

->Hear the depths enclosed by wandering shores,<-
->Drink in these mockeries, you gods, wherever you have withdrawn:<-
->Hear, you infernal ones; hear, you Shadows; hear, you whirlpools <note>original: *charybdes*</note>,<-
->And Night, heavy with the fiery clouds of Phlegethon <note>the river of fire in the underworld</note> and black clouds,<-
->Listen to my voices, and pay heed to my words;<-

For who, as a sincere student of the Truth of Magic <note>original: *Philomagicæ*</note>, would not rebuke these detractors? Who would not consider these insults a monstrous disgrace? Who would not challenge such satires <note>original: *pasquillos*</note> and mockeries to a duel? Whose deepest soul, I ask, would these jokes not wound? I cannot—indeed, I shall not be able to—fail to demand redress <note>original: *clarigare*, a Roman term for formally declaring war</note>, or to throw down the cloak and glove (as the saying goes), and descend into the field of battle with those shameless backbiters;

->Noble virtue, once branded, knows not how to rest,<-
->Nor can it fear even a jot <note>original: *gry*</note> when the cause is just:<-
->I will go, I will go, and I alone will stand in fierce arms,<-
->And in the midst of swords, I will offer my dug-up skull <term>bregma: the anatomical term for the top of the skull</term>.<-

Let no one think, therefore, that I am only courageous in a dedicated wrestling-school,

->And merely a loud-mouth at home, after the manner of a rooster,<-

I, even unarmed—though easily the most remote of all these little circles—summon those scolders into their own sea. I do not fear in the least to clash with them on the Ciceronian or Ovidian plain <note>original: *Tullianâ, aut Ovidianâ*, referring to the refined Latin styles of Cicero and Ovid</note>—that is, on the ancient and hidden plain of the Philosophers.

### §. 12.

The <term>Almond tree <note>original: *Amygdalus*</note></term> is the boldest of trees; as one which, right before the very eyes of a barely-departed winter <note>original: *brumæ*, referring to the winter solstice or the coldest part of the year</note>, seizes possession of the spring, as it were, and thrusts forth its flowers. It fears nothing of the season's inclemency. While other trees and plants, dreading the sharpness and injuries of the air, keep their colors providently tucked away, the almond tree—as if unconcerned by dangers and disdaining all fear—loosens its buds and proffers its blossoms. This, indeed, is the quality to which a diligent leader <note>original: *principem*</note> ought to compose himself: namely, that he be ***the first and the last*** <note>original: *primus & imus*; an idiom suggesting one who is the first to face danger and the most deeply involved in the work</note>. Such a man, despising toil and trampling underfoot all inconveniences, meets the needs of his followers. For the herald of a difficult deed, an emulator of the almond trees, ought not to be an imitator of bees <note>who only emerge in the safety of full warmth</note>. 

Furthermore, to loudly mock those witty jokers <note>his critics</note> in return, I think nothing more opportune could ever be cited than that famous fable, the narration of which is quite pleasant to hear. I ask you, therefore, to look upon this story once, gathered here in passing and, as it were, while on the move:

It is a record of the ancients that the <note>Hippocrenides: another name for the Muses, daughters of the spring Hippocrene</note> **Muses** were called out to a battle by the **Sirens** to contend over the sweetness of their singing. They contended on both sides, and the **Muses** <note>original: *Camœnæ*</note> triumphed in song. From the victory, they plucked the feathers from the Sirens and made themselves little crowns from them as a sign of victory, so say the witnesses of this fiction. The ancients devised all these things to make it known that whatever <note>Thamyris: a mythical singer who challenged the Muses and was punished with blindness</note> **Thamyris**, or whatever the false and deceptive **Sirens**, have written with an envious pen or babbled with a rival tongue against the <note>Aonian choir: a classical reference to the Muses</note> **eloquent Muses**, in order to obscure the most ample virtues and famous deeds of renowned and learned men—all of that turns to their greater glory. They are crowned for the procession with the very feathers with which the detractors hoped to overshadow them. These critics most of all reveal and make illustrious the very honor they wish to drag down and blind. For these monsters among men know that no work is excellent or remarkable, which

->§. 12.<-

The Almond <term>Amygdalus; the almond tree, which in early modern emblem books often symbolized courage or haste because it blooms in late winter</term> is the most daring of trees. As if seizing possession of the spring right before the very eyes of winter <note>original: *brumæ*; specifically the winter solstice or the depth of winter</note> which has scarcely passed, it thrusts forth its flowers, fearing nothing of the season's inclemency. While other trees and plants, fearing the sharpness and injuries of the air, keep their colors prudently shut away, the almond—as if unconcerned by dangers and disdaining all fear—loosens its buds and proffers its flowers. This, indeed, is the manner to which a diligent prince ought to compose himself: namely, that he be **first and last** <note>original: *primus & imus*; a phrase suggesting one who is both the leader in action and the most humble in service to his subjects</note>, who, having despised the sweat of labor and trampled underfoot all inconveniences, runs to meet the needs of his dependents. For the Author <note>original: *Auſpex*; literally an augur or one who takes the lead in an undertaking</note> of a difficult deed ought to be an emulator of the almond tree, not an imitator of bees <note>Bees were often seen as symbols of industry, but here they are contrasted with the almond because they wait for the warmth of the sun to work.</note>. Furthermore, to properly laugh back at those witty jesters, I think nothing more opportune could ever be cited than that fable, the telling of which is quite pleasant to hear; therefore, I ask you to look upon this story here, collected in passing and as if on the run:

It is an original account of the ancients that the Muses <term>Hippocrenides; a name for the Muses, referring to the Hippocrene spring on Mount Helicon which was sacred to them</term>, having been called into battle by the Sirens to contend over the sweetness of their singing, fought on both sides. The Muses <term>Camœnæ; the Roman name for the Muses, often associated with song and prophecy</term> triumphed with their melody, and they plucked the feathers from the Sirens, from which they made crowns for themselves as a sign of victory, so say the witnesses of the story. The ancients devised all these things so that they might make known that whatever the likes of Thamyris <note>A mythical singer who challenged the Muses and was punished with the loss of his sight and his ability to sing.</note>, or the false and fallacious Sirens, have written with an envious pen or babbled with a rival tongue against the eloquent Aonian choir <note>original: *Aonium diſertum chorum*; the Muses, who were said to dwell in Aonia</note>—intending to obscure the most ample virtues and noble deeds of famous and learned men—that effort instead yields to their greater glory. They are crowned for the procession with those very feathers with which the detractors hoped they would be clouded; for these critics most of all reveal and make illustrious the very honor they wish to drag down and darken. They proclaim that Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic war.</note> leapt forth from the head of Jupiter without a mother, and that she arose beside the river Triton, for which reason she is called Tritogenia—for the Boeotians <note>Inhabitants of Boeotia, a region of ancient Greece.</note> call the head *trito*. She is not undeservedly called the Goddess of Wisdom for this reason: because she was born from the brain, which is the seat of wisdom. A golden rain also adorned her birthday at Rhodes (an island named for its rose-beds), so that the moment she was brought into this light might endure in the memory of men. For just as in a public triumph or festival—such as a King’s coronation, a celebration, or the royal birth of an heir—golden coins are sometimes tossed...

->§. 13.<-

Now, let us wander a little into another beautiful, delicate, and no less curious matter. I have often observed—and I believe it is worthy of great admiration—that at night, the brighter and clearer the moon shows itself, the more the dogs bark at it with raised voices and clamor, turning their sharp eyes toward it. Investigating the reason for this while in a deliberative mood, I finally found that I could think of no more fitting explanation than this: the dogs, looking at the moon, see their own image, likeness, and shape within it, as if in a shining mirror. From this, they imagine that another dog similar to themselves is present there, and thus they bark, as dogs are frequently accustomed to do when they see others.

> Dogs gaze at Diana <note>A name for the Moon goddess</note> by night as if into a mirror;
> And while they see another dog, they think it is really there,
> They bark and bay in vain—their voices are lost to the winds,
> While the deaf Moon continues to complete her course.

Hindered not at all by their barking, she proceeds entirely further...

...it proceeds, completing its swift motion. In a not dissimilar way, it is also accustomed to happen to the advocates of more majestic wisdom; so, I say, the malice of the stage-players <term>Thymelariorum; originally stage-performers or mimes, used here to describe foolish, superficial critics or "buffoons" who perform for the crowd</term> cries out and barks against the wise-magicians <term>Magiosophos; those who possess the wisdom of the magi or natural magic</term>, whom they would even wish to blind <note>original: *exoculassere*</note>. This is truly a brutal madness, born of hellish bile <note>original: *choleræ-que tartareæ*</note>, but oh, what hatreds, detested by heaven and kindred to the devil! 

It will perhaps seem a marvel to some for what reason the owl was once dedicated to Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic war</note>; yet beyond other reasons, this principal one (in my judgment) can be assigned: that other birds pursue the owl if she ever appears during the day, for the reason that she has clear, bright, and shining eyes, which the other birds seem to want to gouge out. In just this way, the World would wish to tear away the wisdom, honor, and reputation of the lovers of magic <term>Philomagorum; those who love and study divine or natural magic</term>.

The masters of war <term>Polemopatres; literally "fathers of war," referring to ancient military theorists</term>, in their instructions by which they inform students of military discipline, command a general <note>original: *strategum*</note> who is eager for victory to always arrange the army <note>original: *stratiam*</note> in such a way that he does not fight facing the sun;

->For as they say, *the sun first snatches away both sight and face;*<-

And for that reason, one should never fight against its glimmers—how aptly indeed this applies to those whose minds have been entirely invaded and occupied by hatred and envy of the Spagyric Sun <term>Spagirici Solis; the "Alchemical Sun," symbolizing the gold-making power or the transformative light of alchemical practice</term>! These men, envious of its glory and its incredible mysteries, have wished to bury Alchemy in perpetual oblivion and to banish it from human memory. But, blind and mad, they did not heed the precept of the learned writers on war <term>polemographorum</term>. For they did not only begin to battle against the sun, but even to provoke Hyperion himself <note>A Titan often identified with the sun</note>—the very storehouse <note>original: *myropolium*; literally a perfumery or place of ointments, here a metaphor for the source of nature's wonders</note> of all the wonders of nature—in war, as if to cast Jupiter himself from his throne. From this, it is very easy to guess what these men will suffer in the conflict, having dared to undertake so reckless a thing,

->For the glowing *sun first snatches away both sight and face:*<-

Thus our Titan—that bright torch of the human mind, Physical-Chemistry <term>Physicochymia; a term here for the natural science of alchemy</term>—blinds those mockers according to the merit of their blasphemy, and with the glowing rays of its profound wisdom, it dulls their sight;

Truly, I shall never be able to praise his charity enough!

### §. 14.

I, therefore, at the conclusion of this little literary book, thought it advantageous to have signed it thus: May your scientific majesty, O Thrice-Greatest King <note>original: *Rex Trismegiste*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy</note>, deign to read these things; to polish them with attentive eyes not once, but repeatedly and many times; to value them meticulously <term>ex ungue; literally "from the fingernail," a Latin idiom meaning to judge a work of art with the highest precision</term> and with reverence. Together with your other associates in that most sacred imperial hall, who have already confessed the fates, I ask you to think upon these things with meditation, to summon the invention, to ripen our defenses, and finally to transmit the sum of these burning decrees—not in writing, but by the living voice of this most faithful Wing-Foot <note>original: *Alipedis*; an epithet for the messenger god Mercury, symbolizing swift and divine communication</note>—to the Lovers of Magic <term>Philomagis; those who love the pursuit of secret or divine wisdom</term> who even now face an uncertain gamble, and who are the professors of your name and practice. Send this quickly, most quickly, with all possible haste:

> When I had watered these resounding kisses
> Of words and mind, immediately the Cyllenian Winged One <note>original: *Cyllenius Ales*; another title for Mercury, who was born on Mount Cyllene</note>
> Took up the cause, and entered the halls with ruffled feathers,

And he was seen to have delivered, with the greatest confidence, those biting "storks" <note>original: *ciconias*; a Roman gesture of mockery made by mimicking a stork's beak with the hand; here used to represent the sharp, mocking insults of the critics</note> of the mockers—nay, of the devils—into the very hands of the most fertile Arch-mage <term>Archimagi; a title for a high leader or master of the magical arts</term>. > Burning with the rabid fury of an untamed mind,

Immediately the Maenalian Winged One <note>original: *Mænalius Volucer*; an epithet for Mercury, the messenger of the gods, associated with Mount Maenalus</note> obeyed the decrees. He detested delays and would have already traveled to his destination, had not the Prefect recalled him with these words: "Hey there, where to? In your usual fashion, my faithful minister, you are rushing off without wings and without sandals, you foolish thing; stop, for you shall go as an elegantly outfitted messenger for us." 

He spoke, and immediately bound the winged sandals <term>talaria; the magical winged sandals of Mercury that grant flight</term> to his feet, which weigh him in the air with a famous breeze, high above the earth and across the Vale of Achelous. Then he binds his hair and balances the stars with his traveler's cap <term>petaso; a broad-brimmed hat, often depicted with wings, worn by Mercury</term>. Then he takes the wand <term>virga; the Caduceus, Mercury’s staff entwined with snakes</term> in his fingers, with which he is accustomed to drive the drowsiness of sleep, or again to remove the business of our world from where it is not wanted; with this staff he is able to thrust things away, and trusting in it, he furrows the South Winds and swims through the clouds. With it, he approaches the lurid pools of grim Pluto <note>original: *Ditis*; a name for the god of the Underworld</note>, and leads out the Stygian Spirits <term>Manes; the souls of the deceased</term> from the shallows of the Abyss <note>original: *Erebi*; Erebus, the personification of darkness and a region of the underworld</note>, and at the same time is accustomed to bring life back to the extinguished shadows. Being thus equipped, he circled through the thin air and, swift without rushing, glided down on ready wings, quickly seizing his flight through the void, having first articulated his path with a wide rotation through the clouds.

And then, from that moment, he summoned a circle at close hand under dire omens, in that vaulted and secret chamber of the Silent Ones <note>original: *Silentûm*; likely referring to initiates sworn to silence or the spirits of the dead</note>, which was swelling with scarlet veils and golden keys. There he was to be seen—like Phaëthon <note>The son of Helios who attempted to drive the sun-chariot</note>, with a starry crown, and with spirits of elegant form gathered at his feet like Kings of a heavenly choir—sitting in a shrine upon a throne. This throne was far superior in its workmanship to that of Solomon, that famous and heroic throne to which the world has seen nothing equal or second.

He was entirely covered in silver, and entirely in gold:
As many as were the Initiates <term>Mystæ; those initiated into sacred or secret mysteries</term>, so many Lords <term>Dynastas; powerful rulers or high-ranking members of an order</term> I believed to be present;
They all stood dressed in scarlet garments,
All of them with their brows adorned with uniform garlands.

->§. 15.<-

The secretarial historians of the wonders of their age, when set to describe the triumph of Julian Caesar—that terror of the earth—know not with what grandeur of words, what weight of sentiment, or what charm and vein of eloquence they might most skillfully express it. For who would not marvel greatly at this Emperor? Famous for his victories and spoils, he was carried in a triumphal throne drawn by forty elephants, and thus received into the Roman Capitol with such great pomp, applause, and the joy of the common people. And what of Aurelian, whose chariot was pulled by stags instead of horses? Or Antony, who, after various nations were subdued and brought under his yoke, sat in a carriage to which two pairs of Lions were harnessed? Likewise Domitian, who is recorded as having been introduced not in a two-horse, four-horse, or six-horse litter, but upon the shoulders of men?

And yet, I seem to strive no less here in expressing the magnificence of our Magiarch <term>Magiarchus; the 'Chief of the Magi' or 'Arch-Magician'</term>, and his most haughty night-mysteries <term>nyctelia; secret nocturnal rites or festivals, traditionally associated with Bacchus but here applied to magical gatherings</term>. He was not magnified there in a seated throne, celebrated by lowly herds, thronged by a mortal rabble, or decorated by popular applause. On the contrary, he resounded in that spiritual region with an ineffable symphony, abounding with "Gargaric" <note>likely referring to the immense heights or fertile swarms of Mount Gargarus</note> myriads of Immortal Spirits and a swarming multitude of Philomagi <term>Philomagi; 'lovers of magic' or devoted students of the craft</term>, and every kind of thyme-scented spice and precious thing. 

Ah, what glory! Oh, what pomp! O unspeakable triumph! I truly know not with what style I might best touch upon this: if the whole world were paper, all trees were pens, and all waters were ink, it would not be nearly enough to describe and bring forth the majesty of that place. Therefore, whatever has been settled by us in this matter, he will give answers through the voice of the most learned Messenger <note>original: "Diactoris"; a Greek epithet for Hermes/Mercury meaning 'the guide'</note>. > Continue to feed your mind with sacred studies,

realizing that matters of great weight and importance must have been written in the scrolls, he ordered the full price she had demanded to be paid to her at once. He commanded that the books be preserved with the greatest reverence on the **Capitoline Hill** <note>The religious and political heart of ancient Rome.</note>, to be consulted as oracles by the **Fifteen Men** <term>Quindecimviri: A college of fifteen priests who guarded and interpreted the Sibylline Books in times of crisis.</term> regarding any doubtful matters. The argument concerning these books—whether they were burned or not burned—suggests to me, by the law of satire and by the dictates of the priestly office, that it was also assigned by those **Past Adepts** to their own **Swift-footed Leader of Mysteries** <note>original: "Volucripedi Mystagogo." Likely a reference to the god Mercury (Hermes), the messenger of the gods and guide of souls.</note>.

**Fourth and finally**, everyone agreed in unison that this **little work on true magic** <note>original: "Orthomagiopusculum." A compound of "ortho" (correct/true), "magi" (magic), and "opusculum" (little work).</note>, smelling of the lamp under the torchlight of nightly vigils, should be made known and brought forth from the mouth of the **Wing-footed God** late at night. By this, when I reflect upon it, they clearly indicated the highest pursuit of wisdom. Just as the **Spartans** <note>original: "Lacones."</note>, as we read in the records of history, used to handle their greater and more difficult matters at night, they were certainly mindful of that famous proverb: ***in the night is counsel*** <note>original: "in nocte consilium." This classic proverb suggests that the quiet of night is the best time for reflection and making wise decisions.</note>. Indeed, the rest found at night is most suitable for taking wise and useful counsel regarding all things.

-> §. 18. <-

At the origin of the world, God established the **firmament** in the midst of the waters, so that he might separate one from the other, saying: *Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters*. The **Golden Orator** <note>original: "Orator aureus." Likely a reference to St. John Chrysostom, whose name means "Golden-mouthed."</note> truly reads this as: *Let there be a partition, let a wall intervene to separate the waters, so that some do not communicate with others*. Regarding these waters, I can indeed say that **some** are a symbol of the tumults of the day, while **others** are a type of the peace of night. Let there be, therefore, a space between the waters to separate the flows from the flows, so that the business of each does not run together. For it is impossible for one who has been excessively active during the day to enjoy the hidden things of the night; nor is it granted to find the leisure for arduous and sublime wisdom amidst the tumults of the day and the preoccupations of the light.

Hence also the **Athenians**, who flourished with singular praise for wisdom and all disciplines, abandoned the emblem of the **Eagles** which the **Valentians** <note>Likely referring to the Roman legions under Emperors like Valentinian.</note> carried on their military standards. Instead, they adopted the **Owl**, a bird that flees the light, which they even engraved on their coins as a symbol of wisdom. For this reason, it is also called the bird of **Pallas** and is dedicated to **Minerva**, the goddess of the sciences, to denote—

...during the **dead of night** <term>conticinium: The specific Roman term for the first part of the night when all falls silent.</term>, or the time most suited for studies rather than the day; just as the excellent **Royal Harpist** <note>A traditional title for King David, referring to his authorship of the Psalms.</note>, **Daniel**, **Isaiah**, and **Zechariah** noted: *I meditated in the night with my heart; Night shall be my light in my delights; I beheld in a vision of the night; My soul shall desire thee in the night; I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees in the deep.* <note>These are translated excerpts from Psalm 77:6, Psalm 139:11, Daniel 7:7, Isaiah 26:9, and Zechariah 1:8.</note> For when someone powerful in the weight of their person and authority speaks, all who are present are soon accustomed to fall silent:

> Peace, all are silent, and they hold their faces intent,
> Then Father **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes." The messenger god (Mercury) often associated with the transmission of hidden knowledge.</note> began from his high throne,
> When the late twilight of night reached its midpoint;
> After he restrained the murmurs mixed with bellowing with his voice and hand,
> Soon silence was made among their tongues,
> As the weapons driven by the Leader’s brow came to rest,
> Behold **Prosophus** <note>Likely a character name meaning "The Wise Speaker."</note> again disturbs the silence with words:

Moreover, this silence is never greater than during the night-time, when mortals are surely accustomed to restrain themselves from their daily cares and exercises; as **Solomon** wisely said: *While all things were in quiet silence, your almighty word leaped down from heaven from your royal throne,* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 18:14-15.</note> signifying to us in this matter that the soul which yearns to be free for sublime and secret things ought to cultivate leisure and seclusion, and to shrink from the noise of cares and the tumults of the passions.

> The **Muses** <note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration in literature, science, and the arts.</note> are not well-tended near or through windows,
> They are rarely strong in the sun or the marketplace:
> Nor do they laugh in the middle of the day, or favor the light,
> The sun, the light, and men draw one toward many jests.
> Thus the marketplace, the clear sky, and the streets must be avoided,
> And then the harvest from the Muses will also be greater.

Therefore, the time of night—which is the mother of counsel and the nourisher of every arduous work—is most suitably appointed for the handling of these mysteries.

While I was engaged in such matters, and having been somewhat awakened to all of this, I was more like one keeping watch or dreaming than one who was sleeping. And yet, when **Celeripes** <note>original: "Celeripes." Literally "Swift-foot," a common classical epithet for Mercury (Hermes), the messenger of the gods.</note>, standing present before me, had opened his mouth with the greatest power and soothing sweetness, I seemed to be entirely charmed with immense joy. Immediately, my eyes were led inexpressibly by that clear light of my **Trans-Elysian** <note>Referring to someone from the Elysian Fields, the Greek version of paradise; a soul from the beyond.</note> guide’s countenance, who at that time represented an Archangel in a way not at all dissimilar. By that most orderly golden stylus, inscribed by the fingers of our **High Priest Trismegistus** <note>original: "Propontificis nostri Trismegisti." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as the author of the Hermetic Corpus and a bridge between Egyptian and Greek wisdom.</note>, my ears were melodiously affected. I hung upon the **Attic eloquence** <term>Attic eloquence: A refined, elegant, and polished style of oratory associated with ancient Athens.</term> and the persuasive harmony of the words of my sweet-talking **Mercury**. By the sweet fragrance of his loud-resounding voice—like a certain divine **Orpheus**—he spoke in the tongues partly of men and partly of Angels; that is, using a style of speaking that was now moderate, now full and rhetorical. O blessed, well-tended mouth! My heart was opened within, and it swelled with joy at the account of such great vigilance and concern of the kindly Divinities for their own people, for now at last the day of release had arrived, with our own Patrons taking the matter so heartily upon themselves. And furthermore, there was the Envoy himself, upon whose tongue is the greatest labor, and under his tongue the sweetest honey—but what is above his tongue? Ineffable things, which it is a religious duty for me to speak of, and whose name is the one in whose morning the **Israelite people** shook off the yoke of the hard **Pharaonic mill** <note>A reference to the Exodus from Egypt, here used as a metaphor for spiritual or intellectual liberation.</note>. This is truly a symbol of our entire salvation, redemption, and freedom from the tyranny of the **Tartarean serpent** <note>A classical-style reference to the Devil or the serpent of Eden, Tartarus being the deep abyss of torment in Greek mythology.</note>, as he entices us with such spirit regarding our total success.

### §. 20.

"Now that I have recounted," said **Hermogenes** <note>A name often associated in mystical literature with the Hermetic tradition or a divine messenger of wisdom.</note>, "in the Spartan fashion <note>original: "Laconicè." Meaning briefly and concisely.</note> and with great faith, their opinions concerning that **Stone of the Wise** <note>original: "Lapide Sapientum," the Philosopher's Stone. This was the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>—which is the storehouse of all riches and delights—pay heed to these signs, for they are soon to be offered to mortals. Out of honor for the most holy Trinity and for my excellent initiates, and for the relief of widows and the comfort of the pious, do not despair of divine help. Fortified by His assistance and my own, begin the omen of this 'marketable web'—not one that is rough and uncombed, nor one made controversial by the ambiguity of proverbs. Those who held the right (while they were among the living) to reveal this unique **Art** <note>Meaning Alchemy or "Orthomagia."</note> to whomever they wished, by the nod of God, have commanded that this task be delegated to you as a sacred duty.

Therefore, so that the name of **True Magic** <note>original: "Orthomagiæ." From the Greek 'orthos' (right/true) and 'mageia' (magic).</note> and the lineage of those who granted you this gift may forever sail forward under your guidance among those whom the triple Architect of heaven and earth—that ultimate **First Master of Magic** <note>original: "Protophilomagus." A title likely referring to God as the first source of all wisdom, or perhaps Adam or Hermes Trismegistus in a historical sense.</note>—has called or rather pre-selected for the hidden things of this literature. Deliver the entire business in a simple sequence of tradition, just as I suggest to you: full of meaning but not obscured <note>original: "sententiosè, non septuosè." A wordplay suggesting the text should be pithy and informative rather than "thorny" or partitioned by secrets.</note>, and without any intentional concealment, through a plain and concise order. For it is well known that no one can claim these things for themselves except the one to whom **Jehovah** <note>The Hebrew name for God.</note> has decreed to grant them; He alone clarifies the darkness of these mysteries or dims their brightness, so that no one can grasp even the clearest and most evident things unless illuminated by Him, nor can anyone uncover the most noble secrets if they have not been enlightened by His hand. Furthermore, I adjure you to dispatch these things fluently and without delay."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of etymologies and philosophical definitions, likely following a section describing the prophetic nature of the Sibyls or the "Magic Circus" mentioned in point 8.</meta>

### The Sibyls' Enclosure

1. Commonly used for prophetic virgins; however, in a broad sense, every woman or girl whose breast receives the Divine <note>original: "Numen"</note> and who vaticinates and prophesies is called a **Sibyl**, that is, the counsel of God. For the Aeolians <note>A dialect of Ancient Greek</note> say *Sios* <note>original: "Σιὸς"</note> for "God," and among them *Boule* <note>original: "Βουλὴ"</note> is called "mind" or "counsel." Therefore, we can call the Sibyls **Siobulas**, as it were—those sounding the thoughts of God—to whom the Ancients surely gave this name because they announced the counsels of the Gods.

2. Here is the medium, the practice, the way, etc.: said to be from *climbing* <note>original: "scandendo"</note>, because by this way we climb to the highest points of wisdom.

3. Here it is: to dwell, to remain, etc. Otherwise, <term>morari<gloss>to play the fool</gloss></term> (with a long first vowel), signifies "to act foolishly" according to its Greek etymology. This is seen in the famous saying: *Claudius ceased to linger among men* <note>A punning reference to the death of Emperor Claudius; the author suggests it means he stopped "acting like a fool" rather than simply "staying" among the living.</note>. This should not be interpreted as if the meaning were "Claudius ceased to act and live among men," but rather that through death he ceased to be insane and out of his mind, he who had been senseless while alive.

4. Commonly "lofty" <note>original: "altùm"</note>, as if it were *above the mud* <note>The author provides a folk etymology for "sublimis" (sublime) as "supra limum."</note>.

5. More commonly [one says] of them, as if *you give yourself to the way*, etc.

6. Little animals are of well-known significance. **Ants** <note>original: "Formicæ"</note>, tireless in their labor, dwellers of the countryside, the agile nurslings of the All-Parent Earth, etc., are so named from *carrying crumbs* <note>original: "ferendis micis"</note>—that is, grains, for which "crumbs" is used figuratively, as it is for bits of bread and all other things. For, strictly speaking, "crumbs" <note>original: "micæ"</note> are those tiny specks of dust that sparkle in the sand like gold or silver; hence the verb <term>mico<gloss>I flash or shimmer</gloss></term>, which means to glow or redden repeatedly and at intervals, just as those mentioned dust-specks do.

7. Here it stands for celebrated, distinguished, excellent, etc. Otherwise, <term>nobilis<gloss>noble</gloss></term> is, according to its etymology, a verbal form made and contracted from *noscibilis* <note>knowable or noteworthy</note>, in the same manner as *facilis* (easy), *agilis* (agile), and many similar words.

8. Or the **cornucopia**; it is the same (just as mentioned above regarding the Magic Circus) as the **Horn of Amalthea**. It is endowed with this bright and most indulgent faculty: that whatever we desire, it buds forth for us abundantly from it. Some traditions say there are two such Horns, from one of which ambrosia flowed, and from the other nectar—the food and drink of the Gods. Truly, however, this has no affinity or conformity with our philosophy and the **Golden Truth**: *there is one Sun, one God, and one Earth, which brings forth all things as one through the One.*

# THE UNCOVERED GRAIN <note>original: "GRANUM ERUTUM"; likely a reference to the "Winnowing Fan" metaphor, where the truth (grain) is separated from the husks and dug out for the reader.</note>

1. In this place, it is the same as a seal, a sign, or a sealed diploma <note>original: "sigillum, signum, sive obsignatum diploma"</note>.
2. That is, the powers or properties of the magnet, or more correctly, *magnetism*: otherwise, the term **Divine Will** <note>original: "Numen"</note> properly refers to the command or "nod" of God.
3. In Latin, *breviloquentia* <note>short-speaking</note>, or a brief discourse that contains much within a few words; it is called this as if it were the *custom of the Lacons* <note>original: "Laconum mos"</note>, which is the compression of many things into few words. The name is derived from the customs of the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note>, for whom nothing was more hateful than long-winded talkativeness.
4. Here it is an adjective for that which belongs to meter <note>original: "metri"</note>—that is, it pertains to measurement, song, or verse. At other times, the word **metric** <note>original: "metricus"</note> is also used as a noun, meaning the same thing as a poet.
5. That is, by devotion and holiness of life, by the seal of the soul, etc. This is because **Religion** is used figuratively for anxious care, a scruple of conscience, and so on; it is named from "leaving behind" <note>original: "reliquendo"</note>, or rather from "binding back" <note>original: "religando"</note>, because it surely *binds us back* to God.

<margin>in which it <unclear>truly</unclear> <note>original: "uere"</note> ought to</margin>
6. That is, by the clarity of the soul, by purity, integrity, etc. This is because **sincerity** <note>original: "sinceritas"</note> is etymologically the same as simplicity—that is, the clarity of the heart, *like wax* <note>original: "sicut cera"</note>. Just as the word **simple** <note>original: "simplex"</note> sounds like "without a fold" <note>original: "sine plica"</note>, so that which is **sincere** is said to be "without wax" <note>original: "sine cera"</note>. This is a metaphor drawn from honey, which, before it is without additives—that is, simple, pure, and unmixed—must be *without wax*. Or, we can interpret **sincere** in another way, and perhaps not without wit, as being "together with wax" <note>original: "simul cum cera"</note>: for when we wish to divide the common fruit of the beehives with our partners without deceit, we are accustomed to share the honey *together with the wax*. If, however, we only bring the honey forward and keep the wax for ourselves, we defraud our partners and do not act with them with integrity and **sincerity**—that is, *together with the wax*. And from this, the spelling is good whether it is written **sincerus** with a Latin *i*, or **syncerus** with a Greek *y*.
7. Or graphically <note>original: "graphicè"</note>; in Latin: elegantly, beautifully, accurately, "to the nail" <note>original: "ad unguem"; a Latin idiom for a perfectly finished work</note>, etc.
8. That is, it is first titled, taking a comparison from the ministers of the Church who, when **baptizing** <note>original: "baptizantes"</note>, are accustomed to give names to the persons at the same time.
9. That is, seriously, deliberately, with meditation, etc., as if **by profession** <note>original: "ex professione"</note>.
10. Here it stands for "they affirmed," "they approved," etc. However, the word seems to me to be said as a play on opposites <note>original: "antiphrasticōs"</note> for "I shout" <note>original: "clamo"</note>, as if it were "I love" <note>original: "amo"</note>, that is, "I act secretly" <note>original: "clam ago"</note>, because lovers act very secretly and do not shout at all.

# THE GRAIN UNEARTHED.

1. In this context, this word is the same as a seal, a sign, or a sealed diploma. <note>original: "sigillum, signum, sive obsignatum diploma"</note>

2. That is, the strengths or faculties of the magnet, or more correctly, *magnetism*: otherwise, "Divine Power" <note>original: "Numen"</note> is properly the nod and the wink—the will—of God.

3. The name is derived from the customs of the Lacedaemonians [the Spartans], to whom nothing was more hateful than long-winded talk.

4. Here it is an adjective for that which belongs to meter—that is, it pertains to measure, song, or verse: otherwise, the word *metric* is also sometimes used as a noun, meaning the same thing as a "poet."

5. That is, by devotion and the holiness of life, the seal of the soul, etc., because *Religion* is used figuratively for an anxious care, a scruple of conscience, and so on; it is named from "leaving behind" <note>original: "reliquendo"</note> or rather from "binding back" <note>original: "religando"</note>, because it surely binds us back to God.

6. That is, by a brightness of soul, purity, integrity, etc., because *sincerity* is etymologically the same as *simplicity*—that is, the clarity of the heart, *just like wax* <note>original: "sicut cera"</note>. This is a comparison drawn from honey which, before it is "without deception"—namely, simple, pure, and unmixed—must be "without wax." Or we can interpret *sincere* in another way, and perhaps not without wit, as if it were "together with the wax" <note>original: "simul cum cera"</note>: for when we wish to share the common fruit of the beehives with our partners without deceit, we are accustomed to divide the honey *together with the wax*. # THE WINNOWED GRAIN

4. ...phile <note>This is the conclusion of a word from the previous page, likely "Deiphobe."</note>, yet by me here, and elsewhere by Virgil, she is called **Deiphobe**, as if she were *phobae*, that is, the "hair" and "adornment" of **God** <note>original: "Dei"</note>; you have heard of her deeds in part in our Sibylline Oracles. 5. Likewise, let those three words, **therefore the dark mother** <note>original: "atra igitur mater"</note>, not pass without a notable scrutiny, especially the last one; however, setting aside the tripod <note>A reference to the seat of the Delphic Pythia, meaning "setting aside prophecy."</note> and borrowing the hook of the former: for these have been specifically combined in this way by intention, through long and tedious labor and mature judgment. 6. Here she is distended and stuffed with the best juice; read a little further below the gloss on the word **pregnant**. 7. i.e., Full of veins, or "veined"; because the endings *-osus*, *-lentus*, and frequently *-bundus*, are terminations used by Grammarians to denote fullness. For example, *aurosus* or **aurulentus**, that is, full and **distended** with gold; **Amorosus** or *amorabundus*, or the contracted **amabundus**, that is, full and as if in love **to the very bottom** <note>original: "fundo tenus"</note>; likewise **porosus** (full of pores), **gaudiosus** (full of joys), etc.; **florulentus** (full of flowers), **rosulentus** (full of roses), etc.; **esuribundus** (full of hunger), **deerrabundus** (full of error), etc., which is to say, overflowing and full of pores, joys, flowers, roses, hunger, or error. 8. I consider the history of the **Phoenix** (which is to be understood properly as the **Philosophers' Stone**) renewing itself to be sufficiently well known; however, to me the name **Phoenix** seems to be spoken as if it were the **snow of Phoebus** <note>original: "nix Phoebi"</note>, that is, the luster of the sun. 9. Concerning which, clearly, nothing has yet been born or arisen; hence the "third matter" is excluded, such as all Animals, Vegetables, and Minerals. For the word **virgin** is derived from "incorruption" and is shared with all things that we wish to signify as unpolluted; it is like **virago**, because she **acts with force** <note>original: "vi agat"</note> and is ignorant of female passion. 10. **Nowhere not**, a periphrasis for **everywhere**; for the word **nullibi** is spoken as if **in no place** <note>original: "nullo in loco"</note>; **Necubi** [lest anywhere] has the same sense. 11. That is, it brings forth seed, because **semento** (to sow) is derived from **sementum**, which is the same as **seed** <note>original: "semen"</note>; etymologically it is **sementifico** (to make seed), for which we say the contracted form **semento**, as if **trying the seed** <note>original: "semen tento"</note>. 12. Properly it means "to frisk or play joyfully," spoken as if **frisking with the penis** <note>original: "pene vitulatur," an alchemical pun on "vitulor," to frisk like a calf</note>, from which I believe the contraction was made; it is placed here sharply and aptly, because the **olochrysa** <note>From the Greek for "all-gold."</note>, that is, the ever-living matter of the Sages, continually delights in its own hidden and invisible seed. 13. i.e., It grows, for **olesco** properly means **to grow** <note>original: "cresco"</note>, as if it were **I shall be a vegetable** <note>original: "olus esco"</note>; for the ancients used **esco, escis, escit** for **ero, eris, erit** (I will be, you will be, he will be). 14. i.e., It emits seed, or makes **sperma**, as if it **spermatificates**, for which the contracted form **spermatico** is used; it might be more correctly said as **spermatizo** outside of meter, because the root is Greek. 15. i.e., She is heavy with child, since **praegno** etymologically sounds like being great **before offspring** <note>original: "prae gnatis"</note>, that is, before any fruits. 16. i.e., She gives birth, she makes a fetus; for the verb **foeto** is a contraction of **foetifico**, which is "I make a fetus," "I am in labor," etc. 17. i.e., She increases with offspring, for I think **sobolesco** is said as if **I grow with offspring** <note>original: "sobole cresco"</note>. 18. i.e., She thickens and increases amply, because **alesco** is said as if **I grow by nourishment** <note>original: "alimento cresco"</note>. 19. i.e., And yet she by no means suffers the loss or shipwreck of her virginity, because the **eugium** (with the second-to-last syllable lengthened) is almost the same thing as the *hymen*, namely that thin little membrane in the female parts which is broken at the first coitus and believed to be the enclosure of virginity; therefore, it fits the present purpose rightly through metaphor and metaleptic shift; consult a Greek lexicon. 20. i.e., Not at all, as if in no way; a compound like *solummodo* (only), *tantummodo* (just so), etc. 21. Or used deponentially, **she is shipwrecked** <note>original: "naufragatur"</note>, which absolutely means to suffer loss, spoken as if **I break the ship** <note>original: "navim frango"</note>, from which it was contracted and fused.

-> A Laconic Statement <-
# The Second Metric,
-> under <-
# Conscience and Experience;
-> or <-
## The method, not at all a knot <note>A wordplay on 'modus' (method) and 'nodus' (knot/difficulty)</note>.

How the **unveiled** <note>original: "develata"</note> matter is to be brought to its final completion: for there are **ultimately** <note>original: "demùm"</note> two things upon which the entire mastery of the Philosophers rests: namely, the required matter, and the ritual—or the way of acting—upon it. The matter is the greatest secret, but truly the way of proceeding with it is a secret above a secret. Since, therefore, in the first Laconic statement, the physico-chemical matter was presented **nakedly** <note>original: "nudè"</note> and clearly, in this second one (lest anything be lacking for its use) the method of operating is treated **in good time** <note>original: "intemporè"</note>. In this **most terrible** <note>original: "horribilissimo"; here meaning deeply hidden or awe-inspiring</note> secret, as in the preceding one, I have held myself entirely **in the middle** <note>original: "neutrò"</note>, adding nothing and taking nothing away. But just as I **sketched** <note>original: "catagraphavi"</note> that in **Latin** <note>original: "latinè"</note> from the mouth of **Evander** <note>A mythical figure credited with bringing the alphabet and culture to Italy; here used to signify an ancient source</note>, and as the Philosophers of the Past announced it was **to be delivered** <note>original: "perferendum"</note>, so I also communicate the same here, **most simply** <note>original: "simplicissimè"</note>, to those consecrated to golden literature; otherwise, I would **immediately** <note>original: "continuò"</note> fall back into nothingness.
