# THE SEED UNCOVERED
<note>original: "GRANUM ERUTUM"</note>

<sig>Kk 2</sig>

1. It is worthy of unique weighing and a proper balancing on the golden scales to consider what the name **Vesta** signifies here; that is, a **cheap and common thing** <note>original: "res vilis & tressis"; likely referring to the Prime Matter, which alchemists claimed was found everywhere and ignored by the ignorant</note>, which stands by its own strength and is clothed by all things.
2. That is, bringing joy and pleasure; the word is derived from **helping** <note>original: "juvando"</note>, because those things which are pleasant help both the mind and the senses.
3. That is, festive, pleasing, etc. For it is **salaris** (of salt); or perhaps more correctly **salarius**, an adjective derived from **salt** <note>original: "sale"</note>. In the masculine gender, used both in the singular and plural, it is elegantly employed to mean wisdom, delight, wit, and so forth.
4. That is, **of Jove**; for **Diana** was the daughter of Jupiter <note>Jove</note> by Latona, born at the same birth as Apollo on the island of Delos—wherefore she is called **Delia** and Apollo **Delius**. She is also called **Dictynna, Libera, Noctiluca** (night-shining), **Trivia** (of the three ways), etc. Furthermore, she is called **Hecate**, because she is appeased by a hundred <note>Greek: 'hekaton'</note> sacrifices; likewise **Lucina**, the goddess of childbirth, named **Juno Lucina** by those in labor. **Juno** comes from **helping** <note>original: "juvando"</note>, but **Lucina** because she brings the offspring into the **light** <note>original: "lucem"</note>. This same goddess is similarly called **Luna** (the Moon), because she alone <note>original: "una"</note> shines at night, or because she receives her **light** <note>original: "lumen"</note> from the sun, as if illuminating with another’s light. Further, she is **Omnivaga** (the all-wanderer), not indeed from **hunting** <note>original: "venando"</note>, but because she is numbered among the seven wandering spheres of the planets. In addition, she is **Proserpina**, namely from **creeping forward** <note>original: "proserpendo"</note>, for she seems to creep like a serpent, now "mooning" to the right and now to the left. Moreover, she is **Tergemina** (triple-born), because she is believed to be the **Moon** in the heavens, **Diana** on the earth, and **Proserpina** in the Underworld. Finally, she is **Triceps** (three-headed), because she has three heads: the right of a horse, the left of a dog, and the middle of a wild sow. All these things, though they belong to the fabled theology of the poets, nevertheless contain a mystic interpretation by which they are accustomed to veil these difficult secrets of the mind.
5. That is, **Revealed** <note>original: "Revelata"</note>, with the prefix indicating a negation, as if to say **shown without a veil**.
6. Here it is used for **only**; merely, etc.
7. That is, clearly and frankly, as if **without a game** <note>original: "sine ludo"; a play on "nudè" (nakedly)</note>.
8. Here it is an adverb for **opportunely**, as if in its own time.
9. That is, by the greatest of all; for **horrible** is elegantly and appropriately used for "great," especially in phrases like **a horrible secret** or **a horrible gift**, because great things and deep mysteries usually induce horror, stupor, delay, and wonder.
10. Or **neutrally**, or **in neither place**; that is, neither toward one part nor the other, but as if indifferently in the middle. The word is formed as **ne-utro**, meaning "not to either side."
11. Here it means the same as plainly or openly; properly, **in the Latin manner**.
12. That is, **of Mercury**, because **Evander** (or Evandrus) is a proper name for Mercury. They wish him to be named as if for the **care of merchandise** <note>original: "mercium curam"</note>, because he is thought to preside over merchants. But for our purpose, he is more skillfully called **Viocurius**, that is, **running the way** <note>original: "viam currens"</note>, namely from the Gods to men and back again; or **Medicurius**, because he **runs in the middle** between the Gods and men. For speech **runs in the middle** and is reciprocated between two speakers.
13. I have transcribed this in Latin because **catagrapho** <note>Greek: καταγράφω</note> properly means "I write from the model of another." On this theme, **consult a Greek lexicon**.
14. This means to be spread abroad or published, because **perfero** (to carry through) is used metaphorically for "I make known" or "I proclaim."
15. That is, most openly, purely, and candidly: **without guile or folds** <note>original: "sine dolo & plicis"; the root of the word 'simplicity'</note>.
16. Here it is aptly placed for **soon**, or **suddenly**.

<header>THE HARVESTED GRAIN.</header>

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the form of an oval with text inside and around its border. Arranged around the outer edge of the oval, clockwise from the left, are the words: "it is turned," "by art," "it is." "For," "this," "neither," "of the art," "secondly" (upside down), "through" (abbreviation, upside down), "secondly" (upside down), and "which" (upside down). > ### Symbols
>
> # OF THE LIBYAN PROPHETESS.¹
>
> Let nature, by her own striving,² both cleanse³ and prepare⁴ this,
> For its genius,⁵ by its own inclinations,⁶ within the space of a year,
>
> ->From the raw-<-

---

1. Commonly called the Libyan Sibyl; for *Libyssa* or *Libystis* <note>original: "Libyſſa, vel Libyſtis"</note> refers to one who is from Libya, just as *Persa* refers to one from Persia.
2. Here it stands for the rite, or rather, the manner, guidance, course, or path of nature. In other contexts, "striving" <note>original: "nixus"</note> refers specifically to the labor of childbirth, described as "the extreme force of nature."
3. That is: "And let it purify," because to "purge" <note>original: "purgo"</note> is "to make pure" <note>original: "purum ago"</note>, etc.
4. Outside of the verse, you might perhaps do better—and more suitably to the work being handled—by reading "and let it separate" <note>original: "ſeparétque"</note> rather than "and let it prepare" <note>original: "parétque"</note>. <note>In alchemy, *separatio* (separation) is often a more technical stage than simple preparation.</note>
5. Here used figuratively for those things that are inclined, disposed, or leaning toward a certain state. Otherwise, "prone" <note>original: "pronus"</note> properly refers to a forward-bending motion, as if "born forward."
6. That is: by a "genial" or natural instinct and inclination. Both "genial" <note>original: "geniali"</note> and "genius" are derived from "begetting" <note>original: "gignendo"</note>. For "Genius" is the name given to the God who possesses the power of generating all things; hence water, earth, air, and fire, which are the seeds and elements of things, may rightly be called the "Genius Gods." In this sense, "my genius" refers to that which begot me, the "parent of the race," etc.

## Aphorisms
# OF THE DELPHIC PROPHETESS.

> From your dissolved, ruder Pnigitis <gloss>1</gloss>, there blooms <gloss>2</gloss>
> A certain white-faced <gloss>3</gloss>, divided <gloss>4</gloss>, egg-like <gloss>5</gloss>, consubstantial <gloss>6</gloss> Nymph <gloss>7</gloss>,
> ->Pure and clear,<-

---

1. That is: Black earth; for "Pnigitis" <note>original: "Pnigitis"</note> is interpreted as the black rot of the earth. <note>Pnigitis was a type of medicinal earth described by ancient writers like Pliny, used here to represent the 'nigredo' or black stage of alchemy.</note>
2. That is: It germinates, sprouts, is born, arises, etc. The word is derived from the adjective *vernus* (of the spring) <note>original: "vernus, a, um"</note>, by likeness to **springtime**, because in the spring season things tend to shine, to "ear" (that is, to produce ears of grain), and to bud; it is named from "greenness" <note>original: "virore"</note>, because then the brushwood begins to turn green: or even from "turning" <note>original: "vertendo"</note>, because at that time the season of the year begins to turn itself, etc.
3. That is: Appearing naturally white; perhaps a contraction of *leucopaeus* or *leucophaeus* <note>original: "leucopæus, vel leucophæus"</note>; consult the Greek lexicon.
4. That is: Divided, because *erectus* <note>original: "erectus, a, um"</note> is a participle from *erciscor*, or *ercisceor*, or *ercisco*; which in ancient times was interpreted as "to divide," specifically the land; from which there remains to this day the terms *erectus* and *erciscendus* (to be divided) for that which is divided and must be divided.
5. That is: Single-yoked and transformed, from the likeness of an egg <note>original: "ovi"</note>, whence come the terms *ovatus* and *ovaticus*. This is an epithet of Mercury, and specifically of the Philosophers, who is indeed homogeneous and **egg-like** throughout, in which the principle of indestructibility resides.
6. In English, "consubstantial," or that which is of the same and similar substance, from <term>homoia</term> <note>original: "ὁμοία"</note> (similar) substance, and <term>homos</term> <note>original: "ὁμὸς"</note> (one, similar, or equal).
7. That is: A goddess in the likeness of water, because the Nymph is said to be the water itself, as if the "Spirit of the Water" <note>original: "Numen lymphæ"</note>; hence a bride at a wedding is commonly called a "Nymph" <note>original: "Nympha"</note>, so named from the duty of washing, which also alludes to the name of the one being veiled; for *Nympha* comes from <term>neon</term> <note>original: "νέον"</note> (new) and <term>phainesthai</term> <note>original: "φαίνεσθαι"</note> (to appear), because she appears as a new person.

*Likewise, a portion of this small page awaits an image, placing the matter before the eyes, but it has not been depicted.*

<header>THE UNEARTHED GRAIN.</header>
<meta>catchword: Auto-</meta>

->Diana must be handled¹. Not at random<-

# Inscriptions²
## OF THE CUMAEAN PROPHETESS³.

->Purely cleansed⁴, fire-refined⁵, without dross⁶, crystalline, simple⁷:<-
->Which, yet untouched, must be held by you thus in the fire,<-

---

<image-desc>A circular diagram. In the center is the phrase "The spirit continuously" <note>original: "Spiritus usque"</note>. Surrounding this central text are four words arranged in a circle, oriented to face the center: "is" <note>original: "est"</note> (on the left), "ours" <note>original: "nostra"</note> (bottom left), "this" <note>original: "hæc"</note> (bottom right), and "to whom" <note>original: "quibus"</note> (on the right).</image-desc>

---

**1.** See above in the second "Laconism" <note>A Laconism is a brief, pithy statement, named after the Spartans of Laconia</note>, in the fourth gloss. **2.** That is: Short things written on papers; from the noun "inscriptum" (an inscription). **3.** Here the word is used as a noun; otherwise "saga" (wise/keen) is properly and in itself an adjective. Therefore, a **Saga** <note>original: "Saga"</note> is a woman skilled in sacred rites, or an old woman who knows many things, so called as if she were **sagacious** <note>original: "sagax"</note>. For it refers back to the noun "priestess" <note>original: "sacerdotissa"</note> or something similar, in exactly the same way as, for example, the word "thing" <note>original: "res"</note> or something similar is understood within **money** <note>original: "pecunia"</note>. Indeed, "pecunia" in itself is a mere adjective, derived from the ancient and obsolete "pecu" (cattle), or our "pecus," because among the ancients, **cattle** were the foundation of all wealth. From this resulted the adjectives "pecuarius" (relating to cattle), "pecualis," "pecuinus," and "pecunius," meaning that which belongs to the flock or herd. There are almost infinite examples of this kind in the Latin language which, while being mere adjectives in themselves, are nevertheless mostly used as nouns. Of this kind are, primarily, most names of the arts and sciences, such as Grammar, Poetics, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Logic, Physics, etc. Next are many names of regions, places, months, ranks, offices, trades, etc., in which their specific nouns are always understood. **4.** That is: Pure; for the adjective "putus" (cleansed/bright) seems to me to be a contraction of "putatus" (pruned or reckoned). Hence "purus putus" means pure and unmixed, from which comes "ratio putata," that is, a "settled account" or "pure calculation." **5.** Properly, this means "refined by fire" or "purged." For its origin, look in a Greek lexicon or another more excellent glossary <note>original: "obryza" – from the Greek "obryzon," referring to gold refined by fire</note>. **6.** That is: Clean, as if "without mud" <note>original: "sine limo"</note>, with the "in-" being a negative and the "n" changing into "l" for the sake of better sound. **7.** Here this has the same value as "unmixed" or "not composite." Otherwise, **simple** <note>original: "simplex"</note> properly and etymologically sounds like "without a fold" <note>original: "sine plica"</note>. Hence, when we say **explicit** <note>the traditional ending of a manuscript</note> for "it is finished," as in that line of mine: *It is unfolded, but the manual practice will reveal the rest.* The sense is: by "unfolding" it is loosened, because at the end, when we cease our handling, things are generally evident and clear, having no further "folds" or complications. In the same way, we are accustomed to use **implicitly** and **explicitly** for "secretly" and "openly," as if something were placed **inside** or **outside** of the folds.

*I had also conceived of adding an image here, but for the finding and placing of which I could not, at this time, steal the necessary hours.*

# Aphorisms
## OF THE DELPHIC PROPHETESS.

->From your rougher, dissolved Pnigitis <gloss>1</gloss>, there blooms <gloss>2</gloss><-
->A certain white-appearing <gloss>3</gloss>, divided <gloss>4</gloss>, egg-like <gloss>5</gloss>, consubstantial <gloss>6</gloss> Nymph <gloss>7</gloss>,<-

---

1. **That is: Black earth;** because *Pnigitis* <note>a type of medicinal earth described by Pliny</note> is interpreted as the *black rot of the earth* <note>original: "putredo nigra terræ"</note>.
2. **That is: It germinates, sprouts, is born, arises, etc.** The word is derived from the adjective *vernus* <note>of the spring</note>, by likeness to *spring* <note>original: "ver"</note>, because in the springtime things tend to shine, to form spikes—that is, to make little points—and to bud; named from "greenness" <note>original: "virore"</note>, because then the shoots begin to grow green: or even from "turning" <note>original: "vertendo"</note>, because the season of the year then begins to turn itself, etc.
3. **That is: Naturally appearing white;** perhaps contracted from *leucopaeus* or *leucophaeus* <note>original: "leucopæus, vel leucophæus"</note>; consult the Greek lexicon.
4. **That is: Divided;** because *erctus* is a participle from *erciscor* or *ercisceor* <note>to divide an inheritance</note>, which was anciently interpreted as "to divide," properly applied to land; from which there remains the phrase *erctum erciſcendus* <note>an inheritance to be divided</note>, or *erciſcundus*, for "divided" and "to be divided."
5. **That is: Single-yoked and transformed <note>or "of one form"</note>,** from the likeness of an egg <note>original: "ovum"</note>, whence *ovatus* <note>egg-shaped</note> and *ovaticus* are epithets of Mercury, and specifically of the Philosophers' [Stone/Mercury], which is clearly homogeneous and "egg-like" throughout, in which consists the principle of indestructibility.
6. **In Latin, *consubstantial*,** or that which is of the same and similar substance; from *ousia* <note>original: "οὐσία"</note> substance, and *homos* <note>original: "ὁμός"</note> one, similar, or equal.
7. **That is: A goddess like water;** because the word *Nymph* <note>original: "Nympha"</note> is used for water itself, as if she were the *Divinity of the water* <note>original: "Numen lymphæ"</note>; whence a bride at a wedding is commonly called a *Nymph*, so named from the duty of washing, which also alludes to the name of one marrying; for *Nymph* comes from *neon* <note>original: "νέον"</note> [new] and *phainesthai* <note>original: "φαίνεσθαι"</note> [to appear], because she appears as a new [bride].

<header>THE UNEARTHED GRAIN.</header>

# THE UNEARTHED GRAIN.

->Diana¹ must be treated. Not rashly<-

<image-desc>A text-filled oval with words arranged around its perimeter and within it. There are superscript numbers (1-7) referencing the notes below.</image-desc>

->**Inscriptions²**<-
->**OF THE CUMAEAN PROPHETESS.³**<-

->Purely pure⁴, refined⁵, mudless⁶, Crystalline, simple⁷:<-
->Which nonetheless must be held by you thus untouched by fire,<-

->Spirit continually<-

-><note>The following words are printed in an inverted arc below the oval</note><-
->to which this is set out<-

---

**1.** Look back above at the later *Laconism* <note>original: "Laconismum"; a term for brief, concise speech</note> in the fourth gloss. **2. That is:** Brief things written on papers, from the noun *inscriptum* <note>inscription</note>. **3.** Here it is used as a noun; otherwise *sagus, a, um* <note>prophetic or wise</note> is, properly and in itself, an adjective: therefore a *saga* <note>usually translated as "witch" or "sorceress," but here a "wise woman"</note> is a woman skilled in sacred rites, or an old woman who knows many things, so named as if "sagacious" <note>original: "sagax"</note>; for it refers back to the noun "priestess" <note>original: "sacerdotissa"</note> or something similar, in exactly the same way as, for example, a "thing" or something similar is understood in the word *pecunia* <note>money</note>. For *pecunia* in itself is a mere adjective, derived from the ancient and obsolete *pecu* <note>cattle</note>, or our *pecus* <note>livestock</note>, because among the Ancients livestock was the foundation of all wealth. From this resulted these adjectives: *pecuarius, pecualis, pecuinus, and pecunius, a, um*, for that which belongs to livestock, etc. There are almost infinite examples of this kind in the Latin language which, according to their form, are mere adjectives but are nevertheless mostly used as nouns. Of this kind are, first of all, most names of arts and sciences, such as *Grammar, Poetics, Rhetoric, Dialectics, Logic, Physics*, etc. Then many names of *Regions, Places, Months*, ranks, offices, trades, etc., in which certain nouns of their own are always understood. **4. That is:** Pure; for the adjective *putus* <note>pure/unmixed</note> seems to me to be contracted from *putatus* <note>cleansed or pruned</note>; hence "purely pure" <note>original: "purus putus"</note>, that is, pure and unmixed, from which comes "a settled account" <note>original: "ratio putata"</note>, that is, one made clear. **5.** Properly, it is that which has been boiled out by fire, purged, etc. <note>The term *obryza* refers to gold or silver refined and tested by fire.</note> For the etymology, look in a Greek lexicon or another more excellent Glossary. **6. That is:** Clean, as if "without mud" <note>original: "sine limo"</note>, with the *in-* being negative, and the *n*, for the sake of euphony, changing into an *l*. **7.** Here it has the same value as "unmixed," "not composite," etc. Otherwise, *simplex* <note>simple</note> properly, in itself and etymologically, sounds like "without a fold" <note>original: "sine plica"</note>. Hence when we say *explicit* <note>it ends/the end</note> for "it finishes," as in that verse of mine: *It is unfolded, but the manual practice will reveal the rest.* <note>original: "Explicit at praxis manualis cætera pandet"</note> The sense is, by being "unfolded" <note>original: "explicis"</note> it is loosened, because in the end, when we cease our handling, things mostly become perspicuous and clear—having, of course, no further folds. Thus we are usually accustomed to use *implicitly* and *explicitly* for "hiddenly" or "openly," as if something were *placed inside or outside of the folds*, etc.

*Here likewise I had conceived of adding a picture, for the finding and arranging of which I could not, on this occasion, steal the time for myself.*

->**Original Writings**<-
->**OF THE SAMIAN SIBYL.**<-

> Until the Spirit stands <note>original: "astet"</note>⁴ entirely separate <note>original: "sejugis"</note>³ from the water²:
> Of which the sign will be, if something not previously discovered⁵,

->In a small<-
->con-<-

---

1. **Here it stands for "appointed," "determined," etc.** <note>original: "certo"</note>; otherwise, "certain" <note>original: "certus"</note> is properly clear, open, and undoubted, from "I discern" <note>original: "cerno"</note> instead of "I see," because those things which we discern are clear, undoubted, transparent, etc.
2. **This is taken and understood philosophically here**, namely for the vital humidity, the innermost, best core <note>original: "nucleo"</note> of nature, etc., and not unskilfully; for the word "water" <note>original: "aqua"</note> indeed seems to be forged and composed from "from" <note>original: "a"</note> and "which" <note>original: "qua"</note>, as if it were that "from which" we live <note>This is a speculative alchemical etymology linking the Latin word for water to the source of life</note>.
3. **That is: Separated, set apart, etc.** because "separated" <note>original: "sejugis" or "sejugus"</note> is an adjective contracted from "un-yoked" <note>original: "sejugatus"</note>, that is, "disjoined from the yoke," which comes from "I join," that is, "I drive into one."
4. **Here it has the same value as "becomes" or "is,"** because "to stand near" <note>original: "asto"</note> is correctly used from time to time in place of "to be" <note>original: "sum"</note>.
5. **Outside of the verse, however**, and in your own practical work, you will more correctly read "viewed" <note>original: "conspectum"</note> rather than "discovered" <note>original: "repertum"</note>.

# The Auspices
## OF THE PROPONTIC PROPHETESS.

> In a small mass¹, in the heat, let it coagulate itself;
> His elevenfold lukewarmness² and fluid in turn,

->Let it soon be added<-

---

1. **In a small mass**, here it signifies in a tiny quantity; otherwise, "mass" <note>original: "moles"</note> is etymologically a great and immensely heavy thing, named from "moving" <note>original: "movendo"</note>, because it can only be moved with difficulty.
2. **Here it stands for "slightly cold"** <note>original: "subfrigidus"</note>; otherwise, properly speaking, that is called "lukewarm" <note>original: "extepidum"</note> which has cooled down <note>original: "extepuit"</note>, that is, it is no longer warm—meaning it is either cold or hot. Therefore, "lukewarm and fluid air" is equivalent to these sayings of the Philosophers: "Virgin’s Milk" <term>Lac virginis: A common alchemical term for a mercurial solvent or a white precipitate</term>, "Cool and liquid spirit," etc.

8. Here, this means **to surpass, to overcome**, etc. <note>original: *superet, vincat*</note>.

# THE GRAIN UNEARTHED

<image-desc>A circular typographic diagram. Around the outer border of the circle, words are printed to form a continuous sentence: "What nature¹ joined³ through a separation², in that place⁴ Art⁵ persists⁷, having performed its own good⁶ duty⁴." Inside the circle are headings and a two-line verse.</image-desc>

->Prophecies<-

## THE ERYTHRAEAN SIBYL.

> Thus the true Elixir⁵ of the whole Art shall come forth⁶,
> Which your Virgin⁹ has brought forth⁸—and you will rejoice⁷—for the Vopiscus¹⁰.

---

1. That is, the power of God and the renewer of things; or that divine reason and artificial faculty by which all things are procreated: for **nature** <note>original Latin: *natura*</note> is named from the fact that it makes something be born <note>original: *nasci*</note>.
2. Here used for "separated"; otherwise **sequestro** <note>literally "to surrender for safekeeping"</note> properly means "I deposit with a trustee or mediator" <note>original: *sequestrum*</note>; it is named from this because each party follows the faith of the one who has been chosen as mediator.
3. **Joined**, connected, composed, etc. For the word **jungo** <note>"I join"</note> is said as if bringing things into one.
4. Here used for office, matter, parts, etc. Otherwise it is commonly understood as a gift or merit. It is named from the fact that those who are of a mutual mind give such a thing for the sake of duty or service <note>original: *officii gratia*</note>.
5. i.e. The **Tincture of the Philosophers**, the **fifth essence**, the **masterwork**, the **mystery**, etc. **Elixir** was indeed called an Arabic word, by which they commonly denote a spirit rightly extracted and preserved from gold, or an herb, or wine; perhaps from the word **elixo**, which is interpreted as "I cook with water"; whence the participle **elixatus**, and more compactly and commonly **elixus** <note>meaning "boiled" or "sodden"</note>: Therefore **Elixir** is said as if it were *elixum*, that is, cooked out by water; for the Ancients called water **lixa**, from which also the **lixae** <note>camp-followers</note> are named, who follow the army for the sake of a cheaper trade, such as for the sake of washing or cooking; from ash, which by the Ancients was called **lix**, from which finally comes **lixivia** <note>lye</note>, that is, water in which ash (*lix*) has been boiled for the sake of washing, etc.
6. An archaic form, used here by necessity of the meter, for **exibit** <note>"it shall go forth" or "it shall result"</note>.
7. i.e. And you will be delighted; for **to rejoice** <note>original: *gaudere*</note> is properly to be glad genially, silently, and within oneself, and does not look to another: because we are then said to "rejoice" when the mind is cheered by some thing, yet no outward sign of it appears; on the contrary, someone is said **to be glad** <note>original: *laetari*</note> when the mind is moved so that signs of joy are produced in the face and gestures, etc.
8. i.e. **She has brought forth**; for women who are relieved from the pain of birth are properly called **enixae** <note>"having exerted oneself"</note>, as if conquerors; from the simple **nitor**, which is to strive under a burden; used here metaphorically <note>original: *metaleptice*</note> for: to perfect something with much effort and labor, etc.
9. i.e. Your matter, mother, etc. Look back above at the records of the **Mother of God** <note>original: *Deiparae*</note>, in the eighth section, the ninth gloss.
10. i.e. For the crocodile of the Wise, the basilisk, etc. For a **Vopiscus** <note>traditionally, a twin who survives in the womb after the other has died</note> is an animal which the mother acquires by force <note>original: *apiscor*</note>, that is, acquires with difficulty; or one who is preserved by the help of nature, to whom he also brings help; simply therefore, that which comes to its perfect birth or origin shall be called a **vopiscus**.

*Finally, a part of this page was intended for an image or figure, which haste did not allow to be added.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram. Around the inner perimeter of the circle is the Latin phrase: "It is new in the world. ### THE GROTTO OF THE MIRROR OF MINERVA.

The common line⁵ of nature is woolly⁶ and flexible;
It is unique, simple⁷, and a Sorceress⁸ almost everywhere.
It receives a vile⁹ and crude matter, and thus perfects everything—
Namely, from a lump of raw metal¹⁰, whatever you see in the World.
It is a motion of a single mode, a globe, and a spherical mass¹¹,
From whose fold¹⁴ under the axis¹³ all things come forth¹²:
The Artist, therefore, like a second Ape of nature¹⁵,
In the same way, *taking that which lies constantly before his feet*,
Must take up for himself that well-known ancient matter;
He is a sun upon the earth, who has always gone around, and goes around still.

->Jo.<-

<header>THE CHYMICAL WINNOWING-FAN</header>

1. That is, the Wisdom of the Ancients; for the Ancients used **Minerva**, the Goddess of the sciences, as a mystery to represent wisdom, as if she were the "nerve of the Muses" <note>original: *Musarum nervum*</note>. But to others, she seems so named from "warning" <note>original: *monendo*</note>, because she warns rightly and well; to others, however, from "diminishing" <note>original: *minuendo*</note>, perhaps because she diminishes the "nerves"—namely of the wit and the brain; and further to others from "threatening" <note>original: *minando*</note>, as if threatening force: for she is usually depicted covered in military arms, formidable with her shield, boss, and spear.

2. That is, "very bright," as if bright through the whole at once.

3. Here the word is used connectively for *and*, *also*, *and furthermore*, etc.

4. By **ancient chaos**, he means the beginning of all things, as if before time; for it was born before all Gods and Goddesses, and so named from the Greek word *cheo* <note>original: χέω</note>, that is, "I pour," because it was a foster-mother—that is, a confusion and mixture—of all the elements.

5. Here it signifies a path, a drawing out, or a course, etc.

6. That is, creeping, not hurried, etc. For it is an adjective derived from "wool" <note>original: *lana*</note>, most perfectly suited to Nature, who always proceeds with woolly and slow steps.

7. This is the same as "simple," of which you can read a more copious explanation in *The Undertakings of the Cumean Sibyl*, in the seventh or final gloss.

8. Here it has the same value as if I had said: "She mostly acts or operates in a manner unknown to us." For **Mage** <note>original: *Magus*</note> is said as if "wise" <note>original: *sagus* (a Persian word by which they signify a wise man)</note>; it is both a noun and an adjective, like the beech tree <note>original: *fagus*</note>; derived from **magic**, which is the perfected peak of natural philosophy, or the most absolute science of all natural things, like the "greatest wisdom" <note>original: *maxima sophia*</note>.

9. See below, concerning the **Egg of the Phoenix or of Helen**, in the tenth gloss.

10. That is, from a raw and imperfect thing; for a *Raudus*, *Rudus*, or *Rodus* is a noun signifying a raw and very crude matter.

11. Here it is used properly, namely for a thing that is grand and of immense weight, unlike above in *The Auspices of the Propontiac Prophetess*, in the first gloss.

12. Here it means "they grow," "they come forth," etc.

13. Here it stands for the whole sky, the universal sublunary globe, etc. Otherwise, **axis** properly signifies that smooth piece of wood upon which the wheel of a chariot turns, so named from "acting" <note>original: *agendo*</note>, because the wheel is "acted" (that is, moved) around it.

14. Here it stands for the innermost retreat of nature, the veil, the bosom, etc.

15. If you desire to know the analogy of the word **Ape** <note>original: *Simius*</note>, look back above to *The Arguments of the Phrygian Sibyl*, in the first gloss.

->Jo.<-

# The lattice of Jove¹ is opened,

## It is easy to behold the Opalia² <note>The Opalia were Roman festivals in honor of Ops, the goddess of the earth and abundance; here it refers to the rich works of nature.</note> of the ingenious architectrix³ <note>original: *architectricis*; referring to Nature as the master builder.</note>:

### THE WAY OF JOVE
->M I A.<-

The proper⁷ practice of acting of general nature,
Is a single-yoked⁸, simple⁹, and well-known way;
She perfects all things with a moderate heat shut within,
Which, however, must be duly¹⁰ assisted by external heat.
She separates¹² the pure from the impure at the end of the movement¹¹;
For every¹³ unfinished thing, more or less, is her work:
And continuously one thing is made while another is destroyed;
And conversely, thus the wheel goes in its circle.
And as in every thing the cause of its own death and birth stands
(Which any lover of the Art <note>The "Art" is Alchemy.</note> will well weigh)
So also each individual thing¹⁴ must be destroyed, and there must be achieved¹⁵
From it, that which lies hidden within itself and is fated¹⁶.
He who does not set this aside to be kept¹⁷ in a mindful soul,
Will hardly produce¹⁸ anything useful by wandering through¹⁹ books.

1. That is, of the total natural state; for among the initiates of nature's mysteries, Jupiter is placed in the role of the element of fire, or the entire universe of things. To this point belong those sayings: *All things are full of Jove* <note>original Latin: *Jovis omnia plena*</note>, *Almighty Jupiter, Progenitor of Kings, of things, and of Gods, and Mother of the Gods, one God and all,* etc. This is because there is no thing that so aids and fosters all things as natural heat. Therefore, just as the Ancients named Jove from "helping" <note>original: *juvando*; a common but folk etymology for *Juppiter*</note>, so on the contrary they called the God to whom the faculty of helping had been taken away "Vejovis" <note>Vejovis was an early Roman god, sometimes interpreted as a "little" or "harmful" Jove</note>, that is, the "bad Jove." For Antiquity celebrated certain Gods so that they might be beneficial, and others they appeased so that they might not be harmful, etc. Truly, he is called *Jupiter* as if he were *Jovis pater* [Father Jove], from which the name is composed and fused. Because of this, strictly speaking, it ought not to have the genitive *Jovis*—by a less sound custom—(since the genitive is from the nominative *Jovis*), but rather *Jupitris* or *Jupiteris*. He who was first called Jovis from "helping," as I mentioned, was afterwards "baptized" as Jupiter with the addition of the other word.

2. That is, the Excellencies and festivities of the Goddess Ops, who was the wife and sister of Saturn, by whom the Earth is denoted. Most sharply, indeed, this comes from the ancient adjective *opis*, which our ancestors used for a "wealthy person," just as we still call a poor and needy person *inops* <note>literally "without wealth"</note>. For the Ancients, whose chief wealth consisted in livestock and agriculture, raised the Earth—the giver of this kind of wealth—to divine honors in a certain way, and named her *Ops* herself, that is, the opulent one. This same goddess is also called by those same Ancients, not at all ignorantly, the *Great Mother* and the *Nurturing Mother*, because she nourishes all things; likewise the *Mother of the Gods*, as if all the Heavenly Dwellers had first been brought forth on earth and afterwards, on account of some distinguished merit, were carried across into heaven. Nor perhaps will he wander too far who assigns this to a singular mystery, etc. In the plural, it signifies power, strength, resources, abundance of possessions, etc. Because almost all riches are sought from the earth; they lie hidden and are generated, that is, from the earth, hence these sayings: *Wealth is dug out, Wealth is covered over, Wealth is generated,* etc. It is also thought to be named from this: that by her help <note>original: *ope*</note> the life of men is sustained, or because she is every work <note>original: *opus*</note>, or that there is a need <note>original: *opus*</note> for her for living. Or, just as the soil [*humus*] obtained its name from humidity [*humiditate*], so also *Ops*—in Greek *opos* <note>original Greek: ὀπός</note>—that is, juice, moisture, ointment, or milk, which the most fertile breast of the earth milks and indulges us with, etc.

3. That is, of Nature, than which nothing is more ingenious, nothing wiser, nothing more sagacious, etc. See above, *The Prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl*, in the first gloss.

4. Look at the later *Lanismum* <note>Likely referring to a section on "Wool-working" or purification metaphors</note>, above in the fourth gloss.

5. That is, in a moment, in a point of time.

6. That is, according to the proportion of time.

7. Traverse the *Crocodile's Egg*, below in the tenth gloss.

8. That is, having performed only one [task]; it is called *unijugus* (singular) or *unijugis* (joined), as if drawing, having, holding, or carrying a single yoke.

9. Here it is linear, etc. You have the etymology of this above, in the *Inscriptions of the Cumaean Sibyl*, in the last gloss.

10. That is, decently, rightly, well, etc. Derived from *ritus* [rite], because those things which are done according to the rite are right and regulated.

11. That is, of its operation.

12. Here it stands for "separates," as also in the *Prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl*, second gloss.

13. That is, everything, whatever it may be, etc. Because it is a universal sign.

14. That is, to be corrupted, to be destroyed, etc. Otherwise, *perdo* [to lose/destroy] properly means "to lose."

15. Here used metaphorically for "to be completed, perfected, finished," etc. Otherwise, *patro* properly means to devote effort to children, as if "performing the work of a father."

16. Here similarly it is taken figuratively, namely for "born, generated," etc.

17. Here for "to be guarded, preserved, stored away," etc.

18. That is, it will bring forth into the midst, as if it produces.

19. That is, by searching out, by distinguishing, etc. Because to "wander through" [*peragrare*] is elegantly and metaleptically the same as to track, to arrive, etc. As if for the sake of inquiring, to go around the field [*agrum*], etc.

<meta>This page provides a detailed commentary on the symbolic and linguistic terms used in the previous emblem of the "Egg of Helen" and the "Crocodile." It continues the alchemical explanation of the Prima Materia (First Matter), using mythology and etymology to hide and reveal chemical secrets.</meta>

# THE CHYMICAL SIEVE
### ->(CHYMICÆ VANNI)<-

1. This title, regarding the **Egg of Helen**, finds its place and occasion in that mystical and very ancient discovery of the Ancients. They told the story that Helen, the most beautiful of girls, was the daughter of Nemesis and Jupiter. For it is recorded that Nemesis, while fleeing the embrace of Jupiter, was changed into a goose; Jupiter, however, having turned into a swan, came upon her and entered into her. From that union, Nemesis truly brought forth an **egg**, which a certain shepherd <note>original: "opilionem," a tender of sheep</note> found in a grove. He brought it and gave it to Leda, who then stored it away in a chest. In due time, Helen was born from it, whom Leda raised just as if she had been born from herself.

2. Here, "authentic" <note>original: "germanus"</note> stands for true, sincere, and unfaked. Elsewhere, the word *germanus* properly refers to that which has "germinated" <note>original: "germinavit"</note>, that is, something born from the same stock.

3. I know the Adept of the Art <note>A successful alchemist</note> will wonder greatly when he considers and feels how sharply the word **tetra** <note>meaning foul, grim, or dark</note> fits here. It is taken literally, yet at the same time it alludes so shrewdly to the name of our matter, which is truly spoken of as being, as it were, "foul."

4. That is, the exterior form, appearance, figure, etc. This is because the surface of any thing is absolutely called its "face" <note>Latin: "facies"</note>, as if from the word for "making" <note>Latin: "facierndo"</note>. For just as "appearance" <note>species</note> comes from "looking" <note>aspectu</note>, and "figure" <note>figura</note> from "shaping" <note>fingendo</note>, so also "face" <note>facies</note> comes from "making" or from the "construction" <note>factura</note> of the body.

5. This is a circumlocution for "everywhere." For just as we say "to mix the sea or seas with the sky," or "to confound them," to mean throwing everything into disorder or doing everything possible; so also "to seek by sea and land" means to seek everywhere, in every possible place.

6. That is, twisted, intricate, false, or sophisticated. This is because the **crocodile** is used by analogy to describe a "sophistical question" <note>A "crocodiline" argument was a famous logical trap in ancient rhetoric</note>. Properly, however, it is a four-footed animal of the amphibian genus, living both in water and on land—possessing, as it were, a "double life" because it dwells in both mentioned elements and desires not only terrestrial things but aquatic ones as well. Its figure is said to be not very unlike a lizard, but of almost incredible size, armed with claws, known only to Egypt and those regions washed by the Nile. Its skin is so hardened that it can be disturbed in no part of itself except for the belly alone. It was not for nothing, nor without reason, that we drew a comparison between it and the Philosopher’s Python <note>A reference to the dragon/serpent often representing the raw matter of the Stone</note>. Indeed, there is no animal that grows to such a great size from such tiny beginnings, since its eggs are no larger than those of a goose. Yet this is believed to be unique to it: that as long as it lives, it never stops growing. For four winter months it does not eat, and like certain beasts, it lacks a tongue. Furthermore, this beast is terrifying against those who flee, yet flees from those who pursue it. Its eyes are dull in the water, but its sight is extremely sharp outside of it. When it sees a human, it sheds tears, but soon devours the one who approaches; hence the proverb **Crocodile tears**, which is usually said of those who deceive others under a veil of piety. Furthermore, it seems to me to be named by "antiphrasis" <note>a word used to mean its opposite</note>, as if it were "loving saffron" <note>original: "croci diligens"</note>, which actually means "shunning saffron" <note>original: "crocum vitans"</note>. Because it flees from saffron—the **crocodile** loves nothing about saffron—and even dreads its scent. For this reason, those who gather honey in Egypt are accustomed to spread saffron beforehand, so that the crocodiles do not consume the honey, for they are wonderfully delighted by it.

7. That is, by various and sublime visions, fantasies, and hidden things; consult the Greek lexicon regarding this theme.

8. Here this word means "in the power of," "at," "near," or "beside." As in that phrase: "It flies near the ground," it is placed there for eggs in the hedges.

9. That is, in the last or lowest place, as if on the "base" <note>original: "topo," likely a Greek-derived term for place</note>, because **torus** <note>bed or cushion</note> more frequently means a place, the ground, a dwelling, or a habitation.

10. That is, "one's own" <note>suus</note>, derived from "near" <note>prope</note>; perhaps from the fact that what is "one's own" <note>proprium</note> is most "near" <note>prope</note> to oneself.

11. Here it stands for most despised, most contemptible, etc. Otherwise, the word **cernuus** properly means "inclined," as if "looking downward."

12. That is, "exceedingly," from the particle *re-* increasing the meaning rather than denoting repetition (unlike how it usually works with verbs). In nouns, especially adjectives, it is almost always an intensive particle, like *recanus* (very grey) or *recavus* (very hollow). In the same way, **revilis** means "exceedingly vile," or rather, "doubly vile," named from the "villa" <note>country house or farm</note>, because all things are usually cheaper <note>viliora</note> in country villas than in cities.

13. That is, it "pants" or ardently desires, as if "doubly desiring."

Ph <note>Author's initials</note>

--- Page 336 ---
<meta>This page provides a detailed philological and alchemical commentary on the poem "The Incubation of the Phoenix" from the preceding page. It explains the specific vocabulary used in the allegorical description of the "First Work" of alchemy.</meta>

<header>THE CHYMICAL SIEVE</header>

1. *This refers to commencing, beginning, undertaking,* etc. because to *auspicate* <note>original: "auspico"</note>, or rather to *take the auspices* <note>original: "auspicor"</note>, is properly to take signs from the sky, predicting future physical events from the song and movement of birds; it is to consult the birds regarding the outcome of an affair, etc. However, since the Ancients did nothing except *by augury* or *by auspices*, it has passed into common usage that we use *taking the auspices* in an absolute sense to mean *to begin*, and *to undertake* some business.

2. *This refers to almost finishing, completing,* etc. For *to incline* <note>original: "inclinare"</note> is properly to bend, but metaphorically we say *to incline a matter* for that which is almost finished, or *to forge* it.

3. i.e. *by the clean, bright, and snow-white waters*, with the part standing for the whole: perhaps, moreover, the *wave* <note>original: "unda"</note> was so named as if it were *one* <note>original: "una"</note>, because it is certainly gathered into itself and is as if one.

4. i.e. *A beautiful beast, a wild animal,* etc. For a *beast* <note>original: "belua" or "bellua"</note> is so named by antiphrasis <note>A rhetorical device where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning.</note> from the adjective *beautiful* <note>original: "bello"</note>, that is, good, fair, etc. Or rather (as others prefer) from the noun *war* <note>original: "bellum"</note>, because it is the nature of beasts to wage war upon each other, for which purpose nature seems to have manufactured their weapons.

5. *Here used adverbially* for *above all, first of all, at the start, before everything else,* etc.

6. i.e. *Choose or devise for yourself some secret place*; because a *retreat* <note>original: "recessus"</note> in the present context is the same as a *seclusion* <note>original: "secessus"</note>, that is, a more secret place, empty of crowd and tumult, as if alone and separated from others: for *to secrete* <note>original: "secerno"</note> is properly to divide, separate, discern, etc. By likeness to this, hidden thoughts which can only be investigated with difficulty are fittingly called the *recesses of the mind*.

7. i.e. *In which, where,* etc.

<margin>influx</margin>
8. Here this is almost the same as a *matrix* <note>The "womb" or originating environment of a substance.</note>; for in an absolute sense everything that preserves in some way, as much in metals as in animals and vegetables, is called a *matrix*, as if it were a preserver of matter <note>original: "materiæ conservatrix"</note>, etc. Furthermore, a *nest* <note>original: "nidus"</note> is of well-known meaning, perhaps named from *stench* <note>original: "nidore"</note>, because the dwellings or chambers of birds tend to be of a bad stench, that is, odor.

9. Here it is placed for *continually, always,* etc.

10. That is, *least hard, tender, yielding to the touch,* etc. As if it were *movable* <note>original: "mobile"</note>, because it can be easily drawn and moved in any direction.

11. i.e. *Which brings aid to one giving birth*, for *obstetric* <note>original: "obstetricius, a, um"</note> is an adjective from *midwife* <note>original: "obstetrix"</note>, that is, one having care for those in labor; so named from *standing before* <note>original: "obstando"</note>, because she *stands against* the pain, or certainly the fetus, lest, once the genital enclosures of the womb are loosened, it should fall to the ground.

12. In this place it means *parts, duties,* etc. Revisit the *Oracles of the Erythraean Sibyl* in the fourth gloss above.

**T**herefore, once her snowy **WINGS** have been cut away,
And the heterogeneous parts or dross have been cast aside,
Let him soon pour her into another world <note>Likely referring to a new chemical vessel.</note> as into a nest,
And let him, in her turns, return and provide for her
The nourishment$^5$ of her own tasteless$^4$ and proper vapor,
So that a tame **BIRD** may emerge, fixed from the wild one:
For when she devours her own wings drop by drop$^6$,
Her former **OSTRICH-LIKE**$^7$ <note>original: "STRUTHIA"; the ostrich is a bird that cannot fly, symbolizing the "fixing" of the volatile spirit.</note> life is transformed$^7$;

A rainbow-colored$^{10}$ crest shines$^{11}$ from her rosy head,
And a **RED CROSS** sits$^{12}$ upon her saffron breast;
A **staining**$^{13}$ **POISON**$^{13}$ <note>original: "Tinctile Virus"; in alchemy, "virus" often refers to a potent liquid or "venom" that has the power to transform or "tinge" other metals.</note> spreads through her revived members$^{14}$,
In whose bones much **PURPLE**$^{15}$ glitters$^{16}$;
And her tail shines bright$^{17}$, drenched in **TYRIAN**$^{18}$ **DYE**$^{18}$ <note>original: "TYRIO VENENO"; literally "Tyrian Poison," but referring to the famous royal purple dye of antiquity.</note>,

1. That is: *Of completing, finishing, perfecting,* etc.
2. Here it means: *natural*, not [biting], fleeting, etc.
3. Here it is taken copulatively for the words "and," "also," etc.
4. That is: Not sweet, but of a delightful and harmless flavor, as if a *taste*—that is, entirely devoid of any sharpness or acrimony.
5. A solvent <note>original: "Menstruum"</note>, nourishment, etc. So named from *cherishing* <note>original: "fovendo"</note>, that is, by warming or nourishing.
6. Through individual drops.
7. That is: Its former fleeting nature is changed, or its former terrestrial <note>original: "restris," likely "terrestris"</note> character as an **OSTRICH** <note>original: "Struthia"</note> is *turned* <note>original: "vertitur"</note>. It is so named, as I have explained elsewhere, from *spring* <note>original: "vere"</note>, because the year then begins to *turn* <note>original: "verti tunc annus"</note>, etc. Because the **OSTRICH** <note>original: "Struthius" or "Struthio"</note> is a wild, fierce, and predatory bird, the adjective *Struthius, -a, -um* was created to mean that which belongs to an ostrich—namely something wild or tiger-like. For there are many such words in Latin usage that are both adjectives and nouns: master, companion, servant, craftsman, etc.
8. That is: A tamed bird, which stays shut up like a tame or *enclosed* ox. See above in the Archetypes of the Tiburtine Psaltery <note>Likely referring to a previous section or work titled "Psaltriæ Tiburtis"</note>, in the gloss.
9. This little verse fits very aptly here; for the **SKIN** <note>original: "pellis"</note> is indeed named from *driving away* <note>original: "pellendo"</note>, because it drives away injuries by covering them.
10. That is: Having or reflecting the color of a rainbow <note>original: "iridis"</note>.
11. That is: It restores purity and brilliance; from this comes the noun **VAPOR** <note>original: "nidor"</note>, drawn from an excessive odor.
12. That is: It fits, suits, agrees, etc. For a garment or other clothing is said to "sit" skillfully and elegantly when it is apt and very well accommodated.
13. This is a verbal noun from the supine *tinctum*, or from the substantive *tinctus, -us*, standing for **TINCTURE** <note>original: "tinctura"</note>. In a passive sense, it signifies that which has been dyed or colored, or that which can be dyed and colored, like "dyeable" <note>original: "tinctilis"</note> wool. But in our current context, it is used *actively*; hence "dyeing venom" <note>original: "tinctile virus"</note> here refers to the seed, the medicine, or the venom <note>The Latin "virus" here denotes a potent essence, not necessarily a "poison."</note> possessing the natural power or virtue of dyeing, because "venom" <note>original: "virus"</note> is used in both a good and a bad sense.
14. That is: Endowed with much vigor; again, *living*, etc.
15. That is: A purple and beautiful color.
16. That is: It shines through, it out-shines, etc. Because the verb *to shimmer* <note>original: "mico, as"</note> properly means to flash and shine at intervals, as **GRAINS** <note>original: "micæ"</note> do. These are, as I have interpreted elsewhere, those little dust particles in sand that shine like gold or silver, from which the verb *mico* is derived.
17. Here it means "to shine much" and all around; otherwise, the verb *to shine forth* <note>original: "polluceo"</note> properly pertains to Sacred Rites, meaning to dedicate or vow, or rather to offer libations to Hercules at the altar.
18. That is: With a most ruddy and healthful color. For the word **VENOM** <note>original: "venenum"</note> is a "neutral" word <note>original: "medium," meaning it can have a positive or negative connotation depending on context.</note>, which can be taken in both a good and a bad sense, just like "medicine" <note>original: "pharmacum"</note> and "essence" <note>original: "virus"</note>. These three are general terms for all things that are able to change the nature of the thing to which they are applied. Therefore, we can rightly call healthful medicines "venoms" or "essences," etc.
19. That is: Ductile, easy, flexible, manageable, etc.
20. That is: Glowing, bright, etc. For **GOLD** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> is named from *breeze* <note>original: "aura"</note>—that is, from brilliance or a yellowish glow.
21. That is: A bird born in secret, a winged creature, etc. For a **BIRD** <note>original: "Avis"</note> is named from *out-of-the-way places* <note>original: "aviis"</note>—that is, the more secret locations in which birds especially delight.

# THE EXTRACTED GRAIN

### §. I.

->O what a work, oh what a work! I have performed one single work, and you all marvel! O Nemesis, o Helen, o Jove! <note>original: "Nemesin, Helenam, Jovem" — These mythological figures represent alchemical stages: Nemesis for the correction of substances, Helen for the "beauty" or white stage of the stone, and Jove (Jupiter) for the celestial influence or the metal tin.</note> Oh, how stupendous, how hidden a mystery! O Phoenix, o Crocodile, o Nile! <note>The Phoenix symbolizes resurrection and the final red stage; the Crocodile and the Nile refer to the Egyptian origins of alchemy and the "waters" of the transformation.</note> Do you now understand this profound secret? O bird, o egg, o work! O ornament of works and child of the Sages <note>original: "Sophorum"</note>; O wondrous work of works! These are the marvels of God, the prodigies of the Almighty, and the Work of the Supreme Artist. Because of this, not only the Adepts of this Art <note>original: "Artis Adepti"</note>, but even the Naturalists <note>original: "Physiographi" — those who study and describe the physical laws of nature</note>, though ignorant and inexperienced in these secrets, have inevitably taken up the argument to affirm that there is something of a Divine Being <note>original: "Deitatis"</note> on Earth, which is testified by the various effects we see and experience daily through brilliant signs.<-

They say we know the Earth is the only one who is never angry with man, but gratifies him again and again. Waters turn into rains, swell into waves, and are cast down into torrents. Air thickens with clouds and rages with storms. But this Earth is benign, indulgent, and ever the handmaid for the use of Mortals. What things she generates when compelled! What things she pours forth freely and of her own accord! What scents, flavors, and aromas! What juices, what textures, what colors! With what good faith she returns the interest on what was entrusted to her! What things she nourishes for our sake! Indeed, the consideration of the piety of the Earth’s most merciful vitals and most generous breast could bring anyone to stupor; she is never incensed against man, nor is she ever offended, but supports him in a God-like manner.

Waters are turned into impetuous rains and transformed into harmful hailstorms; they swell and puff up into waves, and rush headlong into torrents, and often, when they overflow, they sweep away beasts, men, and entire buildings with them. The Air, dreadfully dark, gathers into thick and black clouds, and threatens all things with tempests, gales, and destruction.

<summary>This page features an ecstatic celebration of the alchemical "Work," framing it as a divine mystery. The author provides a philosophical contrast between the volatile, destructive nature of Water and Air and the patient, generative, and "merciful" nature of the Earth.</summary>

# THE WINNOWING FAN OF CHEMISTRY

V

<meta>catchword: who nowhere [necubi]</meta>

A voracious fire grazes upon, devastates, and dissolves everything into ashes; yet among all the elements, Earth alone—in all her vastness—serves the needs of Mortals, and most bountifully brings forth everything intended for their use.

What a great abundance of all things she produces of her own accord—not for necessity alone, but even for the ultimate pleasure of those she sustains! How many fragrances for the sense of smell, how many flavors for the palate, how many soft and smooth textures for the touch, how many colors for the sight; how many minerals, how many plants, shrubs, and herbs for our health, does the fertile and lavish Earth <note>original: "Tellus"</note> bring forth!

And though she be trampled under the wicked feet of criminal men, or the heavy and filthy tracks of brute beasts—although, I say, her venerable and ancient face be defiled and dishonored in various ways, and even though her very entrails are crushed and shaken—she does not grow angry because of it, nor is she filled with indignation. Rather, she seems to seize the opportunity to return with interest that which was sparingly lent to her. Indeed, she who acts in such a manner flourishes most courteously and generously. By repaying in this way, she most excellently deserves the name and title of a Deity <note>original: "Deitatis Typum"</note>, and merits being numbered among the Divine Powers. For the Deity also seems to have achieved the greatest work and reached the summit of power when He compensates injuries with graces and offsets offenses with favors.

Is she not that unfading Goddess whom the Ancients worshiped with such fitness? Is she not that most deservedly chaste Virgin of all, who never...

...where she does not grow daily, and yet in no way wastes away within the cloister of virginity? This is the precious pearl of the world; this is that vine most fruitful in produce and never harvestable, producing the whitest and reddest grapes <note>The white and red colors signify the two main stages or "tinctures" of the alchemical Great Work</note>. This is the **Spring of Bernard** <note>original: "fontina Bernhardina," a reference to the famous alchemical allegory of the fountain by Bernard of Trevisan</note>; the **Platonic Fountain**, I say—well-watered, flowing, and ever-streaming—in which an inextinguishable lamp burns. This is the living *Phoenix* renewing itself and reviving itself,

This is that amphibious animal, a **crocodile** of incredible magnitude, who feeds only by the rivers of the Nile. It is surely the **Eagle**, who is said to keep its nest in secret places—an eagle, I say, which transcends far beyond the grasp of fools and is honored by the wise.

But my *web* <note>original: "tela mea"</note> would find no end <note>original: "telos" (Greek: τέλος)</note> if I were carried deeper and longer into the sea <note>original: "amphitrite," the name of a sea goddess used here to mean the ocean</note> of this perpetual subject; and for its praise, whatever might be said from the **creation of the world** <note>original: "cosmopœja"</note> or **mythology** regarding it...

I would report what can be said mysteriously; for the more deeply I enter its inner shrines, the more I continually encounter other even more wonderful analogies. Therefore, for the sake of form, I shall enter the harbor, having first drawn a certain mystical symmetry from that, and having related here a brief but otherwise most certain way of reaching the knowledge of it.

->§. 3.<-

Whoever wishes to be a participant in our profound Wisdom must seek it in the simplicity and humility of his heart, because our matter is not at all sublime in its recognition or appearance, but is vile, humble, and simple; it is hidden entirely from the <note>The author implies those who think themselves wise but lack spiritual insight</note> wise, and is manifested only to those like itself.

Almost every error in this Art arises from an overly subtle imagination, while each person thinks up something new and unusual for himself, when yet nothing is more common, nothing more ancient, than **chaos** <note>In alchemy, "Chaos" refers to the *Prima Materia*—the raw, unrefined substance of the universe from which the Philosopher's Stone is made</note>. "Let the Earth be opened and sprout a Savior" <note>original: "aperiatur Terra & germinet Salvatorem," a reference to Isaiah 45:8, here used to equate the creation of the Stone with a divine birth</note>. What is the need to want to fish in the air, when we ought to fish in the water?

Not long ago, but just a few days past, I was on a ship with a certain Doctor—one more wealthy than he was wise. When a conversation arose (as is prone to happen among the **Sons of Art** <note>A traditional term for practicing alchemists who considered themselves spiritual heirs to the ancient masters</note>) concerning this matter, he answered me in these very words:

> *“I certainly know the true subject of the Philosophers well enough, but I have conceived of it so subtly in my intellect that I cannot explain myself, much less interpret it for others.”*

Oh, what witty childishness! By the best right, then, I may say that this Art is truly a gift of God.

The living and proven matter itself is handed down eloquently and openly everywhere by almost all true Philosophers, and yet one in a hundred thousand does not know it for certain. This cannot be unless God is specifically opposing it, since in this present day there are countless learned men endowed with the sharpest edge of genius.

For you might call this age of ours "Golden" because of the arts thus reborn and the abundance of ingenious men. If Jove’s table <note>The author likely refers to the "Golden Table" or perhaps the prize of beauty (the apple) usually associated with the Judgement of Paris</note> were still to be given (just as formerly to the most beautiful of the three), [the most beautiful] of all...

### §. 4.

For our most majestic art, <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Alchymia." Here treated not just as a laboratory practice, but as a divine science or "sacred art."</note>, is thoroughly likened to Holy Scripture, that sublime school of Christ, which is the deepest river in which a lamb walks—that is, the simple man makes progress—and the Elephant swims—that is, every most learned man fluctuates in his opinions, errors, and doubts. <note>The author uses a famous medieval metaphor: Scripture (and Alchemy) is a river shallow enough for the humble "lamb" to find footing, but so deep that the "elephant" of the proud intellectual loses his ground and must struggle to stay afloat.</note>

> I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth; why, I ask, are you beautiful before the sons of men? Quia abscondisti hanc à sapientibus, & revelâsti eam parvulis," referencing Matthew 11:25</note>, that is, to the humble, the simple, the poor, and those who are fools by the world's judgment.

For upon whom else will the Spirit of God rest—that Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of subtlety and counsel—if not upon the humble, the simple, and the lowly of heart? A humbled heart is the place for the Holy Spirit to rest so that He may fill it; but a heart in which foxes have their holes—that is, which deceitful cunning possesses—or a heart where the birds of the air have their nests—where windy pride takes hold—is not the seat of the Holy Spirit, but of the evil spirit, the spirit of this world, who rules over the children of self-confidence.

God dwells in inaccessible light; He is sublime, immortal, and eternal, whose house is filled with the fragrance of ointment. He resists the proud in heart, but His conversation is with the simple. ### §. 5.

Therefore, whatever true wisdom can be found, whether in this entire earthly dwelling or in that supernal home of the Blessed Minds, is from the Lord God. It is clothed in a humble, simple, and lowly habit, so that high things remain entirely unknown to the [worldly] wise, and are recognized only by the humble and lowly. Where there is *humility*, there is *wisdom*, because humility is the indicator and the guardian of wisdom, just as pride is the indicator of folly. For this reason, Socrates—that almost divine shrine of human wisdom—was the only one declared wise by the oracle of Apollo, because he was so modest in himself that he candidly said he knew nothing.

Similarly, that most illustrious *Lucifer* <note>original: "Lucifer." Here used in its literal Latin sense of "Light-Bringer" or "Morning Star" to describe John the Baptist as the herald of Christ, rather than as a name for the devil.</note> of the Sun of Justice (that was John the Baptist), because he most humbly confessed himself to be a voice, air, and wind, was therefore exalted so much that, by the decree of the Divine mouth itself, no one was greater than he among those born of women.

That most blessed of all, the Virgin Mary, because she responded submissively from the depths of her heart that she was a servant and a handmaid, was for that reason alone found worthy that God should be born from her, and the Messiah should be brought forth from her crystalline viscera.

Among the Prophets which the old law possessed, heaven gifted none with a greater light of spirit than David, as he himself sufficiently indicates when, for so infinite a benefit, he returns immortal thanks to God, saying: 
> *You have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom:* <note>original: "Incerta & occulta ſapientiæ tuæ manifeſtâſti mihi." A quote from Psalm 51:6 (Psalm 50 in the Vulgate).</note>

and so...

# To the industrious Commentator and the noble
## READER.

<margin>1.</margin> Having weighed the deceits and artifices with which the sons of this world trade, and by which they are infected and somehow sustain themselves, upon the more equitable scale of reason; and with this maxim engraved deeply upon the tablets of my heart: *He who seeks to be enriched shall not be innocent* <note>original: "Qui quærit ditari, non erit innocens," a reference to Proverbs 28:20</note>; my spirit was immediately stirred within me to devise a means and a way whereby I might live honestly and without guilt, and be of use to my neighbor. Therefore, to explore the knowledge of more hidden mysteries, I withdrew into the **Chemical Art** <term>Chymica Ars: In this period, the term referred to alchemical practices focused on creating potent medicines</term>, especially since I found that through this very science I could most safely serve and aid my soul and my neighbor without divine offense.

2. Accordingly, since Almighty God—after great expenses were made and great labor endured—heard my prayers and enlightened me through his Spirit of Truth, I was moved, out of true Christian charity toward my neighbor, not to hide this light so mercifully shared with me under a bench or table, but to place it upon the table, so that it might shine around and serve mankind. For I do not intend to bury the talent granted to me out of envy, but to do the greatest good with it. And since this can be done very fittingly through my **Universal Medicine** <term>Pharmacum Catholicum: A "catholic" or universal remedy believed to cure all ailments by purging the body of impurities</term>, I have therefore allowed this little work, committed to the press, to come forth; for the verse says:

> *Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know it.* <note>A famous line from the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 1.27)</note>

3. In this little work, the benevolent reader is instructed in the truth, and will see that I have written not from opinion, but from my own experience, all for the sake of wandering seekers <note>original: "Amatorum," literally "lovers" or enthusiasts of the alchemical art</note>, and for the solace of those longing for the Art, and for the benefit of Doctors. In favor of all these, I have determined within myself to provide such a Universal **True-Medicine** <term>Orthomedicina: From the Greek "ortho" (right/correct), meaning a medicine that aligns with nature and truth</term> (namely, the true **Drinkable Gold** <term>Potabile Aurum: Gold reduced to a liquid state, considered by alchemists to be the ultimate restorative for the human body</term> never...

# Preface to the Commentary
### Concerning
# THE UNIVERSAL MEDICINE

->*How the true Lover of this arduous Mystery ought to be qualified and intentioned.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
As many as desire to walk in this light of nature must, above all, be of as pure and unstained a conscience as possible, and hold a firm and holy intention; likewise, they must be patient, and moreover, extremely silent and devoted to sobriety. Because in a gluttonous, impure, and wavering heart, the spirit of truth—namely, of God—finds for itself neither rest nor a dwelling place; and for that reason, divine grace and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in the **chemical science** <term>Chymica scientia: The study of the transformation of matter, which in this era was inseparable from spiritual devotion and the pursuit of medicinal "essences"</term>, which might benefit the soul and one's neighbor, is by no means to be hoped for. Hence it has even passed into a proverb, that *Chemistry finds a man honest, or makes him honest.* <note>original: "Chymia invenit probum, aut efficit probum." This suggests that the rigorous and "pure" nature of the work either requires an honest worker or forces the worker to become honest through the discipline of the lab.</note> For the closer one approaches the knowledge of temporal and perishing things, the more immediately he draws near to the **Creator** <note>original: "Creatorem"</note> and the knowledge of Him; and again, the better one knows his own Founder and the Founder of all things, the more intimately he loves that very Creator of his, and strives to conform himself to His will.

# A Necessary Word,
### WHICH
## The Translator has to say, before he proceeds.

1. *A page glanced over in passing usually seems worthless, but read ten times it often shines brilliantly.* <note>original: "Pagina obiter transpecta plerumque sordescit, decies perlecta sæpè splendescit." The author uses a play on words to suggest that wisdom is hidden beneath a dull surface.</note> *It is therefore necessary, my dear reader, if you desire to obtain any fruit here, that you repeat your reading several times and weigh it carefully. For although the matter is treated quite crudely and plainly, it is nonetheless wrapped in a great pomp of ceremonies; yet not all things are therefore ancient trifles or darkness, for there is also a light among them, which if you can see, will undoubtedly be a certain guide for you to the Art in the future.* <term>The Art: alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>

2. *But you will say, "I hate that loud-mouthed and stingy kind of men, acting for their own profit, who want to appear to have blessed posterity with huge treasures, when they either do not know them themselves, or having plucked them from elsewhere, they set out to present them with a Sphinx-like mouth."* <note>original: "Sphingico ore," referring to the Greek myth of the Sphinx who spoke in deadly riddles. It suggests the obscure, coded language used by alchemists.</note> *Let it be as you say; what does it matter? Are gems any less valuable because they are given twice? If you can dig them out from their filth, do not be worried about the one who obscured them.*

<header>COMMENTARY ON THE UNIVERSAL MEDICINE <note>original: *COMM. DE PHARM. CATHOLICO*. The title refers to a "catholic" or universal pharmacy/medicine sought by alchemists to cure all ills and transmute metals.</note></header>

# Chapter one.

## *On the universal solvent of all metals and minerals.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Here, in this chapter, I will instruct and inform the fair and eager Lovers <note>A common term for students of alchemy or "Lovers of Wisdom."</note> of this art in the highest truth and with a sincere heart. I shall do so with simple words that are to be understood literally; therefore, pay attention to my words and repeat your reading as many times as necessary until you have attained a fundamental understanding and the true meaning of this little book.

2. Furthermore, you should know that two types of solutions are found among the philosophers. The *first* occurs when matter is reduced through the "primary matter" <note>original: *materiam primam*. The primitive, formless base of all substance in alchemical theory.</note> back into its own primary matter—that is, into its first original principles—as if into a certain "dry water," which is called not only Mercury but also Sulfur. This dry solution is achieved through *magical* <note>original: *Magica*. In alchemical texts, "magical" often refers to the hidden, spiritual, or "sympathetic" powers of nature rather than supernatural sorcery.</note> elements with an open fire. The *other* solution is astral, occurring through the "seed," which is a dry liquid that flows and melts like wax. In this solution, we usually observe a separation, because the solvent <note>original: *menstruum*. A term for a substance that dissolves a solid, named for its perceived relationship to natural cycles.</note> takes for itself only the most noble soul from the metallic Sulfur already previously obtained, leaving behind certain dregs.

3. And just as this solvent relates to Sulfur, in the same way it behaves toward the magnet of Sulfur, namely Salt. For these things have proceeded from its blood and state; therefore, this metallic fire works only upon its like, remaining as a solvent inseparable from that which it has dissolved. But how and by what means both of these sublime reductions and solutions are performed, you will gather from my following teaching—specifically, by means of the *magical* elements.

...as if from a mother, they are brought forth and formed into this world. When compounded things <note>original: *elementata*. Refers to any physical substance composed of the four basic elements.</note> are corrupted, those same elements resolve themselves once again. Indeed, none of these visible elements exists by itself, nor is any pure; rather, they are mixed to a greater or lesser degree, and they are mutually transmutable into one another. For from earth comes water, and from water again earth; from evaporated water comes air, and from the condensation of air, water once more; from ignited air comes fire, and this fire, through extinction, becomes water, and this water, through intense cold, becomes earth, and through heat, stone or sulfur. 

All of this is accomplished through the opposing and agreeing qualities of the elements. From clashing qualities, an **antipathy** <note>original: *antipathia*. In early science, this described a natural repulsion between substances, like oil and water.</note> or battle arises; however, from agreeing qualities, as if through **sympathy** <note>original: *sympathiam*. A natural attraction or harmony between substances.</note>, support and victory follow—that is, destruction, which is the cause of new generation. From this, it is proven and remains an unshakeable truth from its very root: that everything here below is born of the elements, and similarly, one thing is transmutable into another. Every compounded thing is destroyed because of its own opposing and agreeing qualities, and thus, under another form, it is resolved anew into its elements. But destruction is nothing other than the abolition of the old form, and the elevation of the compounded substance into a new form and a better essence.

2. Just as everything in the sublunary world <note>original: *sublunare*. The realm below the moon (the Earth), which was believed to be subject to change and decay, unlike the unchanging heavens.</note> has its origin from thick and visible elements, so also do the elements derive their beginnings from their superiors. For just as in the Archetypal World <note>original: *Archetypo Mundo*. In Platonic and Hermetic thought, the divine realm of ideal forms or the mind of God.</note> *all things are in all things*, so in the body of this World *all things are found in all things, yet in different ways, according to the nature of those receiving them.* 

And in this way, elements exist not only in the celestial bodies, but also in the Angels, etc. In the lower world, there are crude forms and material elements; but above, they consist of their own virtue and nature, belonging to a certain more excellent and heavenly essence. From there, our crude material elements draw their origin. Because fire has its principle from the Sun, Mars, and their domiciles; air from Jupiter and Venus; water from Saturn and Mercury; but the earth now takes its origin from the Moon and all of these combined:

# ON THE UNIVERSAL MEDICINE

3. To the degree that qualities harmonize within a compounded substance <note>original: *elementato*. A physical body formed from the four elements.</note>, that composite becomes either "fixed" or "volatile"—that is, difficult or easy to dissolve. Gold and silver are both fixed bodies, especially gold, in which the qualities of the elements harmonize and agree so perfectly that no single element gains dominance or control. If gold is to be destroyed <note>original: *corrumpendum*. We see that a great fire overcomes water (its enemy) and forces it to become air; conversely, a large amount of water suppresses and extinguishes fire. In the same way, when the **Sulfur** of the Sun is abundantly fed and kindled through Sulfur, the bond is weakened. The joining spirit—namely, the **Mercurial water** <note>The fluid, feminine principle that was believed to act as the "glue" or medium holding the solid parts of a metal together.</note>—must dry up due to the intensity of the fire and migrate into another element that shares its qualities. Consequently, it is immediately taken up by its neighboring element and transmuted into the nature of the receiver.
